dateConvention: Chinese courts counted years by reign eras on a lunisolar calendar; dates here are the Julian (before 1582) or Gregorian conversions in standard references, with BC years shown as negative. Grouped cards cover runs of short reigns and eras of division. From 1912 the deck follows whoever held real power: presidents, warlords, the Nationalist leader, then Communist Party leaders.

reigns.tagline: He made China one country and still feared death
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Son of King Zhuangxiang of Qin
reigns.previously: Seven kingdoms have fought each other for 250 years. Qin is winning.
paragraphs: For two and a half centuries, the Warring States, seven kingdoms had battled over China. Qin, the hard state in the west, ran on harsh laws, farming and war. Its king, Ying Zheng, took the throne as a boy in 246 BC. In 227 BC an assassin, Jing Ke, came to court to present a map. Rolled up inside was a poisoned dagger. The king dodged round a pillar until he could tug out his long sword. Then Qin swallowed the other six kingdoms one by one.

In 221 BC he made up a new title, huangdi, "emperor", and called himself the First. With his minister Li Si he pressed the old kingdoms into one mould: one script, one coin (round with a square hole), the same weights and measures, even the same axle widths for carts. He linked older walls into a long northern wall and built roads and canals. In 213 BC he had books burned, and the next year scholars were said to be buried alive.

He was terrified of dying. He sent the magician Xu Fu out to sea to find the elixir of life, and Xu Fu never came back. The emperor died on tour in 210 BC. His chief eunuch Zhao Gao and Li Si hid the death, and a forged order told his eldest son, Fusu, to kill himself. Fusu obeyed. Under a hill near Xi'an, the emperor's tomb was guarded by thousands of life-size clay soldiers, found by farmers digging a well in 1974.

claims.text: He burned the books and buried 460 scholars alive.
claims.note: The story comes from Sima Qian, writing a century later under the Han, who needed Qin to look monstrous. The book burning is widely accepted; the live burial is doubted by many modern historians.

claims.text: He sent Xu Fu with thousands of young men and women across the sea to find the elixir of life.
claims.note: Sima Qian records the voyage. The later tale that Xu Fu landed in Japan and stayed has no evidence behind it.

claims.text: Farmers digging a well in 1974 found the Terracotta Army.
claims.note: The discovery near Xi'an is well documented; excavation has gone on ever since, and the tomb mound itself is still unopened.

reigns.hook: The First Emperor is dead in a closed carriage, and only a handful of men know. A cart of salted fish rolls beside it to hide the smell. In the capital, his younger son Huhai is about to become emperor.

images.caption: The Terracotta Army in Pit 1 near Xi'an, made to guard the First Emperor's tomb. No portrait of him survives from his lifetime.
images.alt: Rows of life-size clay soldiers standing in long earthen corridors in Pit 1 of the Terracotta Army

reigns.tagline: The puppet emperor who let Qin burn
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Younger son of the First Emperor
reigns.previously: The First Emperor is dead, and a forged order has killed his heir.
paragraphs: Huhai was the younger son who happened to be on the trip when his father died. The eunuch Zhao Gao and the chancellor Li Si forged an edict ordering the heir, Fusu, to kill himself, and he did. The great general Meng Tian was made to take poison too. Huhai became the Second Emperor. Then he turned on his own family: Sima Qian says a dozen princes were put to death in the capital and ten princesses torn apart.

He kept building his father's tomb and palaces and left the government to Zhao Gao. In 209 BC two conscript leaders, Chen Sheng and Wu Guang, rose in revolt, and rebels sprang up everywhere. In 208 BC Zhao Gao had Li Si cut in half at the waist. To test who dared defy him, he brought a deer to court and called it a horse. Those who said "deer" were quietly destroyed.

As the armies of Chu closed in, Zhao Gao decided the emperor was a liability. In 207 BC his son-in-law led troops into the Wangyi palace. Huhai begged to be made a king, then a marquis, then just a commoner. He was refused and killed himself, still only in his twenties.

claims.text: Zhao Gao called a deer a horse to see who dared contradict him.
claims.note: It's in Sima Qian and became a Chinese idiom for twisting the truth. Nobody can check it, and it fits the Han picture of Qin as rotten.

claims.text: Huhai's succession was faked by Zhao Gao and Li Si.
claims.note: Sima Qian says so. A bamboo text in the Peking University collection, the Zhao Zheng shu, has the dying emperor name Huhai himself.

claims.text: Huhai begged to be spared as a king, then a marquis, then a commoner.
claims.note: The haggling scene is Sima Qian's, written about a century later by a Han historian with every reason to mock Qin.

reigns.hook: Zhao Gao has killed one emperor and needs another. With rebels on every side, he drops the grand title and picks a royal kinsman named Ziying to be a mere King of Qin.

images.caption: A small bronze plaque carrying one of the Second Emperor's edicts, from 209 BC. No portrait of him survives.
images.alt: Small bronze plaque inscribed with columns of ancient Chinese characters, in a museum display

reigns.tagline: Forty-six days as the last ruler of Qin
reigns.previously: Zhao Gao forces the Second Emperor to kill himself.
paragraphs: Ziying knew exactly what Zhao Gao was. On the day he was due to be enthroned he stayed home, claiming to be ill. When Zhao Gao came to fetch him in person, Ziying's men were waiting. They stabbed the eunuch dead, and Ziying had his whole family wiped out. It was the one bold act of a very short reign.

By then there was little left to save. The rebel Liu Bang had slipped through the passes ahead of everyone else. After 46 days Ziying gave up. He came out to Zhidao, near the capital, in a plain carriage pulled by white horses, a cord around his neck, holding the imperial seals. Liu Bang spared him and kept his troops from looting.

Then Xiang Yu arrived with a far larger army. He killed Ziying and the Qin royal clan, looted Xianyang and set the palaces on fire. Sima Qian says the flames burned for three months. The dynasty that was meant to last ten thousand generations had lasted fifteen years.

claims.text: Ziying surrendered with a cord around his neck, in a carriage drawn by white horses.
claims.note: Sima Qian gives the scene. These were ritual signs of surrender, so it may be stylised, but nobody doubts that he gave up.

claims.text: The fire in Xianyang burned for three months.
claims.note: The three months come from Sima Qian. Archaeologists have found burnt palace foundations, but the length is a figure of speech.

reigns.hook: Qin is ashes. Xiang Yu, the greatest warrior of the age, shares out the empire as he likes, and sends Liu Bang to a remote corner in the west called Han.

images.caption: A wall painting from a Qin palace at Xianyang, the city Xiang Yu burned. No portrait of Ziying survives.
images.alt: Fragment of an ancient painted wall from a Qin palace site, displayed in the Xianyang Museum

reigns.tagline: The aristocrat against the peasant, winner takes China
reigns.cameToPower: Xiang Yu shares out the empire
reigns.reignEnded: Xiang Yu dies at the Wu River
reigns.previously: Xiang Yu kills Ziying and burns Xianyang. Qin is gone.
paragraphs: At a feast at Hongmen, Xiang Yu's adviser Fan Zeng had a sword dance staged so that Liu Bang could be killed mid-performance. Liu Bang slipped out to the latrine and fled. Xiang Yu then named himself Hegemon-King of Western Chu, split China into 18 kingdoms and sent Liu Bang to Han, in the far west. He also had the rebels' figurehead, Emperor Yi of Chu, murdered. Liu Bang put his army in mourning and marched out.

Xiang Yu won almost every battle. In 205 BC he smashed a much larger Han army at Pengcheng and captured Liu Bang's father and wife. He threatened to boil the old man alive. Liu Bang told him to send over a cup of the soup. But Liu Bang kept his supply lines, kept raising new armies, and his general Han Xin conquered the north. In 203 BC the two sides agreed a truce and Liu Bang's family came home. Then Liu Bang broke it.

In 202 BC Xiang Yu was trapped at Gaixia. At night he heard the songs of Chu from the enemy camp and thought his homeland had gone over. He sang a farewell to his beloved Lady Yu, broke out with a few horsemen and reached the Wu River. A boatman offered to take him home. He refused, fought on foot and cut his own throat. Soldiers tore his body apart for the reward.

claims.text: Liu Bang offered to share the soup if Xiang Yu boiled his father.
claims.note: The exchange is in Sima Qian. It may be polished, but the hostage-taking itself is not in doubt, and the father was later sent back unharmed.

claims.text: Fleeing Pengcheng, Liu Bang pushed his own children out of his carriage to go faster.
claims.note: Sima Qian says he did it more than once and his driver Xiahou Ying kept stopping to pick them up. No other account survives.

claims.text: Lady Yu killed herself after Xiang Yu's farewell song.
claims.note: Sima Qian gives the song but not her death. Her suicide comes from later writers and was made famous by the opera Farewell My Concubine.

reigns.hook: Liu Bang, a village official who once drank on credit, is the last man standing. A peasant has won the empire. Now he has to work out how to run it.

reigns.tagline: The village constable who founded a dynasty
reigns.previously: Xiang Yu is dead at the Wu River. Liu Bang is the last man standing.
paragraphs: Liu Bang was a farmer's son who became a village constable in Pei. He was loud, lazy, generous and popular, and he drank at the local taverns on credit. In 202 BC he became the first commoner to found a Chinese dynasty. He called it Han, after the land Xiang Yu had fobbed him off with, and built a new capital at Chang'an.

He kept Qin's machinery of government but softened its savage laws. When he first entered the Qin heartland he had promised just three: no murder, no wounding, no theft. He trusted few of his old comrades. The greatest general of the war, Han Xin, was lured into the palace by Gaozu's wife, Empress Lü, and executed in 196 BC.

In 200 BC Gaozu marched north against the Xiongnu, the horse nomads of the steppe, and was surrounded at Baideng for seven days. He got out, and never tried again. Instead he began heqin: brides called princesses and yearly gifts of silk, wine and grain to buy peace. In 195 BC he was hit by an arrow fighting the rebel Ying Bu. When the wound turned bad he sent the doctor away, saying his fate lay with Heaven, and died.

claims.text: Tavern keepers let him drink on credit, then tore up his debts after seeing a dragon hovering over him.
claims.note: Sima Qian tells it. Stories of omens around a founder's youth were standard, and this one was written under his own dynasty.

claims.text: He promised the people of Qin a law code of just three articles.
claims.note: Sima Qian reports the promise, but Han law codes found at Zhangjiashan show the Han soon kept most of the Qin rules.

claims.text: He escaped Baideng by bribing the Xiongnu ruler's wife.
claims.note: Sima Qian says the adviser Chen Ping sent gifts to the chanyu's consort. The plan itself was kept secret, which invited later guesses.

reigns.hook: Gaozu is dead and his heir is a gentle boy of 15. The real power now belongs to the widow, Empress Lü, and she has a long list of scores to settle.

images.caption: An imagined portrait by the Qing artist Shangguan Zhou, printed in 1743, nearly 2,000 years after Gaozu died.
images.alt: Black-and-white woodblock portrait of Emperor Gaozu of Han

reigns.title: Empress Dowager Lü
reigns.tagline: The first woman to rule China, and the most feared
reigns.cameToPower: Ruled through her son Emperor Hui
reigns.reignEnded: Died; her clan was wiped out
reigns.previously: Gaozu dies of an arrow wound. His teenage son becomes Emperor Hui.
paragraphs: Lü Zhi had married Liu Bang when he was nobody, and spent two years as Xiang Yu's hostage during the war. As empress she helped him destroy the generals he feared. When he died she put her son on the throne as Emperor Hui and ran the empire herself. She was the first woman to rule China in all but name.

She had not forgotten Lady Qi, Gaozu's favourite, who had tried to get her own son Ruyi made heir. Ruyi was poisoned. Lady Qi had her hands and feet cut off, her eyes put out and her ears burned, and was thrown into a privy as the "human swine". Emperor Hui was taken to see her. He wept, fell ill, said he could no longer rule, and drank his life away until he died in 188 BC.

Empress Lü then put two boy emperors on the throne in turn and ruled through them. She broke Gaozu's rule that only his own Liu clan could be kings and made her Lü relatives kings too. A new dynasty seemed to be growing inside the old one. When she died in 180 BC, Gaozu's old generals and the Liu princes struck. They killed the Lü clan, young and old.

claims.text: She turned Lady Qi into the "human swine".
claims.note: Sima Qian tells it in full, writing about a century later under emperors descended from the men who destroyed the Lü clan.

claims.text: Seeing Lady Qi broke Emperor Hui and he gave up governing.
claims.note: Sima Qian says so, and Hui did leave power to his mother. The direct cause is the historian's reading.

claims.text: Her government was good for ordinary people.
claims.note: Even Sima Qian, who told the horror stories, ended her annals saying the empire was at peace, punishments were rare and harvests plentiful.

reigns.hook: Rewind to 195 BC. All this time an emperor sat on the throne: Gaozu's gentle son Liu Ying, Emperor Hui. What was it like to be her son?

images.caption: A Western Han empress's jade seal, dug up near Xianyang close to the tomb she shared with Gaozu. It's often thought to be hers.
images.alt: White jade seal with a crouching tiger knob, displayed in the Shaanxi History Museum

reigns.tagline: The gentle son who could not protect anyone
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Son of Gaozu and Empress Lü
reigns.previously: Empress Lü dies in 180 BC and her whole clan is wiped out.
paragraphs: Liu Ying nearly lost the throne before he got it. Gaozu thought him soft and wanted to make Ruyi, his son by Lady Qi, heir instead. Empress Lü turned to the strategist Zhang Liang, who told her to win over four old hermits the emperor had never managed to hire. When Gaozu saw the white-bearded sages standing behind his son at a banquet, he gave up the idea.

As emperor, the boy tried to shield his half-brother Ruyi, eating and sleeping beside him. One winter morning in 194 BC he went hunting early and left Ruyi asleep. When he got back, Ruyi had been poisoned. Then his mother showed him Lady Qi, mutilated and kept in a privy. He fell ill for a year, said a son of hers could never govern, and turned to drink.

His reign was not empty. Chang'an got its great earth walls, built by huge levies of labourers between 194 and 190 BC, and in 191 BC the old Qin ban on owning books was lifted. His mother married him to his own niece, a girl of about 11, and when no child came, sons of palace women were passed off as hers. Hui died in 188 BC, about 22.

claims.text: Four elderly hermits, the Four Whiteheads of Mount Shang, saved Liu Ying's place as heir.
claims.note: Sima Qian tells it as a dramatic set piece. Some later scholars, Sima Guang among them, thought it too neat to be true.

claims.text: Hui saved his half-brother the King of Qi from a poisoned cup by raising it to drink the toast himself.
claims.note: Told in the Shiji: Empress Lü knocked her own son's cup over in a panic. Only one source, and a hostile one to her.

claims.text: Seeing the 'human swine' broke Hui's will to rule.
claims.note: His words are quoted in the Shiji. Historians agree he left government to his mother; whether one shock caused it is a storyteller's reading.

reigns.hook: Hui is dead at 22. His young widow has no children of her own, but the palace holds little boys said to be hers. Empress Lü picks one and keeps on ruling.

reigns.title: The Emperors Shao
reigns.tagline: Two little boys on a throne their grandmother owned
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Said to be sons of Emperor Hui
reigns.previously: Emperor Hui dies at 22, worn down by drink and despair.
paragraphs: History calls them simply the Former and Latter Young Emperors. The first, said to be named Liu Gong, was a child of Hui by an unnamed palace woman. He was raised as the son of Hui's empress, and his real mother was put to death so she could never claim him. Empress Lü now issued edicts in her own name.

Around 184 BC the boy learned what had happened to his mother and said that when he grew up he would make them pay. Empress Lü had him shut away, announced that he was mad, and had him killed. Another of Hui's sons, Liu Hong, took his place. Meanwhile she made her nephews kings and let a Liu prince, the King of Zhao, starve to death under guard in 181 BC.

When she died in August 180 BC, the old generals Zhou Bo and Chen Ping struck, and the Lü were slaughtered. The officials then declared that Liu Hong and his brothers were not really Hui's sons at all. On the night the new emperor arrived in the palace, the boy was carried out and killed.

claims.text: The Young Emperors were not Emperor Hui's real sons.
claims.note: The men who killed them said so, and the Shiji records it. It conveniently justified murdering children; many historians doubt it.

claims.text: The first boy threatened revenge for his mother and was killed for it.
claims.note: Both the Shiji and the Hanshu tell this, though his exact words and age are uncertain.

reigns.hook: The Lü are dead and so is the boy emperor. The generals need someone harmless. They pick a son of Gaozu by a minor wife, whose mother's family is too weak to cause trouble.

reigns.title: Emperors Wen and Jing
reigns.tagline: Two thrifty emperors and forty quiet years
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Wen: son of Gaozu by a minor wife
reigns.previously: Empress Lü is dead and the generals have wiped out her whole clan.
paragraphs: The generals picked Liu Heng because his mother's family was too weak to be a threat. As Emperor Wen he became the model ruler later Confucians dreamed about. He cut the land tax, for years to nothing at all. He wore plain clothes and dropped plans for a new terrace when told it would cost as much as ten ordinary families owned. Father and son between them made "the rule of Wen and Jing" a byword for good government.

In 167 BC a girl named Chunyu Tiying wrote to the emperor. Her father, a doctor, faced mutilation as a punishment, and she offered to become a government slave to spare him. Wen was moved and abolished mutilating punishments. His son, Emperor Jing, took over in 157 BC and kept the thrift going.

Jing had a harder edge. As a prince he had killed a cousin, the heir of the kingdom of Wu, with a game board after a quarrel. In 154 BC that boy's father and six other kings rose in the Rebellion of the Seven States. To calm them, Jing had his own adviser Chao Cuo, who had urged cutting the kings down, executed in his court robes. The rebels fought on anyway and were crushed within three months.

claims.text: Wen was so frugal that he wore coarse clothes and wouldn't spend money on buildings.
claims.note: Sima Qian praises his thrift, but Wen also gave a favourite, Deng Tong, a copper mountain and the right to mint coins.

claims.text: A girl's letter made Wen abolish mutilation.
claims.note: The abolition in 167 BC is real. The tidy story of the dutiful daughter, told by Sima Qian, may have been polished in the retelling.

claims.text: As a prince, Jing killed his cousin with a game board.
claims.note: Sima Qian gives it as the root of the Wu king's grudge. It's the only account, and it serves to explain the rebellion.

reigns.hook: Jing dies in 141 BC. The new emperor is 15 and has no intention of being thrifty. He's going to spend that treasury on armies, horses and the far west.

reigns.tagline: The emperor who pushed China west
reigns.previously: Wen and Jing leave a calm empire and a treasury full to bursting.
paragraphs: Emperor Wu reigned for 54 years, a record no Chinese emperor beat for about 1,800 years. He made Confucian learning the official creed of the state and in 124 BC founded an Imperial Academy to train officials in the classics. Then he went to war. In 138 BC he sent Zhang Qian west to find allies against the Xiongnu. Zhang Qian was captured and held ten years, escaped, and came home in 126 BC with news of kingdoms China had never heard of.

His generals Wei Qing and Huo Qubing drove the Xiongnu deep into the steppe, opening the road that became the Silk Road. He fought a war for the "heavenly horses" of Ferghana and conquered lands in Korea, the far south and the south-west. To pay for it all he took over the salt and iron trades. In 99 BC the historian Sima Qian defended a defeated general, Li Ling, and was castrated for it. He lived on to finish his great history, the Shiji.

Old and suspicious, Wu came to believe witchcraft was being used against him. In 91 BC the hunt reached the crown prince, Liu Ju, who was framed and rose in desperation. He lost, and killed himself; so did his mother, the empress. Wu then issued the Luntai edict, regretting the cost of his wars. He died in 87 BC and left the throne to a small boy.

claims.text: Sima Qian chose castration over death so he could finish his history.
claims.note: He says so himself in his Letter to Ren An, preserved in the Hanshu.

claims.text: Ferghana's "heavenly horses" sweated blood.
claims.note: Han writers said so. If it was real, a skin parasite that makes horses bleed is the usual modern guess.

claims.text: In the Luntai edict, Wu publicly apologised for his wars.
claims.note: The text survives in Ban Gu's Hanshu. Some historians think Ban Gu shaped it to make Wu look repentant.

reigns.hook: Emperor Wu dies in 87 BC. The new emperor, Liu Fuling, is a boy of seven, and a tough general named Huo Guang is left in charge. He will make and unmake emperors.

reigns.tagline: A boy emperor whose mother had to die first
reigns.cameToPower: Named heir as Wu lay dying
reigns.previously: Emperor Wu dies after 54 years, leaving a small boy on the throne.
paragraphs: Liu Fuling was Wu's youngest son, by Lady Gouyi. Before naming the boy heir, the old emperor had his mother put to death. The reason, the histories say, was Empress Lü: a young emperor with a strong mother meant a mother who ruled. Wu left the child to a team of regents. The general Huo Guang led them, with Jin Midi, a captured Xiongnu prince, and Shangguan Jie.

In 81 BC the court held a great debate on whether the state should keep its monopolies on salt and iron, and the arguments were written up as a famous book. That year Su Wu came home after 19 years as a captive of the Xiongnu, herding sheep. In 80 BC Shangguan Jie and his allies plotted to topple Huo Guang. The plot was crushed and Huo Guang was left with no rivals.
Zhao was married at about 11 to Huo Guang's granddaughter, then a little girl of six. He died in 74 BC, aged about 20, without a son. That left Huo Guang to choose the next emperor.

claims.text: Emperor Wu had Lady Gouyi killed so she could not rule through her son.
claims.note: That is the motive the histories give. The Hanshu only says she offended him and died, and the explanation comes in a later passage added to the Shiji.

claims.text: At 14, Zhao saw through a forged letter accusing Huo Guang of treason.
claims.note: The Hanshu tells it to show the boy's wisdom. It is hard to tell how much was the boy and how much Huo Guang's own men.

reigns.hook: Huo Guang needs a new emperor, and quickly. He sends for one of Emperor Wu's grandsons, a young prince called Liu He. It will not go to plan.

reigns.tagline: Emperor for 27 days, sacked for 1,127 misdeeds
reigns.previously: Emperor Zhao dies at about 20 and leaves no son.
paragraphs: Liu He was the Prince of Changyi, a grandson of Emperor Wu. Summoned to the capital, he brought his own household with him and started handing out jobs. After 27 days Huo Guang had had enough. With the teenage Empress Dowager Shangguan seated in state, a charge sheet was read out listing 1,127 misdeeds, from partying during mourning to misusing the imperial seals. Liu He was stripped of the throne and sent home.

His followers paid for it: more than 200 of them were executed. Liu He himself was kept under watch, then made Marquis of Haihun, a small fief in the south, where he died in 59 BC. His tomb near Nanchang was found in 2011. It held tonnes of bronze coins, gold, bamboo texts and a lacquered screen with one of the oldest known pictures of Confucius.

claims.text: Liu He was deposed for 1,127 misdeeds in 27 days.
claims.note: The charge sheet is in Ban Gu's Hanshu. It was drawn up by Huo Guang, the man who had just removed him.

claims.text: His followers shouted on the way to execution that they should have struck first.
claims.note: The Hanshu records the cry. It hints that Liu He's men had been planning to remove Huo Guang.

claims.text: His tomb near Nanchang held about ten tonnes of Han coins.
claims.note: Excavated from 2011 to 2015 by the Jiangxi archaeological institute; the finds are on display in Nanchang.

reigns.hook: Huo Guang tries again. This time he picks someone with no friends at court at all: a great-grandson of Emperor Wu who grew up in prison and in the streets.

reigns.tagline: The prison baby who grew up to rule
reigns.previously: Huo Guang throws out Liu He after just 27 days.
paragraphs: Liu Bingyi was a few months old when the witchcraft purge of 91 BC destroyed his grandfather, the crown prince. He was thrown in prison, where a kindly official, Bing Ji, found women prisoners to nurse him. He grew up a commoner and married Xu Pingjun, daughter of a minor official. When Huo Guang made him emperor, the court wanted Huo's daughter as empress. Xuan asked them to find the old sword he had owned when he was poor. They got the hint.

In 71 BC Empress Xu died after childbirth, poisoned by a doctor working for Huo Guang's wife, and Huo's daughter became empress after all. Xuan waited. Huo Guang died in 68 BC and in 66 BC his family were caught plotting and wiped out. Xuan then ran a tight, hard-working government. In 60 BC Han set up a Protectorate of the Western Regions, and in 51 BC the Xiongnu ruler Huhanye came to court to submit.
He was not a soft man. When his heir urged him to use more Confucian scholars, Xuan snapped that the Han had its own way of ruling, mixing force with virtue. He died in January 48 BC.

claims.text: Xuan sent for "the old sword" to make his commoner wife empress.
claims.note: The edict is recorded in the Hanshu, and "the old sword" became a phrase for loyalty to a first wife.

claims.text: Huo Guang's wife had Empress Xu poisoned.
claims.note: The Hanshu says the doctor confessed. The Huo family had been destroyed by the time it was written, so nobody spoke for them.

claims.text: Xuan said, "The one who will ruin my house is the crown prince."
claims.note: The Hanshu reports it. It looks a lot like hindsight, given how weak the dynasty grew under his son.

reigns.hook: Xuan is dead, and the crown prince he worried about is now emperor: a gentle scholar who trusts his eunuchs and loves his books.

reigns.tagline: The bookish emperor and the woman sent north
reigns.previously: Xuan dies, worried his gentle heir will ruin the dynasty.
paragraphs: Emperor Yuan was the son of Empress Xu, who had been poisoned. He loved Confucian learning and music, and he was often ill. Real power drifted to the eunuch Shi Xian, who controlled the paperwork. When the emperor's old tutor Xiao Wangzhi crossed him, Shi Xian had him hounded until he took poison. Yuan wept for him and did nothing.

On the frontier things went better. In 36 BC the officer Chen Tang, acting without orders, marched far to the west and killed the Xiongnu chief Zhizhi. In 33 BC a palace lady, Wang Zhaojun, volunteered to go north as a bride for the Xiongnu ruler Huhanye. She became one of the most famous women in Chinese history. Yuan died that summer.
His empress, Wang Zhengjun, would outlive him by 45 years. Her brothers and her nephew Wang Mang were about to take over the government.

claims.text: Wang Zhaojun was never noticed at court because she would not bribe the painter of the palace women's portraits.
claims.note: The story of the painter Mao Yanshou comes from a later collection of anecdotes, not from the Hanshu.

claims.text: His consort Lady Feng stepped between the emperor and an escaped bear.
claims.note: The Hanshu tells it, and it became a favourite subject for court painters.

claims.text: Chen Tang wrote that anyone who offended mighty Han would be punished however far away.
claims.note: The line is from his report to the throne, as given in the Hanshu.

reigns.hook: Yuan's son takes the throne, and his mother's family come with him. The Wang brothers will run the empire while the new emperor enjoys himself.

reigns.tagline: The pleasure-loving emperor and the flying swallow
reigns.previously: Emperor Yuan dies. His widow's Wang family are rising fast.
paragraphs: Emperor Cheng let his mother's brothers run things. Her eldest brother, Wang Feng, became commander-in-chief, and in 27 BC five more Wang brothers were made marquises on a single day. The emperor went out in disguise to party in the city. There he met a dancer, Zhao Feiyan, "the flying swallow", and her sister Hede. Feiyan became empress in 16 BC, and Hede his favourite.

Neither sister had a son, and no other child of his survived. After his death an inquiry claimed that babies he had with other women were killed in the palace on Hede's orders. Not everything went badly: from 26 BC the scholar Liu Xiang sorted and catalogued the imperial library, saving much of early Chinese literature.
In 7 BC Cheng died suddenly in Hede's rooms. She killed herself. His heir was a nephew. The Wang clan's leader was now Wang Mang, the commander-in-chief, famous for his modest and pious life.

claims.text: Zhao Feiyan was so light she could dance on the palm of a hand.
claims.note: The story grew up long after her death, in fiction and poetry. Her nickname is early, the palm dancing is not.

claims.text: Cheng's infant sons were killed in the harem on Zhao Hede's orders.
claims.note: The Hanshu quotes an official inquiry held under the next emperor, when the sisters' enemies were in charge.

reigns.hook: Cheng is dead and the Wang family are on the back foot. His nephew is the new emperor, and he arrives with his own grandmother and her relatives.

reigns.tagline: The emperor who cut his sleeve for love
reigns.previously: Emperor Cheng dies suddenly. His nephew takes over.
paragraphs: Ai came in determined to be strong. He pushed the Wang family aside, and Wang Mang left court. Ai's grandmother, Lady Fu, and his mother's family, the Ding, took their place. He was often ill, and in 5 BC, swayed by a prophecy, he even renamed himself and his reign to renew Heaven's favour. Weeks later he changed it all back.

His great love was a young official, Dong Xian. Ai showered him with titles and money and, at 22, made him commander-in-chief. At a banquet he mused about handing the throne to Dong Xian, as the sage king Yao once gave his throne to a worthy man. A Wang courtier told him the empire was not his to give away.

In 1 BC Ai died, aged about 25, with no son. The very same day his grandmother's old rival, the Grand Empress Dowager Wang, took the imperial seals and called back Wang Mang. Dong Xian was dismissed and killed himself.

claims.text: Ai cut off his own sleeve rather than wake Dong Xian, asleep on it.
claims.note: The Hanshu tells it; "the passion of the cut sleeve" became a polite phrase for love between men.

claims.text: Ai suggested he might give the throne to Dong Xian.
claims.note: The Hanshu reports the banquet remark. It was written by historians hostile to Dong Xian, and it may have been half a joke.

reigns.hook: Wang Mang is back, and he needs a child on the throne. He picks an eight-year-old cousin of the dead emperor, and keeps the boy's mother far away.

images.caption: A 17th-century painting of the cut-sleeve story, made more than 1,600 years after Ai's death.
images.alt: Ink painting of two men on a couch, one cutting the sleeve of his robe while the other sleeps

reigns.tagline: The child emperor in Wang Mang's shadow
reigns.previously: Emperor Ai dies young. Wang Mang returns the same day.
paragraphs: Liu Kan, a grandson of Emperor Yuan, was eight when he was brought from his little kingdom of Zhongshan. Wang Mang was regent, and he made sure the boy's mother and her Wei relatives stayed out of the capital. In AD 3 Wang Mang's own son tried to scare his father into changing course by splashing blood on his door. Wang Mang made his son kill himself and had the Wei family destroyed, all but the mother.

Meanwhile Wang Mang played the perfect Confucian minister. He took the title Duke Who Secures the Han, gave away land and money and refused honours he could have taken. In AD 4 the emperor married his daughter. In early AD 6 Ping fell ill. Wang Mang prayed to offer his own life in the boy's place, as the Duke of Zhou was said to have done. Ping died at 14, without a son.

claims.text: Wang Mang poisoned Emperor Ping.
claims.note: Rebels against Wang Mang said so. The Hanshu only reports the rumour, and Ping was a sickly boy.

claims.text: Wang Mang wrote a prayer offering to die in place of the sick emperor.
claims.note: The Hanshu says he did, copying the Duke of Zhou. Whether he meant it is another question.

reigns.hook: Another child emperor has died. Wang Mang looks over the dozens of eligible Han princes and picks the youngest of all, a baby barely a year old.

reigns.tagline: The baby heir who lost an empire before he could talk
reigns.previously: Emperor Ping dies at 14. Wang Mang chooses the next one.
paragraphs: Liu Ying was chosen in AD 6 because he was the youngest of the possible heirs. He was never crowned. He was simply "Ruzi", the infant, and Wang Mang ruled as "acting emperor". Omens kept turning up, including a stone from a well with red writing telling Wang Mang to be emperor. In AD 7 a governor, Zhai Yi, rose in revolt to defend the Han. His army was crushed.

In January of AD 9, after one omen too many, Wang Mang took the throne and founded the Xin dynasty. The Hanshu says he held the little boy's hand and wept, saying Heaven had left him no choice. Ying was made a duke and shut away under guard, so cut off that he grew up unable to name the farm animals. In AD 25 rebels proclaimed him emperor, and he was killed when they were beaten.

claims.text: A white stone with red writing, found in a well, told Wang Mang to become emperor.
claims.note: The Hanshu records the omen, along with others his supporters produced. Even then many people suspected they were faked.

claims.text: Ruzi Ying was kept so isolated he could not name the six farm animals.
claims.note: The Hanshu says so. It was written under the restored Han, who wanted Wang Mang to look as cruel as possible.

reigns.hook: Wang Mang has the throne and a plan. He will tear up the old Han world and rebuild a lost golden age, starting with who owns the land and what money is.

reigns.tagline: The reformer who tried to rebuild a golden age
reigns.previously: Wang Mang sets the infant Ruzi Ying aside and takes the throne.
paragraphs: Wang Mang named his dynasty Xin, "New", the only break in four centuries of Han rule. He wanted to bring back the perfect age of the ancient Zhou kings. He declared all land to belong to the throne, to be shared out fairly, and banned the buying and selling of slaves. He changed the money again and again, and as regent he had already brought out bronze coins shaped like knives. Each change wiped out people's savings.

Then nature turned on him. Around AD 11 the Yellow River burst its banks and swung onto a new course, drowning farmland and sending crowds of refugees across the north. Famine bred rebels. The Red Eyebrows painted their brows red to tell friend from foe. The Lülin, the "Green Forest" bands, rallied around princes of the old Han family.

In AD 23 Wang Mang sent a huge army against them. At Kunyang a Han prince, Liu Xiu, broke it with a small force as a storm burst over the field. In October rebels stormed Chang'an. Wang Mang was killed in the palace, still clutching his ritual knife and reciting from the classics. His head was hung up in the market for the crowd to pelt.

claims.text: At Kunyang Liu Xiu routed an army of 420,000 men, helped by a storm.
claims.note: The Hou Hanshu's numbers are huge and the storm is dramatic; both may be inflated in honour of the man who became emperor.

claims.text: Wang Mang's head was kept in the imperial treasury for over 270 years.
claims.note: The Jin Shu says it was lost in a palace fire in 295, along with Gaozu's sword and Confucius's shoes. Nobody can check it now.

claims.text: He nationalised all land and freed the slaves.
claims.note: The orders were real, but they were watered down or cancelled within three years. How far they were ever carried out is unclear.

reigns.hook: Wang Mang is dead. The rebels who stormed Chang'an fight for a Han prince, Liu Xuan, the Gengshi Emperor. His best general, Liu Xiu, is the brother of a man Gengshi has just had executed.

reigns.tagline: The rebel emperor who drank his empire away
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Han prince, Wang Mang's rebel rival
reigns.previously: Rebel armies close in on Wang Mang and his New dynasty.
paragraphs: Liu Xuan was a minor member of the Han royal clan who had joined the Green Forest rebels. In March 23 their leaders made him emperor, partly because he looked easy to control. He took the reign title Gengshi, "a fresh start". His armies broke into Chang'an that autumn and Wang Mang was killed. For a moment the Han seemed to be back.

It went wrong fast. Gengshi had Liu Yan, a popular cousin and a rival, put to death in 23, and Liu Yan's brother Liu Xiu swallowed his grief and kept serving. Gengshi then sent him north to Hebei, which was a mistake: Liu Xiu built an army there. In Chang'an, Gengshi handed out top posts to cooks and cronies and left the government to others while he drank.

In 25 the Red Eyebrows marched on Chang'an with their own puppet, a teenage cowherd named Liu Penzi picked by drawing lots. The city fell that autumn. Gengshi surrendered and was given a prince's title, then was strangled on the orders of a Red Eyebrow commander before the year was out. By then Liu Xiu had already declared himself emperor.

claims.text: On the day he was made emperor, Gengshi was so overwhelmed he blushed, sweated and could not say a word.
claims.note: The Hou Hanshu tells it, but it was written under the rival line of Liu Xiu, which had every reason to make him look feeble.

claims.text: Chang'an mocked him with a song: "Cooks in the kitchen are made generals; rotten sheep's stomachs, cavalry commanders."
claims.note: The ditty is quoted in the Hou Hanshu. Street songs like this were popular evidence of bad rule, and it's a hostile source.

claims.text: His consort Lady Han would shout at officials who interrupted their drinking to bring him state business.
claims.note: Another Hou Hanshu story, the kind later historians used to explain a fall. She appears in later collections of cautionary tales about women.

reigns.hook: Gengshi is dead and the Red Eyebrows are looting Chang'an. The man he sent north, Liu Xiu, already wears the yellow robe, and his army is the best in the empire.

reigns.tagline: The farmer prince who glued the Han back together
reigns.previously: The Red Eyebrows take Chang'an. The Gengshi Emperor surrenders.
paragraphs: Liu Xiu was a distant Han kinsman, a gentleman farmer who had studied in Chang'an. After Kunyang he served the Gengshi Emperor, another Han prince, who held Chang'an from 23 to 25 until the Red Eyebrows overran it and killed him. By then Liu Xiu had his own army in the north. In 25 he declared himself emperor and moved the capital east to Luoyang. That's why his line is called the Eastern, or Later, Han.

It took him over ten years to put the empire back together. The last big rival, Gongsun Shu in Chengdu, fell in 36. In the far south two sisters, Trưng Trắc and Trưng Nhị, led a revolt in what is now Vietnam in 40. Guangwu's general Ma Yuan crushed it by 43. The sisters are still national heroes in Vietnam.

At home Guangwu freed many slaves, shrank the army and lightened taxes. He kept his old comrades-in-arms rich and honoured, but gave the real work of government to officials, so none of them could turn on him. In 57 he sent a gold seal to the king of Na in Japan. A gold seal found by a farmer in Kyushu in 1784 is thought to be that very gift. He died the same year.

claims.text: The gold seal found in Kyushu in 1784 is the one Guangwu sent.
claims.note: The Hou Hanshu records the gift in 57, and the seal's wording fits. A few scholars have questioned whether the seal is genuine.

claims.text: He kept his generals rich but out of power, so none could rebel.
claims.note: The Hou Hanshu praises him for it. In fact several old comrades did hold office; the policy was looser than the legend.

claims.text: The Trưng sisters drowned themselves rather than surrender.
claims.note: That's the Vietnamese tradition. The Chinese sources say Ma Yuan captured and beheaded them.

reigns.hook: Guangwu leaves a restored empire to his son Liu Zhuang, Emperor Ming. Within a few reigns, though, the throne will belong to children, and the palace to their mothers' kin and the eunuchs.

reigns.tagline: The emperor who dreamed of a golden man
reigns.previously: Guangwu dies at Luoyang, leaving the Han restored, his son in charge.
paragraphs: Liu Zhuang was the son of Guangwu's beloved Yin Lihua. He became heir when the first crown prince stepped aside after his own mother was demoted. As Emperor Ming he was clever, hard-working and strict. He kept a tight leash on officials, and his own in-laws got almost nothing. His wife's late father, the great general Ma Yuan, was even left out when he had 28 of Guangwu's commanders painted on the Cloud Terrace.

Ming's half-brother Liu Ying, Prince of Chu, was an early patron of Buddhism. Accused of plotting in 70, he killed himself, and thousands were dragged into the inquiry. In 73 Ming sent armies against the northern Xiongnu, and with them went a junior officer named Ban Chao, who would spend 30 years winning over the oasis kingdoms of the Tarim Basin.
Ming died in 75, aged about 47. His reign and his son's are remembered as the high summer of the Later Han.

claims.text: Ming dreamed of a flying golden man, sent envoys west, and they came back with Buddhist monks on a white horse.
claims.note: The story turns up in later Buddhist texts and the Hou Hanshu. Buddhism was probably already arriving along the trade routes, as Liu Ying's case shows.

claims.text: He left his father-in-law Ma Yuan off the Cloud Terrace portraits so as not to favour his wife's family.
claims.note: The Hou Hanshu says so in Ma Yuan's biography; it fits Ming's well-attested hard line on in-laws.

claims.text: Guangwu had said: "If I marry, let it be Yin Lihua."
claims.note: The Hou Hanshu puts it in his mouth as a young man in Chang'an. A charming line, impossible to check.

reigns.hook: Ming is dead. His son Liu Da, 18, inherits a strong empire and a stepmother, Empress Ma, who has firm views on what her relatives deserve. Nothing.

reigns.tagline: The kind emperor with a ruthless empress
reigns.previously: Emperor Ming dies after 18 strict years. His son takes over.
paragraphs: Liu Da was born to a junior consort and raised by Ming's empress, the daughter of Ma Yuan. As Emperor Zhang he was gentle and generous. He eased harsh punishments, and in 79 he called scholars to the White Tiger Hall to settle arguments over the Confucian classics. His stepmother, now Empress Dowager Ma, at first refused to let him make her brothers marquises.
In the west, the court ordered a pull-out from the Tarim in 76. Ban Chao ignored it and stayed. With a few troops and a lot of local diplomacy he won the oasis kingdoms back one by one.

In the palace things were darker. Zhang's Empress Dou had no son, so she adopted Liu Zhao, the baby of Consort Liang. Then she struck. The crown prince's mother, Consort Song, was accused of witchcraft and killed herself in 82, and the crown prince was demoted. Liu Zhao became heir. Consort Liang's family was ruined, and she died of grief. Zhang died in 88, aged about 31.

claims.text: Empress Dowager Ma scolded her relatives for showing off, with "carriages like flowing water, horses like dragons".
claims.note: The phrase comes from her edict quoted in the Hou Hanshu, and it became a stock Chinese idiom for luxury.

claims.text: Empress Dou framed Consort Song and destroyed Consort Liang's family to secure the succession for her adopted son.
claims.note: The Hou Hanshu tells it this way. It was written after the Dou family fell, so they had no defenders.

claims.text: When Ban Chao tried to leave, the people of Khotan clung to his horse's legs and begged him to stay.
claims.note: The scene is in his biography in the Hou Hanshu, a flattering family-style portrait of a famous general.

reigns.hook: Zhang is dead and Empress Dou's adopted son, Liu Zhao, is nine. Her brother Dou Xian takes the army north to win glory, and the boy has no idea who his real mother was.

reigns.tagline: The boy who turned the eunuchs on his regents
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Son of Zhang, raised by Empress Dou
reigns.previously: Emperor Zhang dies young. A boy of nine takes the throne.
paragraphs: Empress Dowager Dou ruled for the young Emperor He, and her brother Dou Xian ran the army. In 89 Dou Xian smashed the northern Xiongnu and had the historian Ban Gu carve a victory inscription on a Mongolian mountainside. The Dou clan grew rich, loud and dangerous.

In 92 the 13-year-old emperor struck. With the eunuch Zheng Zhong he had Dou Xian stripped of command and forced to kill himself. Ban Gu, a Dou client, died in prison, and his sister Ban Zhao finished his history of the Former Han. Zheng Zhong was later made a marquis, the first Later Han eunuch with real power, and far from the last. After the dowager died in 97, He learned that his true mother was Consort Liang, and he honoured her family.

In 97 Ban Chao's envoy Gan Ying set off for Rome and got as far as the sea before turning back. In 105 the eunuch Cai Lun presented his new paper. Many of He's sons died as babies, so others were raised in secret outside the palace. He died in early 106, aged about 26.

claims.text: Ban Gu's victory inscription for Dou Xian has been found on a cliff in Mongolia.
claims.note: Mongolian and Chinese researchers identified the carving in 2017. Its text matches the one preserved in the Hou Hanshu.

claims.text: Parthian sailors scared Gan Ying off by saying the voyage to Rome could take two years.
claims.note: The Hou Hanshu says so. Historians suspect the Parthians wanted to keep their middleman role in the silk trade.

claims.text: Cai Lun invented paper.
claims.note: He presented an improved paper in 105, but older paper from the Western Han has been dug up, for example at Fangmatan.

reigns.hook: He is dead. One son is thought too sickly to rule. The other, Liu Long, is barely three months old, and the new empress dowager, Deng Sui, picks the baby.

reigns.tagline: Emperor at 100 days old
reigns.previously: Emperor He dies at 26. His surviving sons: a sickly boy and a baby.
paragraphs: Liu Long is the youngest emperor in Chinese history. Like several of Emperor He's children he had been raised outside the palace, and he was about 100 days old when the throne came to him in early 106. The real ruler was the widowed Empress Dowager Deng Sui. His elder brother Liu Sheng was passed over as too sickly.

Deng was clever and well read; the historian Ban Zhao had tutored her. She cut palace spending, sent home many palace women and turned away luxury tributes. The baby emperor did not live out the year: he died later in 106. Deng now had to choose again, and again she chose a child.

claims.text: Deng Sui picked a baby over his older brother so that she could keep power.
claims.note: Critics said so, and her choices both times kept her in charge. The Hou Hanshu, which admires her, stresses Liu Sheng's illness.

claims.text: Deng Sui studied the classics with Ban Zhao.
claims.note: Ban Zhao's biography in the Hou Hanshu says she taught the empress and the palace women, and that Deng valued her advice.

reigns.hook: The baby is dead. Deng passes over Liu Sheng again and fetches a 12-year-old cousin, Liu Hu, whose father was the crown prince Empress Dou pushed aside.

reigns.tagline: Fifteen years under his aunt, four on his own
reigns.previously: The baby Emperor Shang dies within months. Deng must choose again.
paragraphs: Liu Hu was the son of the crown prince who had been demoted back in 82. Empress Dowager Deng kept power for 15 years, and needed all her skill. A huge Qiang uprising in the north-west from 107 cost a fortune and years of fighting, and floods and famine hit the heartland.

Deng died in 121 and An went after her family at once. His wet nurse Wang Sheng and the eunuchs accused the Dengs of plotting, and several of them killed themselves. Cai Lun, the paper man, was ordered to answer for his part in the plot against An's grandmother decades earlier. He bathed, put on his best robes and took poison.

An's own court was run by his wet nurse, the eunuchs and his Empress Yan, whose family filled the top posts. In 124 they had the only son, Liu Bao, removed as heir. In spring 125 An fell ill on a journey south and died, aged about 31. The empress kept it quiet until the party was safely back in Luoyang.

claims.text: Cai Lun dressed in his finest robes and drank poison rather than face trial.
claims.note: His biography in the Hou Hanshu describes it. It is a short, plain account without obvious embroidery.

claims.text: Empress Yan had poisoned Liu Bao's mother, Consort Li, years before.
claims.note: The Hou Hanshu says so. It was written after the Yan family's fall, and no one tested the charge at the time.

reigns.hook: An is dead. Empress Dowager Yan wants another child she can control, and she has just the boy: a little cousin, Liu Yi. The deposed heir Liu Bao has friends among the eunuchs.

images.caption: Cai Lun, the eunuch who presented paper to the throne and died in Emperor An's purge, as imagined about 1,600 years later. Not a portrait of the emperor.

reigns.tagline: The forgotten boy emperor of 125
reigns.previously: Emperor An dies on the road. His only son is already disinherited.
paragraphs: Liu Yi was a grandson of Emperor Zhang and still a child. In the spring of 125 Empress Dowager Yan and her brother Yan Xian put him on the throne, passing over An's son Liu Bao, so that the Yan family could keep running the court. They cleared out the rival eunuchs and the old wet nurse.

Then the boy fell ill, and by the end of the year he was dead. While the Yans hesitated, the eunuch Sun Cheng and eighteen others swore an oath, struck at night and brought Liu Bao to the throne. Yan Xian was killed and the empress dowager was locked away. Liu Yi was buried with a prince's honours, and many lists of emperors leave him out.

claims.text: The Yans kept Liu Yi's death secret and shut the palace gates while they hunted for another child.
claims.note: The Hou Hanshu says so. The victors wrote the account, and the Yan side of the story is lost.

reigns.hook: Nineteen eunuchs have just made an emperor. Liu Bao, ten years old, owes them everything, and they expect to be paid.

reigns.tagline: Put on the throne by nineteen eunuchs
reigns.previously: Nineteen eunuchs storm the palace and fetch the disinherited Liu Bao.
paragraphs: Liu Bao took the throne as Emperor Shun at ten. All nineteen eunuchs who had made him were named marquises. In 135 eunuchs were allowed to pass their titles to adopted sons, and their power started to run in families.

Shun was mild and easily led. In 132 he made Liang Na his empress, and her father Liang Shang became generalissimo. After Liang Shang died in 141 the post went to her brother, Liang Ji, a man of no restraint at all.

It was also a clever age. Zhang Heng, the court astronomer, built a bronze vessel in 132 that could sense distant earthquakes, and he mapped the stars. Shun died in 144 at about 29, leaving one son, Liu Bing, not yet two.

claims.text: Zhang Heng's seismoscope detected an earthquake in the far north-west that nobody in Luoyang had felt.
claims.note: The Hou Hanshu says a messenger arrived days later to confirm it. How the device worked is still argued over; modern replicas are guesses.

claims.text: The nineteen eunuchs were all made marquises.
claims.note: The Hou Hanshu lists them, led by Sun Cheng. It was a turning point in eunuch power.

reigns.hook: Shun is dead. The new emperor, Liu Bing, is a baby. His mother the empress dowager and her brother Liang Ji will rule, and Liang Ji means to keep it that way.

reigns.tagline: A one-year-old in Liang Ji's hands
reigns.previously: Emperor Shun dies at 29. His only son is not yet two.
paragraphs: Liu Bing was a toddler, so Empress Dowager Liang Na ruled for him, with her brother Liang Ji as generalissimo. Rebels were rising in the south-east, and the Liangs filled the court with their own people.

In early 145 the little emperor died. The senior official Li Gu urged the court to pick a grown man, and named Liu Suan, Prince of Qinghe, a sensible adult. Liang Ji wanted nothing of the kind. He chose a seven-year-old instead.

claims.text: Li Gu pushed hard for an adult emperor and made a lifelong enemy of Liang Ji.
claims.note: Li Gu's biography in the Hou Hanshu records his proposals; Liang Ji later had him killed in 147.

claims.text: Empress Dowager Liang Na was a capable and honest regent, betrayed by her brother's greed.
claims.note: The Hou Hanshu treats her kindly. How far she could, or wanted to, restrain Liang Ji is unclear.

reigns.hook: The baby emperor is dead. Liang Ji's choice, Liu Zuan, is seven, bright and outspoken. Being outspoken around Liang Ji is a dangerous habit.

reigns.tagline: The boy who called Liang Ji a bully
reigns.previously: The toddler emperor dies. Liang Ji passes over an adult for a boy.
paragraphs: Liu Zuan was seven when Liang Ji put him on the throne. He was a sharp child. One day in 146, in front of the assembled court, he looked at Liang Ji and called him "an overbearing general".

Not long after, the boy ate a cake and fell desperately ill. He asked for water. He died in the summer of 146, aged about eight. Li Gu tried again to bring in the adult Liu Suan. Liang Ji instead chose a 14-year-old marquis, Liu Zhi, who happened to be engaged to Liang Ji's own sister.

claims.text: Liang Ji had the boy poisoned with a cake for calling him overbearing.
claims.note: The Hou Hanshu tells it, written by historians who saw Liang Ji as the arch-villain. The boy did die suddenly.

claims.text: Liang Ji refused the dying emperor water, saying he would only vomit.
claims.note: This detail comes from the same account of the death; it reads like a story told to blacken Liang Ji.

reigns.hook: Another boy emperor is dead. The new one, Liu Zhi, will marry Liang Ji's sister and do as he's told. For thirteen years.

reigns.tagline: The emperor who freed himself with five eunuchs
reigns.previously: The boy Emperor Zhi dies after eating a cake. Liang Ji picks again.
paragraphs: Huan married Liang Ji's sister and spent thirteen years as a figurehead. Liang Ji's mansions and parks were the talk of Luoyang. In 159 the empress died, and Huan moved. In a palace privy, the only private place he had, he plotted with five eunuchs. Palace guards surrounded Liang Ji's house, and Liang Ji and his wife killed themselves. Their whole clan was wiped out.

The five eunuchs were all made marquises on the same day, and from then on the eunuchs ran the court. Scholars and students protested. In 166 their leader Li Ying and some 200 others were arrested and later banned for life from office: the first Partisan Prohibition.

In 166 men claiming to be envoys of "Andun", king of Da Qin, the Roman empire, arrived by sea. That year Huan made offerings to Laozi and the Buddha in his palace. He died in early 168 at about 35, with no son.

claims.text: Huan sealed his oath with the eunuchs by biting one of them, Shan Chao, on the arm until it bled.
claims.note: The Hou Hanshu says so. It is a vivid detail in a story told by historians who loathed the eunuchs.

claims.text: Liang Ji's confiscated fortune equalled half the empire's taxes for a year, so taxes were halved.
claims.note: The figure is from the Hou Hanshu and may be rounded up for effect.

claims.text: The "Roman envoys" of 166 were sent by Marcus Aurelius.
claims.note: The Hou Hanshu's "Andun" sounds like Antoninus. Their gifts were local goods from South East Asia, so they were probably private merchants.

reigns.hook: Huan is dead without an heir. His widow and her father Dou Wu choose a twelve-year-old, Liu Hong, and Dou Wu plans to finish the eunuchs off for good.

reigns.tagline: The emperor who sold the government
reigns.previously: Emperor Huan dies without a son. A twelve-year-old cousin is chosen.
paragraphs: Liu Hong arrived from the provinces in early 168. That autumn the regent Dou Wu and the old minister Chen Fan plotted to wipe out the eunuchs, but word leaked. The eunuchs struck first, with the boy in their hands. Dou Wu killed himself and Chen Fan was cut down. A second, harsher Partisan Prohibition followed in 169, and scholars died in prison.

Ling grew up among the eunuchs and trusted them completely. From 178 he sold offices for cash, with fixed prices. He did one thing that lasted: from 175 the classics were carved on stone tablets outside the Imperial Academy, so scholars had an agreed text.

In 184 the faith healer Zhang Jue raised the Yellow Turbans, chanting that the blue sky was dead and the yellow sky would rise. Generals crushed them, but the empire was now full of armed men. Ling never named an heir. He died in May 189 at about 33.

claims.text: Ling called the eunuchs Zhang Rang and Zhao Zhong "my father" and "my mother".
claims.note: The Hou Hanshu quotes him. It's in the eunuchs' biographies, written by historians who blamed them for the fall of Han.

claims.text: Cui Lie bought a top ministry for five million cash, and people said he smelled of copper.
claims.note: A Hou Hanshu anecdote. The selling of offices is well recorded; this joke about it may be polished.

claims.text: The Xiping Stone Classics were carved under Ling, from 175.
claims.note: Fragments of the tablets have been dug up at Luoyang and are in museums today.

reigns.hook: Ling is dead with two sons and no heir named. The elder, Liu Bian, 13, has a powerful uncle, He Jin. The eunuchs have no intention of going quietly.

reigns.tagline: Five months on the throne, then a cup of poison
reigns.cameToPower: Raised by his mother and uncle He Jin
reigns.previously: Emperor Ling dies, leaving two young sons and a court at war.
paragraphs: Liu Bian was Emperor Ling's elder son by Empress He, a butcher's daughter who had climbed to the top of the harem. Ling had never named him heir, and was thought to prefer the younger boy, Liu Xie. But when Ling died in May 189, the empress and her half-brother He Jin, the commander-in-chief, moved fast. The 13-year-old Liu Bian was on the throne within two days, with his mother as regent.

He Jin wanted to wipe out the palace eunuchs, and called generals with armies towards the capital to back him up. The eunuchs struck first. In September they lured him into the palace and cut off his head. His officers, led by Yuan Shao, stormed the palace and killed some 2,000 eunuchs. The last eunuch leaders fled north with the two boys, and threw themselves into the Yellow River when the soldiers caught up.

Waiting on the road was Dong Zhuo, a hard frontier general who had been marching on Luoyang. He took the boys back to the city and took the city too. On 28 September he deposed Liu Bian, made him Prince of Hongnong and put his little brother on the throne. In 190, as rebel armies gathered against him, Dong Zhuo sent a man with poisoned wine. Liu Bian was about 14.

claims.text: When Dong Zhuo met the boys on the road, Liu Bian wept and couldn't speak, while his eight-year-old brother calmly told the whole story, and Dong decided then to swap them.
claims.note: Told in later anecdote collections quoted by Pei Songzhi and in the Hou Hanshu. It reads as a tidy excuse for the deposition.

claims.text: Before he drank the poison, Liu Bian sang a farewell song with his consort, Lady Tang.
claims.note: The Hou Hanshu gives the words of both songs. Lady Tang survived and remarried, so the story could come from her, but the verses may be polished.

claims.text: Some 2,000 eunuchs were killed in the palace massacre, and men without beards were cut down by mistake.
claims.note: The Hou Hanshu and Sanguozhi both give the figure and the detail; the exact number is a round estimate.

reigns.hook: Dong Zhuo has his own emperor now: Liu Bian's eight-year-old half-brother, Liu Xie. Across the east, the governors are raising armies to come and take the boy back.

images.caption: Dong Zhuo deposes Liu Bian, in a Qing-dynasty illustration to the Romance of the Three Kingdoms, made some 1,500 years later.

reigns.tagline: A boy emperor passed from warlord to warlord
reigns.cameToPower: Set on the throne by Dong Zhuo
reigns.reignEnded: Taken in hand by Cao Cao
reigns.previously: Dong Zhuo deposes Liu Bian and crowns his little brother.
paragraphs: Liu Xie's mother, Consort Wang, was poisoned by the jealous Empress He soon after he was born, and he was brought up by his grandmother. At eight he was Dong Zhuo's emperor. In 190 the eastern governors formed an alliance against Dong, with Yuan Shao at its head. Dong Zhuo's answer was to burn Luoyang, dig up the imperial tombs for their treasure, and drag the court and a vast crowd of people west to Chang'an.

In May 192 the minister Wang Yun talked Dong's bodyguard and adopted son, Lü Bu, into killing him. It didn't help. Dong's old officers, Li Jue and Guo Si, stormed Chang'an, killed Wang Yun and ran the government themselves. In 195 they fell out and fought in the streets of the capital, one holding the emperor and the other holding his ministers as hostages.

That summer the teenage emperor slipped away east with a handful of officials, chased and harried the whole way. In 196 he reached Luoyang. It was a ruin. Officials scratched for wild plants to eat, and some starved to death among the broken walls. Then a general with a strong army and a good sense of what an emperor was worth came to call. His name was Cao Cao.

claims.text: Wang Yun turned Lü Bu against Dong Zhuo by using a beautiful girl named Diaochan.
claims.note: Diaochan is invented by later drama and the Romance of the Three Kingdoms. The Sanguozhi says only that Lü Bu was having an affair with one of Dong's maids and feared being found out.

claims.text: Dong Zhuo's body was so fat that the guards lit a wick in his navel, and it burned for days.
claims.note: Recorded in the Hou Hanshu and Sanguozhi commentary. A grim detail that may well be true, and the kind of story historians love to tell about a villain.

claims.text: In a famine in 194 the boy emperor tested the relief porridge himself and caught the official in charge cheating.
claims.note: From the Hou Hanshu. It fits the later picture of a clever, helpless emperor; there is no other account.

reigns.hook: Cao Cao has the emperor. He can now give orders to the whole empire in the Han's name, and every rival who defies him is a rebel against the throne.

reigns.tagline: The novel's great villain, and a fine poet
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Son of a eunuch's adopted son
reigns.cameToPower: Took the emperor into his care
reigns.reignEnded: Died at Luoyang, King of Wei
reigns.previously: Emperor Xian escapes Chang'an and limps home to ruined Luoyang.
paragraphs: After Emperor Ling died, the eunuchs murdered the general He Jin, and his men slaughtered the eunuchs. The warlord Dong Zhuo seized the boy Emperor Xian, burned Luoyang in 190 and dragged the court west. In 192 his adopted son Lü Bu killed him. The emperor drifted, half starved, among feuding warlords. In 196 Cao Cao, a sharp and ruthless general, brought him to his own base at Xu and gave orders to the empire in his name.

Cao Cao's great rival was Yuan Shao, master of the north. In 200 Cao beat him at Guandu by raiding and burning his supply depot. In 208 he sailed down the Yangtze to finish off the south, but Sun Quan and Liu Bei beat him at the Red Cliffs, sending fire ships into his fleet. China was now split three ways.

He became chancellor, then King of Wei in 216, but never took the throne. He was also a fine poet, and his verses are still learned today. The 14th-century novel Romance of the Three Kingdoms made him its scheming villain, and the stage gave him a white face. In 2009 archaeologists announced they had found his tomb near Anyang. He died at Luoyang in March 220.

claims.text: Cao Cao said, "I'd rather betray the world than let the world betray me."
claims.note: It comes from a later anecdote collection quoted by Pei Songzhi in his notes to the Sanguozhi; the novel made it famous.

claims.text: He lost at the Red Cliffs to a fire-ship attack.
claims.note: The Sanguozhi's accounts are brief and differ. Some mention fire, others blame disease in Cao's army; the novel's details are invented.

claims.text: The tomb found near Anyang in 2009 is Cao Cao's.
claims.note: Chinese archaeologists announced it with confidence, but critics have questioned the finds and the identification of the bones.

reigns.hook: Cao Cao ruled for 24 years in the name of an emperor. Go back to 196 and that emperor, Liu Xie, a hungry teenager who has just swapped one master for another.

reigns.tagline: The last Han emperor, a hostage in his own court

end.note: Abdication edict; Cao Pi was enthroned on 11 December

reigns.cameToPower: Taken to Xu by Cao Cao
reigns.previously: Cao Cao dies at Luoyang in 220, King of Wei but never emperor.
paragraphs: In 196 Cao Cao moved the starving court from ruined Luoyang to his own city of Xu. Liu Xie was fed, housed and honoured, and every order went out in his name. But his guards and officials were Cao's men. He was an emperor in a gilded cage, and he knew it.

In 200 a plot against Cao was uncovered. Its leader, the general Dong Cheng, said he had a secret edict from the emperor sewn into a belt. Dong and his family were executed, among them his daughter, the emperor's pregnant consort. Liu Xie begged for her life and was refused. In 214 it was Empress Fu's turn: an old letter of hers against Cao came to light, she was dragged away barefoot and died in prison, and her two sons were poisoned.

Cao Cao gave the emperor three of his own daughters as consorts, and one, Cao Jie, became empress. After Cao Cao died, his son Cao Pi made the move his father never had. In late 220 Liu Xie gave up the throne, after the polite three refusals, and became Duke of Shanyang. He lived quietly until 234. Four centuries of Han rule were over.

claims.text: Empress Cao Jie threw the imperial seal down and cursed when her brother's men came for it.
claims.note: The Hou Hanshu says so. It makes a fine scene, and a later court history had every reason to flatter her loyalty to the Han.

claims.text: In 221 Shu wrongly reported that Liu Xie had been murdered, and Liu Bei mourned him before declaring himself emperor.
claims.note: Recorded in the Sanguozhi. The former emperor was alive and well as a duke under Wei.

claims.text: As Duke of Shanyang he worked as a village doctor, treating the poor for free.
claims.note: A local tradition from later centuries. The early histories only say he lived on his estate with imperial honours.

reigns.hook: The Han is gone. Cao Pi is emperor of Wei, but in the west Liu Bei claims the Han inheritance, and in the south Sun Quan has his own ideas. China now has three thrones.

reigns.tagline: He ended the Han and wrote poetry about it
reigns.cameToPower: The last Han emperor abdicated to him
reigns.previously: Emperor Xian hands the throne to Cao Pi. The Han is over.
paragraphs: Cao Pi took over his father's titles in March 220 and wasted no time. That December, after the ritual three refusals, he accepted the throne from Emperor Xian, who became Duke of Shanyang and lived on quietly for 14 more years. After four centuries the Han was over, and Cao Pi was the first emperor of Wei. His new nine-rank system had local officials grade men for office, and it soon became a ladder for the great families.

He didn't stay the only emperor. In Chengdu, Liu Bei declared himself emperor in 221, as heir to the Han. Sun Quan took the title King of Wu from Wei, then broke away in 222. Liu Bei marched on Wu to avenge his sworn brother Guan Yu, and was crushed at Yiling in 222. He died at Baidicheng the next year. Cao Pi tried three times to cross the Yangtze and beat Wu, and got nowhere.

He was a writer as much as a ruler. His essay on literature, which called fine writing a great work that never dies, is one of the first pieces of literary criticism in China. He also forced his first wife, Lady Zhen, to kill herself in 221, and kept his brothers on a very short leash. He died in June 226, about 39, naming his son Cao Rui heir only at the end.

claims.text: Cao Pi ordered his brother Cao Zhi to compose a poem in seven steps or die, and Cao Zhi did it: beans weeping in the pot over a fire of bean stalks.
claims.note: The story first appears in the Shishuo Xinyu, about 200 years later. The brothers' rivalry was real; the poem's date and authorship are doubted.

claims.text: Emperor Xian refused the throne three times before handing it over.
claims.note: The Sanguozhi and Pei Songzhi's commentary preserve the exchange of edicts. The refusals were ritual; the outcome was never in doubt.

claims.text: Lady Zhen was killed because she complained of being neglected for Cao Pi's new favourite.
claims.note: The Sanguozhi says she was ordered to die after resentful words. Later stories blame the favourite, Guo Nüwang, and add lurid details.

reigns.hook: Cao Pi is dead at about 39. His heir is the son of the wife he forced to die, a young man nobody quite knows, and in the west Zhuge Liang is getting ready to march.

reigns.tagline: He beat back Zhuge Liang and built palaces
reigns.cameToPower: Named heir on his father's deathbed
reigns.reignEnded: Died young, leaving a boy heir
reigns.previously: Cao Pi dies at about 39, naming his son heir at the last moment.
paragraphs: Cao Rui was Lady Zhen's son, and after her death his own future hung in the balance for years. He turned out to be a sharp, cool ruler. When Zhuge Liang, the chancellor of Shu Han, began marching north in 228, Wei's generals held him off again and again. Sima Yi, the most patient of them, refused to be drawn into battle, and in 234 Zhuge Liang died in camp at the Wuzhang Plains. In 229 Sun Quan of Wu had declared himself emperor too.

With Shu on the back foot, Cao Rui spent heavily on palaces and gardens at Luoyang, and his ministers sent memorial after memorial complaining. In 238 he sent Sima Yi north-east to destroy the warlord Gongsun Yuan in Liaodong. Sima Yi took his city and slaughtered thousands of its men. With Liaodong open, envoys from Queen Himiko of Wa, in Japan, reached Wei and went home with a gold seal and gifts.

His own sons all died young, so he adopted a boy, Cao Fang. Falling ill at the end of 238, he first picked his uncle as regent, then changed his mind. On his deathbed in January 239 he held Sima Yi's hand and gave him the boy, with his kinsman Cao Shuang as co-regent. He was only in his early thirties.

claims.text: Out hunting, Cao Pi shot a mother deer and told Cao Rui to shoot the fawn. He wept and said, "Your Majesty has killed its mother. I can't bear to kill the child," and his father decided then to make him heir.
claims.note: From an anecdote collection quoted by Pei Songzhi. A neat story about Lady Zhen's son that may have been made up later.

claims.text: Himiko's envoys reached Wei in 238.
claims.note: The Japanese chapter of the Sanguozhi says 238, but Liaodong was still at war that year, and many historians think 239 is right.

claims.text: He changed the regency on his deathbed after two ministers talked him round.
claims.note: The Sanguozhi and its commentary describe the switch from his uncle Cao Yu to Cao Shuang and Sima Yi. The scene's details vary.

reigns.hook: A seven-year-old sits on the throne of Wei. His two regents, a Cao kinsman and the old general Sima Yi, smile at each other in public. Only one of them will be alive in ten years.

reigns.tagline: The boy who watched the Sima family take over
reigns.cameToPower: Adopted heir of the dying Cao Rui
reigns.previously: Cao Rui dies young, leaving a boy of seven and two regents.
paragraphs: Nobody knew for sure where Cao Fang came from; the court kept it secret. At first Cao Shuang and Sima Yi shared power. Then Cao Shuang filled the court with his friends and pushed the old general out. Sima Yi said he was ill and stayed at home for years. In 249 Cao Shuang took the young emperor out of Luoyang to visit Cao Rui's tomb at Gaoping. Sima Yi, suddenly well again, shut the city gates behind them.

He promised Cao Shuang his life if he gave up. Cao Shuang did, and was executed with his whole clan within days. From then on the Sima family ran Wei. Sima Yi died in 251 and his son Sima Shi stepped into his place. In 254 a group of courtiers plotted to replace Sima Shi. He found out, killed them, and had the emperor's empress deposed because her father had been one of them.

Then he came for the emperor himself. In October 254 he made the empress dowager sign a decree accusing Cao Fang, now 22, of drinking and debauchery, and sent him off as Prince of Qi. It was a soft landing. Cao Fang lived another 20 years, outlasting the dynasty, and died in 274 as a duke under the Jin.

claims.text: Sima Yi faked his illness so well that he let soup dribble down his chin in front of Cao Shuang's spy.
claims.note: From an anecdote collection quoted by Pei Songzhi. The novel loves it; the scene is too perfect to take at face value.

claims.text: Cao Fang was secretly the son of a minor prince.
claims.note: The Sanguozhi says his origins were kept secret. One commentary names Cao Kai, Prince of Rencheng, as his father; others disagree.

claims.text: The charges of debauchery against him were trumped up.
claims.note: The decree survives in the Sanguozhi. It was written for Sima Shi, who needed a reason; how much was true can't be known.

reigns.hook: Sima Shi needs a new emperor. He picks Cao Pi's 13-year-old grandson, Cao Mao, a clever boy who loves books. Clever boys can be a problem.

reigns.tagline: The teenage emperor who charged with a sword
reigns.previously: Sima Shi deposes Cao Fang and picks a bright teenager instead.
paragraphs: Cao Mao impressed everyone. He painted, wrote and went to the Imperial Academy to argue about the classics with its scholars. He had no power at all. Sima Shi crushed a rebellion in 255 and died soon after, and his brother Sima Zhao took over. Another rising, by Zhuge Dan at Shouchun, ended in blood in 258. Sima Zhao kept piling up titles, and everyone could see where it was heading.

In June 260 the 19-year-old emperor snapped. He called in his ministers and told them he would not sit and wait to be deposed. One of them ran to warn Sima Zhao. Cao Mao drew his sword, climbed into his carriage and led a few hundred palace servants and guards out of the palace. Sima Zhao's men met them at the south gate. They backed away from the emperor, and nobody wanted to strike him.

Then Sima Zhao's officer Jia Chong told a soldier named Cheng Ji that this was what they'd been fed for. Cheng Ji ran Cao Mao through with his spear. Sima Zhao wept in public, had Cheng Ji and his family executed, and had the dead emperor condemned in a decree and buried without imperial honours. Nobody was fooled.

claims.text: Cao Mao told his ministers, "Sima Zhao's heart is known to every man in the street."
claims.note: The line comes from the Han Jin Chunqiu, quoted by Pei Songzhi, and is still a Chinese proverb for an obvious plot. The wording may be polished.

claims.text: Sima Shi died after his eye burst out of its socket during a night attack.
claims.note: The Jin Shu says he had just had a growth cut from his eye and the shock of the attack made it burst. Vivid, and recorded by the dynasty his family founded.

claims.text: Cao Mao wrote a poem about a dragon stuck in a well, meaning himself, which angered Sima Zhao.
claims.note: From later commentary. It may have been told afterwards to explain the break.

reigns.hook: Sima Zhao needs another Cao to sit on the throne. He chooses a teenage grandson of Cao Cao, Cao Huan, who will do exactly as he's told.

reigns.tagline: The last emperor of Wei signs it all away
reigns.previously: Cao Mao charges Sima Zhao's men and is run through with a spear.
paragraphs: Cao Huan was a grandson of Cao Cao, and he understood his job. Sima Zhao ran everything; the emperor signed. In 263 Wei finally went for Shu Han. While the main army was stuck at the passes, the general Deng Ai led a force over the mountains by a back route, at times rolling down slopes wrapped in felt. He appeared outside Chengdu, and Liu Bei's son, the emperor Liu Shan, surrendered.

The victory went sour fast. The other commander, Zhong Hui, arrested Deng Ai and tried to set himself up in Shu, and in 264 both men were killed in the chaos. Sima Zhao collected the credit: Duke of Jin, then King of Jin. Liu Shan was brought to Luoyang, made a duke and treated kindly. He seemed happy with that, which was perhaps the wisest thing he ever did.

Sima Zhao died in September 265, one step short of the throne. His son Sima Yan took the last step. In February 266 Cao Huan handed him the throne, just as Emperor Xian had handed it to Cao Pi 45 years earlier. He was made Prince of Chenliu, allowed to keep Wei's rites and calendar at home, and died around 302.

claims.text: Asked at a feast if he missed Shu, Liu Shan said, "I'm so happy here I don't think of Shu."
claims.note: From the Han Jin Chunqiu, quoted by Pei Songzhi. It became a byword for a feckless ruler, but a captive had good reason to look content.

claims.text: Deng Ai wrapped himself in felt and rolled down a mountainside to reach Shu.
claims.note: The Sanguozhi says so. The march over the Yinping route was real and daring; the felt detail is hard to check.

claims.text: Cao Huan died in 302.
claims.note: The Sanguozhi commentary gives 302; some sources say 303.

reigns.hook: Sima Yan is now Emperor Wu of Jin, and he sits on the throne his grandfather spent a lifetime stalking. Only Wu, down on the Yangtze, still stands in his way.
