reigns.tagline: He glued China back together and handed out the knives
reigns.cameToPower: Pushed the last Wei emperor aside
reigns.previously: Cao Huan, the last Wei emperor, hands the throne to Sima Yan.
paragraphs: Sima Yan was the third generation of a family that had spent decades taking Wei apart from the inside. In 266 he simply finished the job and called his dynasty Jin. One rival was left: Wu, down on the Yangtze. In 280 his fleets came down the river, the last Wu ruler gave up, and China had one emperor again for the first time in about 90 years.

Then he relaxed. He cut back the provincial armies, but gave the princes of his own family armies of their own, hoping relatives would be loyal. Peace brought a famous splurge. His harem swelled with Wu's palace women, and two courtiers, Shi Chong and Wang Kai, held a contest to see who could waste more money. Worst of all, his heir was famously slow-witted, and he kept him anyway.
When the emperor died in 290, the throne passed to that son. Behind him stood a tough, ambitious wife, and around him stood a ring of uncles and cousins, each with soldiers.

claims.text: He picked which woman to visit by riding through the harem in a goat cart, and women put salt and bamboo leaves outside their doors to make the goats stop.
claims.note: Told in the Jin Shu, written over 350 years later. It's a moral tale about a lazy, lustful ruler as much as a report.

claims.text: Shi Chong smashed Wang Kai's prize coral tree, a gift from the emperor, then offered him a choice of bigger ones.
claims.note: A favourite story in later anecdote collections and the Jin Shu. The wealth contest was real enough; the details are polished.

claims.text: Told the people had no grain to eat, his heir asked, "Why don't they eat meat porridge?"
claims.note: From the Jin Shu, written by a later dynasty that had every reason to make the Jin look foolish.

reigns.hook: A slow-witted emperor named Sima Zhong, a ruthless empress and a dozen princes with private armies. The Jin is about to tear itself to pieces, and the peoples of the north are watching.

reigns.tagline: Everyone fought over him; nobody listened to him
reigns.previously: Emperor Wu dies. His slow-witted son becomes emperor.
paragraphs: Sima Zhong was the heir everyone had warned Emperor Wu about. His wife, Jia Nanfeng, was quick and ruthless. In 291 she had the regent, the old empress's father Yang Jun, killed, then used one prince to kill another and had the first executed for it. For nine years she ran the empire, and some say ran it well. Then in 299 she framed the crown prince, who was not her son, and in 300 had him killed.

That gave Sima Lun, Prince of Zhao, his excuse. He arrested Jia Nanfeng and made her drink poisoned wine, and in 301 took the throne himself. Other princes rose and killed him. The War of the Eight Princes was in full swing, and the emperor was the prize. He was carried off to Ye, to Chang'an, and back to Luoyang. At Dangyin in 304 he was hit by arrows and left almost alone on the field.

While the princes fought, the peoples they used as soldiers began to fight for themselves. In 304 Liu Yuan, a Xiongnu noble, declared his own Han kingdom in the north, and in Sichuan the Li family set up a state of their own. In January 307 the emperor, now in the hands of Sima Yue, Prince of Donghai, ate some cakes and died. He was 47. His younger half-brother took the throne.

claims.text: At Dangyin his minister Ji Shao shielded him with his body and was killed, and the emperor wouldn't let anyone wash the blood off his robe: "This is Ji Shao's blood."
claims.note: Told in the Jin Shu. Ji Shao's death is well attested; the line about the robe is the kind of scene the histories liked to polish.

claims.text: Hearing frogs croak, he asked whether they were croaking for the government or for themselves.
claims.note: From the Jin Shu, written by the Tang, who had every reason to make the Jin look foolish.

claims.text: He was poisoned by Sima Yue.
claims.note: The Jin Shu hints at it and many later writers said so. There's no proof, and he may simply have died.

reigns.hook: The new emperor, Sima Chi, is clever and willing. But the empire he inherits is broken, and the Xiongnu armies of Liu Yuan's Han are already raiding towards Luoyang.

reigns.tagline: He lost Luoyang and poured wine for his captor
reigns.cameToPower: Named heir in the civil war
reigns.previously: Emperor Hui dies after eating cakes. His half-brother takes over.
paragraphs: Sima Chi was the 25th son of Emperor Wu, a scholarly young man who had kept out of the princes' wars. As emperor he had little power. Sima Yue, Prince of Donghai, ran the court and fought anyone who crossed him. Meanwhile Liu Yuan declared himself emperor of Han in 308, and his generals, among them a former slave named Shi Le, roamed the north.

In 310 Sima Yue led the main army out of Luoyang. He died in 311, and Shi Le caught his army as it marched away with his coffin and destroyed it. Tens of thousands died. Luoyang was left almost undefended. In July 311 Liu Yao and Wang Mi stormed the capital, burned the palaces, killed thousands and took the emperor prisoner. The Chinese remember it as the Yongjia disaster.

He was taken to Pingyang, the capital of the new emperor of Han, Liu Yuan's son Liu Cong. At first Liu Cong gave him a title and a wife. Then at a New Year feast in 313 he made the Jin emperor dress as a servant and pour the wine. Some of the Jin officials present burst into tears. Liu Cong had them killed, and in March he had the emperor put to death. He was 29.

claims.text: Liu Cong made the captured emperor serve wine in a servant's blue robe at a New Year banquet.
claims.note: From the Jin Shu. The humiliation is well attested in outline; the scene is written for maximum shame.

claims.text: Liu Cong reminded his prisoner that they had met years before in Luoyang, when Liu Cong was a guest and Sima Chi a prince.
claims.note: The Jin Shu gives their conversation. They may well have met, but the dialogue is a historian's set piece.

claims.text: Over 30,000 people were killed when Luoyang fell.
claims.note: The Jin Shu's figure. Numbers like this in the histories are rough at best.

reigns.hook: With the emperor dead, the Jin loyalists in the west crown his nephew, a teenage boy, in what's left of Chang'an. The Xiongnu armies are already on their way.

reigns.tagline: The boy emperor who surrendered in a sheep cart
reigns.previously: Luoyang falls and Emperor Huai dies a captive at Pingyang.
paragraphs: Sima Ye was Emperor Wu's grandson, a boy who had escaped Luoyang in 311 and been brought to Chang'an by loyal officers. When news came of his uncle's death, they proclaimed him emperor in May 313. His capital was a shell. The Jin Shu says it had fewer than a hundred households, weeds and thorns had grown into thickets, and the whole government had four carts.

Help never came. Jin's princes and generals in the east and south had their own worries, and Sima Rui in Jiankang sent nothing much. In 316 Liu Yao, the Han general who had taken Luoyang, besieged Chang'an. Food ran out. Grain was sold for gold, people ate each other, and more than half the people in the city died. In December the emperor said he couldn't let them suffer any more.

He rode out in a cart drawn by sheep, stripped to the waist with jade in his mouth and a coffin carried behind him, the old ritual of a ruler who gives himself up. At Pingyang Liu Cong made him a marquis and a servant. He led the hunt in armour carrying a halberd, and poured wine and washed cups at feasts. Jin officials who wept at the sight were killed, and early in 318 so was he. He was about 17.

claims.text: He surrendered in a sheep cart, half naked, with jade in his mouth and a coffin behind him.
claims.note: The Jin Shu describes the full surrender ritual. It was an ancient form, so the details are likely, though the writer leans on the pathos.

claims.text: Chang'an had fewer than a hundred households and only four carts when he was crowned.
claims.note: The Jin Shu's words. It's a deliberate picture of ruin and probably exaggerated, but the city was devastated.

claims.text: In the siege a measure of grain cost two catties of gold.
claims.note: The Jin Shu's figure, a stock way of describing famine prices.

reigns.hook: The northern Jin is finished. In the south, in Jiankang, a distant cousin named Sima Rui hears the news. He'll be emperor before long, but only of half a country.

reigns.tagline: The refugee prince who rebuilt Jin on the Yangtze
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Cousin of Min; great-grandson of Sima Yi
reigns.reignEnded: Died after Wang Dun took Jiankang
reigns.previously: Chang'an has fallen. Emperor Min is a prisoner of the Xiongnu.
paragraphs: Sima Rui was a minor prince of Langya with no real claim to anything. In 307, as the north burned, he slipped south to Jianye on the Yangtze (soon renamed Jiankang, today's Nanjing) with a clever adviser, Wang Dao. Northern families followed him in their thousands. When Chang'an fell he called himself King of Jin, and when news came in 318 that Emperor Min was dead, he became emperor.

He owed everything to the Wang clan. Wang Dao ran the government and his cousin Wang Dun commanded the armies upriver. People joked that the Wang and the Sima shared the realm. The emperor tried to build up men loyal only to him, and in 322 Wang Dun lost patience. He marched downriver, took Jiankang and had the emperor's friends killed. Sima Rui kept his throne but lost his power, and within months he was dead.

claims.text: A popular saying ran: "The Wang and the Sima share the realm."
claims.note: Quoted in the Jin Shu. It sums up how the southern court really worked in the 310s and 320s.

claims.text: Sima Rui's real father was a junior official named Niu, his mother's lover.
claims.note: The Jin Shu repeats the rumour and the northern Wei Shu leans on it. It fits an old prophecy too neatly to trust.

reigns.hook: Wang Dun now holds the capital in all but name. The dead emperor's son, Sima Shao, is in his early twenties, and he has no intention of being anyone's puppet.

reigns.tagline: The young emperor who outlasted his overmighty warlord
reigns.previously: Wang Dun storms Jiankang. Emperor Yuan dies a humbled man.
paragraphs: Sima Shao was the brightest of the Jin princes, a boy famous for his quick answers. As emperor he moved carefully. Wang Dun sat upriver with the best army in the south, and everyone knew he was thinking about the throne.

In 324 Wang Dun moved again. This time the emperor was ready, and Wang Dun was ill. Loyal troops held the capital, the old general died in his camp, and the rising fell apart. The emperor had his body dug up and his head displayed. Then, after barely three years on the throne, Sima Shao fell sick himself and died in 325, still in his mid-twenties. His heir was a little boy.

claims.text: Asked as a child whether the sun or Chang'an was farther away, he gave a clever answer one day and the opposite clever answer the next.
claims.note: A favourite anecdote in the Shishuo Xinyu. Told to show a born ruler's wit, not as a record.

claims.text: He rode in disguise to spy on Wang Dun's camp, and Wang Dun, warned of a "yellow-bearded" rider, sent men after him too late.
claims.note: From the Jin Shu. The emperor's fair beard is mentioned elsewhere; the chase reads like a storyteller's set piece.

reigns.hook: Wang Dun is gone, but Jin has a four-year-old emperor. His mother will govern for him, and her ambitious brother is about to start a fight he can't finish.

reigns.tagline: A child on the throne while rebels burn his capital
reigns.cameToPower: Succeeded his father as a child
reigns.previously: Wang Dun's rising collapses. Emperor Ming dies young.
paragraphs: Sima Yan (the same name as Jin's founder, in a different character) was four when he became emperor. His mother, Empress Dowager Yu, governed for him, and her brother Yu Liang ran the court. Yu Liang tried to take away the troops of a frontier general, Su Jun. In 327 Su Jun rebelled instead, and early in 328 he took Jiankang.

The rebels looted the city and held the boy emperor in the Stone Fortress on the river. His mother died that year, in disgrace and despair. Loyal generals, led by Tao Kan and Wen Jiao, fought back. Su Jun was killed in battle in 328 and the revolt was crushed in 329. The old statesman Wang Dao then kept the court steady until his death in 339. The emperor grew up, but died at about 21, leaving only baby sons.

claims.text: When the rebels sacked Jiankang, courtiers and palace women were stripped and had to cover themselves with mats and grass.
claims.note: From the Jin Shu's account of the rebellion. The sack is certain; the detail is meant to shock.

claims.text: Su Jun died when, drunk, he charged the loyalist lines and his horse stumbled.
claims.note: The Jin Shu and Zizhi Tongjian tell it this way. A dramatic end for a rebel, told by the winners.

reigns.hook: The dying emperor's sons are babies. The Yu family has another idea: skip them and crown his grown-up brother.

reigns.tagline: Two years on a throne his uncles chose for him
reigns.cameToPower: Picked by the Yu clan over Cheng's sons
reigns.reignEnded: Died of illness after two years
reigns.previously: Emperor Cheng dies at 21. His sons are still babies.
paragraphs: Sima Yue owed his crown to his mother's family. Yu Bing, brother of the late Yu Liang, argued that the realm needed a grown man, not a baby, with enemies all around. Keeping the throne with Cheng's brother also kept the Yu family as uncles of the emperor. Not everyone agreed. The minister He Chong said plainly that sons should come before brothers.

The reign was short. Yu Yi, another Yu brother, planned a march north against the Later Zhao, but little came of it. In 344 the emperor fell ill. This time He Chong won the argument: the dying emperor named his own son, a baby barely a year old, as heir. Soon afterwards Sima Yue was dead, aged about 22.

claims.text: When the new emperor thanked He Chong and Yu Bing for his throne, He Chong replied that if his own advice had been taken, the emperor would never have seen the day.
claims.note: Told in the Jin Shu and the Shishuo Xinyu. He Chong's opposition is real; the neat put-down may be polished.

reigns.hook: A one-year-old is now emperor. Real power is about to pass to a general named Huan Wen, who will spend thirty years making and unmaking rulers.

reigns.tagline: The baby emperor whose general won back Sichuan
reigns.cameToPower: Succeeded his father as a baby
reigns.reignEnded: Died at about 18 with no son
reigns.previously: Emperor Kang dies after two years. His baby son is named heir.
paragraphs: Sima Dan was about a year old when he became emperor. His mother, Empress Dowager Chu, governed from behind a screen. The man who mattered was Huan Wen, governor in the middle Yangtze. In 347 he marched up into Sichuan and conquered the Cheng-Han kingdom. In 356 he took back the old capital, Luoyang, for the first time in over forty years.

These were good years for the south. In 353 the calligrapher Wang Xizhi held his famous poetry party at the Orchid Pavilion. The young emperor took power himself in 357, but he died in 361, aged about 18, with no son. The throne went to his cousin, a son of Emperor Cheng.

claims.text: When Huan Wen camped near Chang'an in 354, a poor scholar named Wang Meng talked politics with him while picking lice from his clothes.
claims.note: From the Jin Shu. Wang Meng later became chief minister to Fu Jian of Former Qin; the lice make the story.

claims.text: Wang Xizhi wrote the Orchid Pavilion Preface after drinking, and could never match it sober.
claims.note: A Tang-era tale. The gathering of 353 is real; the original Preface is lost.

reigns.hook: The new emperor, Sima Pi, is a grown man. He has decided he would rather live forever than rule.

reigns.tagline: He wanted to live forever. The pills had other plans
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Cousin of Mu; son of Emperor Cheng
reigns.cameToPower: Chosen when Mu died without a son
reigns.previously: Emperor Mu dies at 18 with no son. A cousin takes the throne.
paragraphs: Sima Pi was a son of Emperor Cheng, passed over as a baby twenty years earlier. Now he had the throne, and he wanted something else. He fell under the spell of Daoist masters who promised long life. He gave up eating grain and swallowed their pills of cinnabar and minerals.

By 364 he was too sick to rule, and Empress Dowager Chu took over the government again. Huan Wen pushed through a great new census that put northern refugee families on the tax rolls. Meanwhile the northern Former Yan closed in on Luoyang, which was soon lost again. Early in 365 the emperor was dead, aged about 24. He left no son, so his younger brother took the throne.

claims.text: The emperor was poisoned by the immortality drugs he took.
claims.note: The Jin Shu blames the elixirs directly. Cinnabar and mercury cures killed others too, but the exact cause can't be checked.

reigns.hook: Huan Wen now dominates the court. The new emperor, Ai's brother Sima Yi, is about to learn how far the general will go to make himself look strong.

reigns.tagline: Deposed by a rumour about his bedroom
reigns.previously: Emperor Ai dies, poisoned by his own elixirs.
paragraphs: This Sima Yi shares a name, in English, with the grandfather of the whole dynasty, but nothing else. He was a quiet man, and Huan Wen was the real power. In 369 the general marched north against Former Yan and was badly beaten at Fangtou by the Yan prince Murong Chui. Huan Wen needed to win back his prestige.

So he went after the emperor. Early in 372 Huan Wen announced that the emperor was impotent, that his favourites had fathered the princes, and that he must go. The empress dowager signed. The boys were killed, and the emperor was sent away as Duke of Haixi. He lived another fourteen years in quiet retirement, drinking and keeping his head down, and died in 386.

claims.text: The charge that he was impotent and his sons were not his own was invented by Huan Wen.
claims.note: The Jin Shu says many people believed it was false. No one could prove either way, which was the point.

claims.text: Huan Wen said that if he couldn't leave a good name for a hundred generations, he could at least leave a bad one for ten thousand years.
claims.note: Quoted in the Jin Shu and the Shishuo Xinyu. A famous line, but it is the kind historians like to give a would-be usurper.

reigns.hook: Huan Wen picks the next emperor himself: an old, gentle prince who has spent his life talking philosophy. Everyone expects him to keep the seat warm for Huan Wen.

reigns.tagline: The philosopher-prince kept as a placeholder
reigns.previously: Huan Wen deposes the emperor on a rumour about his sons.
paragraphs: Sima Yu was the youngest son of the dynasty's founder, and he had been chancellor for decades. He was a star of "pure conversation", the elegant philosophical talk that fashionable southerners loved. He was not a fighter. Huan Wen made him emperor because he expected no trouble from him, and he got none.

Sima Yu spent his eight months as emperor in fear. When he fell ill in 372 he drafted a will that came close to handing Huan Wen the throne. Ministers led by Wang Tanzhi had it rewritten so that Huan Wen was only a regent. The emperor died, his ten-year-old son took the throne, and Huan Wen died the next year still asking for honours that the court kept finding reasons to delay.

claims.text: Wang Tanzhi tore up the draft will that would have let Huan Wen take the throne.
claims.note: From the Jin Shu. The dispute over the will is well attested; the dramatic tearing may be embroidered.

claims.text: A prophecy said Jin would end with someone called Changming, and he gave his son that very name before he heard it.
claims.note: Told in the Jin Shu. Later writers used it to explain what came after; it's almost certainly written backwards.

reigns.hook: A ten-year-old is emperor and Huan Wen is dead. Up north, Fu Jian of Former Qin has united almost everything. He is looking south.

reigns.tagline: He saw off the greatest invasion, then a bad joke
reigns.cameToPower: Succeeded his father as a child
reigns.previously: Emperor Jianwen dies. Huan Wen never gets the throne.
paragraphs: Sima Yao was a boy when he took the throne, and the great minister Xie An guided the court. In 383 Fu Jian of Former Qin came south with an enormous army, meaning to finish the Jin for good. At the Fei River, Xie An's nephew Xie Xuan and the tough northern Beifu troops smashed it. Fu Jian's empire fell apart within two years. The south was safe.

After that the emperor lost interest. He drank hard and handed the government to his brother Sima Daozi, whose cronies grew rich. In 396 he teased his favourite, Lady Zhang, that she was nearly thirty and he should find someone younger. That night he was smothered in his bed. No one was punished. The heir was his eldest son, who could barely function.

claims.text: Xie An was playing weiqi when the news of the Fei River came. He read it, said only that "the boys" had beaten the enemy, and went on playing.
claims.note: From the Jin Shu, which adds that he broke a clog in his hidden excitement. A famous scene, polished to show calm.

claims.text: Lady Zhang had her maids smother the emperor with a quilt after his joke about her age.
claims.note: The Jin Shu says so. Nobody investigated, which tells you how weak the court already was.

reigns.hook: The new emperor can't speak or tell hot from cold. Around him, the Jin's generals, princes and rebels are lining up to take what's left.

reigns.tagline: An emperor who could not speak, fought over for 22 years
reigns.previously: Emperor Xiaowu is smothered in his bed after a joke.
paragraphs: Sima Dezong could not look after himself, and everyone around him knew it. His uncle Sima Daozi ruled, badly. In 399 the Daoist leader Sun En raised a rebellion along the coast, raiding from island bases. That same year the monk Faxian left Chang'an on foot for India. In 402 Huan Xuan, son of Huan Wen, took Jiankang, killed Daozi's family and then made himself Emperor of Chu. The Jin emperor was moved aside but kept alive.

In 404 a Beifu officer named Liu Yu rose against Huan Xuan and beat him. He put the Jin emperor back on the throne and became the real ruler. Liu Yu won war after war, and in 417 he took Chang'an itself. Then, at the start of 419, the emperor was strangled in his palace. He was about 36.

claims.text: He could not speak and could not tell cold from heat or hunger from fullness.
claims.note: The Jin Shu says so plainly, and every account treats him as unable to rule. The exact condition is unknown.

claims.text: Liu Yu had him killed because a prophecy said two more emperors would follow Changming (his father), so he needed a second one before taking the throne.
claims.note: From the Jin Shu and Song Shu. The murder is accepted; the prophecy motive may be later colour.

reigns.hook: Liu Yu has the dead emperor's brother crowned. Everyone at court can count: one more Jin emperor, and the prophecy is fulfilled.

reigns.tagline: The last Jin emperor signed himself out
reigns.previously: Liu Yu has the helpless Emperor An strangled.
paragraphs: Sima Dewen was a devout Buddhist who knew exactly why he had been crowned. Liu Yu was the master of the south and needed one more Jin emperor before he could take the throne himself. In the summer of 420 Sima Dewen was asked to step down. He did it calmly and wrote out the abdication edict in his own hand. Liu Yu became the first emperor of the Song, and the Jin, founded in 266, was over.

Liu Yu did not let him live long. In 421 he sent a man with poisoned wine, who drank it himself rather than kill his old master. Then soldiers came. The former emperor refused the poison, saying his faith forbade suicide, and they smothered him with a quilt.

claims.text: He told his attendants that Jin had really been lost long ago under Huan Xuan, and Liu Yu had given it twenty more years, so he gave it up gladly.
claims.note: Told in the Jin Shu and Zizhi Tongjian. A gracious exit scene; how much he meant it, no one knows.

claims.text: He refused poison because Buddhism taught that a suicide would not be reborn as a human.
claims.note: From the Zizhi Tongjian. The killing on Liu Yu's orders is accepted; the details of his last words are not certain.

reigns.hook: Liu Yu's Song now rules the south. In the north, a teenage prince of the Tuoba clan is about to inherit the Northern Wei, and he intends to swallow everything above the Yangtze.

reigns.tagline: The horseman who conquered the north and banned the Buddha
reigns.previously: Liu Yu ends the Jin and founds the Song in the south.
paragraphs: The north now belonged to the Tuoba, a Xianbei clan from the steppe who had ruled as the Northern Wei since 386, with their capital at Pingcheng (Datong). Tuoba Tao came to the throne as a teenager and spent his life in the saddle. He took the Xia capital in 427, swallowed Northern Yan in 436 and finished off Northern Liang in 439. For the first time in over a century, one ruler held the whole north.

His chief adviser Cui Hao, a Chinese aristocrat, and the Daoist master Kou Qianzhi turned him against Buddhism. In 446, after weapons were found in a monastery at Chang'an, he ordered monks killed and images smashed across his lands. In 450 Cui Hao himself was executed with his whole clan. That year Tao rode south against the Song and reached the Yangtze opposite their capital before turning back.
His heir died in 451, hounded by the slanders of the eunuch Zong Ai. In March 452 Zong Ai, afraid the emperor would find him out, had him murdered.

claims.text: Cui Hao was destroyed because his official history of the Tuoba, carved on stone steles by a main road, told their humble and barbarous origins for all to read.
claims.note: The Wei Shu's account. Historians also see a clash between Cui Hao's Chinese aristocrats and the Xianbei nobles behind it.

claims.text: The 446 edict ordered every monk in the realm put to death.
claims.note: The edict is quoted in the Wei Shu's treatise on Buddhism and Daoism. The crown prince delayed it, so many monks escaped.

claims.text: Crown Prince Huang died of grief and fear after Zong Ai accused his men of crimes.
claims.note: Wei Shu and Zizhi Tongjian. The emperor is said to have regretted it when he learned the truth.

reigns.hook: The emperor is dead and Zong Ai holds the palace. He kills the prince the officials want and puts a younger son on the throne, a man he thinks he can control.

reigns.tagline: The eunuch's puppet who tried to cut his strings
reigns.cameToPower: Put up by the eunuch Zong Ai
reigns.previously: The eunuch Zong Ai murders Emperor Taiwu in his palace.
paragraphs: Tuoba Yu, Prince of Nan'an, was one of Taiwu's younger sons. He owed everything to the man who had just killed his father. Zong Ai had blocked the officials' choice by having that prince killed, and now he ran the court, handing out titles to himself and filling posts with his own men.

Yu soon tired of being a puppet and began to plot to take Zong Ai's power away. The eunuch struck first. Some eight months into the reign, Zong Ai had him killed while he was at a night-time sacrifice in the ancestral temple. A eunuch had now murdered two emperors in one year, and the court finally moved against him.

claims.text: Zong Ai had Tuoba Yu killed during a night-time ancestral sacrifice.
claims.note: Told in the Wei Shu and the Zizhi Tongjian. The setting is specific, but these are later histories written from the winners' side.

claims.text: When Zong Ai fell, his whole clan was put to death with him.
claims.note: Both main histories record the execution of his clan, the standard punishment for treason.

reigns.hook: Loyal guards and officials seize Zong Ai and put him to death. The throne goes to Taiwu's grandson Tuoba Jun, a boy of 12 whose own father died of fear.

reigns.tagline: The boy who brought the Buddhas back, carved in stone
reigns.cameToPower: Placed on the throne by loyal officials
reigns.previously: The eunuch Zong Ai kills his puppet emperor Tuoba Yu.
paragraphs: Tuoba Jun was the son of the crown prince Zong Ai had hounded to death. Once the eunuch was gone, the boy undid his grandfather's war on Buddhism. Monks came back, temples were rebuilt and a stone Buddha was carved in the emperor's own likeness.

The monk Tanyao then began cutting five colossal Buddhas into the sandstone cliffs at Yungang, west of Pingcheng. They're still there, the start of one of the great Buddhist sites of Asia. The Northern Wei also kept a grim old custom: when a son was named heir, his mother was made to die so she could never rule through him. Jun's heir lost his mother this way in 456.
Jun was a quiet ruler and his reign was mostly peaceful. In 465 he died, aged about 25, leaving a boy of about 10.

claims.text: The stone Buddha made in 452 had black stones set in its face and feet to match moles on the emperor's body.
claims.note: Recorded in the Wei Shu's treatise on Buddhism. Real enough as a record; whether the statue matched him is anyone's guess.

claims.text: Tanyao's five great Buddhas at Yungang stand for five Northern Wei emperors.
claims.note: A common modern reading, built on the Wei Shu's note that Buddha images were made for the emperors. No inscription names them.

claims.text: The heir's mother, Lady Li, was forced to die under the Tuoba custom.
claims.note: The Wei Shu records her death in 456 and the custom itself, which ran from the dynasty's founder until about 512.

reigns.hook: When Jun's belongings are burned at his funeral, his young widow Lady Feng throws herself into the flames. She's pulled out alive. Soon she'll be running the empire.

images.caption: Not a portrait: Cave 16 at Yungang, one of the five colossal caves the monk Tanyao began in his reign.
images.alt: Large carved stone Buddha in Cave 16 of the Yungang Grottoes near Datong

reigns.tagline: He quit the throne at 17 and still couldn't escape
reigns.previously: Emperor Wencheng dies at 25. His widow Lady Feng survives the fire.
paragraphs: Tuoba Hong was about 10 when he took the throne. A minister called Yifu Hun grabbed power at once, and within months Empress Dowager Feng had him killed and took the regency herself. Then in 467 the young emperor had a son, and she stepped back to raise the baby.

Hong did well while he ruled. The Song in the south fell into a civil war in 466, and its northern governors went over to Wei, handing him the lands north of the Huai River. But he clashed with his stepmother. In 470 he had her favourite, Li Yi, put to death.

In 471, aged 17, he gave up the throne. He wanted his uncle to have it, but the court objected, so it went to his son, aged four. As retired emperor he still led armies against the Rouran. He died in 476, aged 22.

claims.text: Empress Dowager Feng had him poisoned in revenge for Li Yi.
claims.note: The Wei Shu hints at it and later histories say it outright. Her power after his death was so great that few questioned it at the time.

claims.text: He first tried to hand the throne to his uncle, Tuoba Zitui, Prince of Jingzhao.
claims.note: Both the Wei Shu and the Zizhi Tongjian record the court's protest that a father's throne must pass to his son.

claims.text: He gave up the throne to devote himself to Buddhism and the Dao.
claims.note: His stated reason. Pressure from the empress dowager may matter more.

reigns.hook: The new emperor is a little boy of four. The real power is the woman who raised him, Empress Dowager Feng, and she has big plans for the Tuoba state.

images.caption: Not a portrait: carvings in Cave 7 at Yungang, one of the caves cut after 465 as the site grew under his family.

reigns.tagline: He made his own people dress, talk and eat Chinese
reigns.previously: Emperor Xianwen gives up the throne to his four-year-old son.
paragraphs: For his first 19 years, Empress Dowager Feng ruled. Under her came the equal-field system of 485, which handed out farmland by the number of mouths in a family, and new village heads to count every household. In 479 the Song in the south fell to a general who founded the Southern Qi. When Feng died in 490, the young emperor mourned her for years.

Then he set out to remake his people. In 493 he marched south from Pingcheng, saying he was going to war with Qi. At Luoyang, in heavy rain, his nobles begged him to stop. Fine, he said: then we stay here. Luoyang became the capital. He banned Xianbei dress, then Xianbei speech at court, married his family into Chinese noble clans and in 496 changed the royal surname from Tuoba to Yuan.
Many Xianbei hated it. His own heir tried to flee back north and was made to die in 497. In 499 the emperor fell ill on campaign against Qi and died at about 31.

claims.text: The march on Qi in 493 was a trick to get his nobles to Luoyang.
claims.note: The histories tell it that way. He may well have meant to fight too, but the scene in the rain is how they remember it.

claims.text: On his deathbed he ordered his empress, Feng Run, to be made to kill herself for her affair.
claims.note: Wei Shu and Zizhi Tongjian. The order was carried out after his death; the affair itself rests on palace accounts.

claims.text: The equal-field system began under his reign in 485.
claims.note: Recorded in the Wei Shu's treatise on food and money. The Sui and Tang later used versions of it.

reigns.hook: The emperor dies on the road home. His teenage son inherits a Chinese-style court, a new capital, and a mother's family that wants all the power.

reigns.tagline: The pious emperor whose uncle ran the court
reigns.previously: Emperor Xiaowen dies on campaign. His teenage son inherits.
paragraphs: Yuan Ke was shy and devout. He liked to lecture on Buddhist sutras himself. At first his uncles ran things. When one of them rebelled in 501, Ke turned to his mother's brother, Gao Zhao, who soon ran the court. In 508 Gao had the emperor's respected uncle Yuan Xie, the Prince of Pengcheng, forced to drink poison.

In 502 the southern Qi fell and a new dynasty, the Liang, took over. Wei and Liang fought along the Huai River, and in 507 a huge Wei army was smashed at Zhongli. At Longmen, south of Luoyang, the emperor paid for the Binyang caves in honour of his parents, with reliefs of the imperial couple and their courts.
His only surviving son was born in 510 to Lady Hu. Under the old custom she should have died. She didn't. In February 515 the emperor died, aged about 31.

claims.text: He spared Lady Hu from the custom of killing an heir's mother.
claims.note: The Wei Shu says so, and that she had prayed for a son despite the danger. The custom does seem to end with her.

claims.text: Gao Zhao had Yuan Xie poisoned with wine sent in the emperor's name.
claims.note: Recorded in the Wei Shu and Zizhi Tongjian. Yuan Xie's widow is said to have cried out that heaven would punish the Gao.

claims.text: The Binyang caves took 24 years and over 800,000 days of labour.
claims.note: The Wei Shu's figures. Only one of the three planned caves was finished under the Northern Wei.

reigns.hook: The emperor is dead and his heir is four. Gao Zhao rides back from a campaign to find the court turned against him. And Lady Hu, the mother who should have died, is about to rule.

reigns.tagline: His mother built the tallest pagoda and outlived him
reigns.previously: Emperor Xuanwu dies. His four-year-old son becomes emperor.
paragraphs: Gao Zhao was killed the moment he got back to Luoyang, and Lady Hu became regent. She was clever, strong-willed and spent like no one before her. In 516 she began the Yongning pagoda at Luoyang, a wooden tower of nine storeys said to be visible from miles away. In 518 she sent pilgrims to India for sutras.

In 520 her brother-in-law Yuan Cha and a eunuch locked her up and ran the empire for five years. Meanwhile the Six Garrisons, the old frontier forts full of neglected Xianbei soldiers, rose in revolt in 523–524. The north burned for years. Lady Hu got back in charge in 525, but she now ruled a crumbling state.
By 528 Xiaoming, now grown, hated her men. He secretly called in the warlord Erzhu Rong. In March he died suddenly, still in his teens.

claims.text: His mother had him poisoned to stop Erzhu Rong.
claims.note: The Wei Shu and Zizhi Tongjian point to her. With the timing, few doubt it, but no one saw it done.

claims.text: She then announced that his baby daughter was a son and made her emperor, before admitting the truth days later.
claims.note: Recorded in the Wei Shu and Zizhi Tongjian. The girl is sometimes counted as a ruler for a day or so.

claims.text: A monk called Bodhidharma said that in all his travels he had never seen anything like the Yongning pagoda.
claims.note: From Yang Xuanzhi's Record of the Buddhist Monasteries of Luoyang (547). Whether he's the Bodhidharma of Chan legend is unclear.

reigns.hook: The fake boy emperor is quietly replaced by a real one: a toddler. Erzhu Rong is already marching on Luoyang, and he's not coming to pay respects.

reigns.tagline: A toddler on the throne, for seven weeks
reigns.previously: Emperor Xiaoming dies suddenly. His mother is blamed.
paragraphs: Yuan Zhao was a great-grandson of Emperor Xiaowen, and about two years old. Empress Dowager Hu chose him because a toddler would leave her in charge. It didn't work. Erzhu Rong, chief of a powerful clan of northern horsemen, said the young emperor had been murdered and declared a new emperor of his own, Yuan Ziyou.

Luoyang's defences melted away. In May 528 Erzhu Rong's men took Empress Dowager Hu and the little boy to Heyin, on the banks of the Yellow River, and threw them both in. Then he called the court officials out to meet the new emperor and had his horsemen cut them down. Some two thousand died. The old Luoyang nobility was all but wiped out in a day.

claims.text: Empress Dowager Hu had shaved her head as a nun before she was drowned.
claims.note: Both the Wei Shu and the Zizhi Tongjian say she and the palace women took vows as the Erzhu approached.

claims.text: Over two thousand officials were killed at Heyin.
claims.note: The figure varies between sources, from about 1,300 to over 2,000. All agree it was a massacre of the court.

reigns.hook: Erzhu Rong's emperor enters a capital with no ministers left. Yuan Ziyou is about 21, owes everything to the man who did this, and is quietly working out how to kill him.

reigns.tagline: The puppet who killed his master with his own hands
reigns.previously: Erzhu Rong drowns the boy emperor and massacres the court at Heyin.
paragraphs: Yuan Ziyou was a grandson of Emperor Xianwen, and took Erzhu Rong's daughter as his empress. Rong stayed at his own base, Jinyang, and ran the empire from there. In 529 a rival Wei prince, Yuan Hao, came north with a small Liang army under Chen Qingzhi and actually took Luoyang. Xiaozhuang fled, and it took Erzhu Rong two months to put him back.

In autumn 530 Rong came to court. Xiaozhuang lured him into the palace with news that a crown prince had been born, and killed him there, striking the first blow himself. The Erzhu clan rose in fury and named a rival emperor, Yuan Ye. In January 531 Erzhu Zhao took Luoyang, carried Xiaozhuang off to Jinyang and strangled him in a Buddhist temple.

claims.text: Xiaozhuang hid a blade under his knee and stabbed Erzhu Rong himself.
claims.note: The Wei Shu and Zizhi Tongjian describe him striking first. Details like the hidden blade vary in the retelling.

claims.text: Before his death he prayed never again to be born a king.
claims.note: A line given in the histories, along with a short death poem. It makes a good ending, which is why it's suspect.

reigns.hook: With Xiaozhuang dead, the Erzhu have their own emperor already. But Yuan Ye is a distant cousin, and the Erzhu are already looking for someone more useful.

reigns.tagline: The rival emperor nobody needed for long
reigns.reignEnded: Set aside for a better puppet
reigns.previously: Emperor Xiaozhuang murders Erzhu Rong in the palace.
paragraphs: When Xiaozhuang killed Erzhu Rong, Rong's nephew Erzhu Zhao and cousin Erzhu Shilong needed an emperor of their own, fast. They picked Yuan Ye, Prince of Changguang, a minor member of the imperial clan, and proclaimed him at Changzi in November 530.

With him as their banner, Erzhu Zhao swept down on Luoyang and seized Xiaozhuang. But once the rival was dead, Yuan Ye had served his purpose. The Erzhu thought him too distant from the main line to look like a real emperor. In spring 531 he was made to step down and given the lesser title of Prince of Donghai. When the general Gao Huan took Luoyang the next year, Yuan Ye was put to death.

claims.text: He was dropped because his descent from earlier emperors was too remote.
claims.note: The Wei Shu and Zizhi Tongjian both give this as the Erzhu's reason.

claims.text: Erzhu Zhao's men looted Luoyang when they took it.
claims.note: Recorded in the histories and in Yang Xuanzhi's account of the city's monasteries.

reigns.hook: The Erzhu need a new face. They find a prince who hasn't spoken a word in eight years.

reigns.tagline: He played mute for eight years, then spoke up
reigns.previously: The Erzhu set aside Yuan Ye as too remote a relative.
paragraphs: Yuan Gong was a grandson of Emperor Xianwen who had kept his head down through the bloody 520s by pretending to be mute. The Erzhu liked the sound of a silent emperor. When he finally spoke, people took it as a sign from heaven, and he took the throne in 531.

But the Erzhu clan were hated, and one of their own officers, Gao Huan, a northerner from the garrisons, turned on them. He set up his own emperor, Yuan Lang, and in 532 beat the Erzhu armies at Hanling. The Erzhu fell apart. Gao Huan entered Luoyang, deposed both Yuan Gong and his own man Yuan Lang, and had Yuan Gong poisoned soon after.

claims.text: Yuan Gong pretended to be mute for about eight years to stay out of danger.
claims.note: The Wei Shu tells it. It fits the times, but it's also the sort of story told to explain an unlikely emperor.

claims.text: At Hanling, Gao Huan beat a far bigger Erzhu army.
claims.note: The histories give Gao Huan fewer than 30,000 men against about 200,000. The numbers are almost certainly inflated.

reigns.hook: Gao Huan is master of Luoyang. He picks a new emperor, a young prince called Yuan Xiu, and marries him to his own daughter. What could go wrong?

reigns.tagline: He ran away from one warlord, straight into another
reigns.previously: Gao Huan beats the Erzhu at Hanling and takes Luoyang.
paragraphs: Yuan Xiu was a grandson of Emperor Xiaowen. Gao Huan made him emperor and his daughter empress, then went back to his base at Jinyang to rule from there. Xiaowu wanted none of it. He built up his own guard and looked west, to the general Yuwen Tai in the Wei River valley around Chang'an.

In 534 the break came. Xiaowu mustered troops at Luoyang as if to attack Gao Huan, then lost his nerve and fled west to Yuwen Tai. Gao Huan put a boy on the throne and moved the court to Ye. Now there were two Wei emperors: Eastern Wei under Gao Huan and Western Wei under Yuwen Tai. Xiaowu soon learned his new protector was no softer. Early in 535 he was dead, poisoned on Yuwen Tai's orders.

claims.text: He fell out with Yuwen Tai over his affair with his cousin, Princess Pingyuan, whom Yuwen Tai had killed.
claims.note: The Zhou Shu and Zizhi Tongjian tell it. Yuwen Tai had plenty of other reasons to want an independent emperor gone.

claims.text: The Northern Wei split into Eastern and Western Wei in 534.
claims.note: From this point two rival courts, at Ye and Chang'an, each claimed to be the true Wei.

reigns.hook: Yuwen Tai needs a new emperor of his own. He picks Yuan Baoju, a prince with no army and no illusions, and settles in to fight Gao Huan for the whole north.

reigns.tagline: A puppet in Chang'an while two strongmen fight
reigns.cameToPower: Picked by the general Yuwen Tai
reigns.previously: Emperor Xiaowu dies in Chang'an, poisoned. Yuwen Tai needs an emperor.
paragraphs: Yuan Baoju was a grandson of Emperor Xiaowen, so he had the right blood and no army. Yuwen Tai put him on the throne at Chang'an in 535. From now on there were two Wei emperors: this one in the west, and Gao Huan's boy emperor at Ye in the east. Each strongman ruled; each emperor signed. In 537 Yuwen Tai, badly outnumbered, ambushed Gao Huan's army at Shayuan and smashed it.

The steppe mattered too. To buy peace with the Rouran nomads, the emperor set aside his empress, Lady Yifu, and married their khan's daughter. When the Rouran raided anyway, he ordered Lady Yifu to kill herself. In 546 Gao Huan threw everything at the fortress of Yubi and failed. He died early the next year, and his general Hou Jing defected, ending up with the Liang in the south.

Hou Jing then turned on his new master, took the Liang capital Jiankang, and the old Emperor Wu of Liang died his prisoner in 549. In 550 the Gao family dropped the pretence in the east and made themselves emperors of Northern Qi. Yuwen Tai kept his puppet and built up a new army of farmer-soldiers. In 551 Emperor Wen died, aged about 44.

claims.text: The Rouran raid of 540 was blamed on the ex-empress Lady Yifu, and the emperor ordered her death to appease them.
claims.note: Told in the Bei Shi. That she was forced to die is solid; the reasoning reads like court gossip.

claims.text: Lady Yifu was buried in a cave at Maijishan, the Buddhist cliff site in Gansu.
claims.note: The Bei Shi says she was entombed in a cave there; which cave held her is an identification by modern scholars.

claims.text: Emperor Wu of Liang starved to death as Hou Jing's prisoner.
claims.note: The histories say he was refused food and water at the end, but he was 85 and already ill.

reigns.hook: The emperor is dead. His son Yuan Qin takes his place, married to Yuwen Tai's own daughter. He hates his father-in-law anyway.

reigns.tagline: The emperor who plotted against his father-in-law
reigns.previously: Emperor Wen dies. Yuwen Tai still holds the real power.
paragraphs: Yuan Qin had a strange marriage. His wife was a daughter of Yuwen Tai, the man who ran his empire. Yuwen Tai treated the throne as a rubber stamp. When a Yuan prince, Yuan Lie, plotted against him in 552, he had him killed, and the young emperor took it personally.

Outside the palace the map was changing fast. In 552 the Turks under Bumin threw off their Rouran masters and became the new power on the steppe; Western Wei had already sent them a bride. In the south Hou Jing was hunted down and killed. In 553 Western Wei's general Yuchi Jiong marched into Sichuan and took Chengdu from the feuding Liang princes.
The emperor wanted Yuwen Tai dead, and talked about it. Word got out. Early in 554 Yuwen Tai deposed him and later had him poisoned. History calls him Fei, which simply means "the deposed".

claims.text: Yuan Qin plotted to kill Yuwen Tai because Yuwen had executed his kinsman Yuan Lie.
claims.note: The Bei Shi and Zizhi Tongjian give this motive; both drew on records kept by Yuwen Tai's own successors.

claims.text: He was given no proper posthumous title: Fei just means "the deposed".
claims.note: The Bei Shi lists him that way, as later Chinese histories did for other emperors who lost the throne.

reigns.hook: Yuwen Tai needs another Yuan face for the throne. He picks the deposed emperor's teenage brother, then sends his army south.

images.caption: Not a portrait: a Western Wei stone beast dated 551, the year he came to the throne.
images.alt: Carved stone animal sculpture from the Western Wei, displayed in the Forest of Steles museum, Xi'an

reigns.tagline: The last Wei emperor, a footnote to a regent
reigns.reignEnded: Forced to abdicate to Yuwen Jue
reigns.previously: Yuwen Tai deposes the emperor who plotted to kill him.
paragraphs: Yuan Kuo was about 17 and did what he was told. Late in 554 Yuwen Tai's army stormed Jiangling on the Yangtze, the capital of Emperor Yuan of Liang. Before he surrendered, the Liang emperor set fire to his library. He was killed, and tens of thousands of his people were marched north to Chang'an as captives. Western Wei left a puppet Liang emperor at Jiangling.

In the same year the Yuan family were told to take back their old Xianbei surname, Tuoba. Yuwen Tai also handed out Xianbei names to his Chinese generals. He was building a new state on ancient Zhou rituals, with six ministries named after an old classic. Then in 556 he died on a journey, aged about 50.

His nephew Yuwen Hu took charge for Yuwen Tai's teenage son. Early in 557 the emperor was made to step down in the boy's favour, and he was killed soon after. In the south a general named Chen Baxian ended the Liang the same year and founded the Chen.

claims.text: Emperor Yuan of Liang burned some 140,000 scrolls before Jiangling fell, saying that all his reading had brought him to this.
claims.note: The burning is well attested; the number and his bitter words come from later histories and vary between them.

claims.text: The Yuan imperial family were ordered back to the surname Tuoba in 554.
claims.note: Recorded in the Zhou Shu and Bei Shi, part of Yuwen Tai's return to Xianbei names.

reigns.hook: A 15-year-old son of Yuwen Tai takes the throne and calls himself the Heavenly King of Zhou. His cousin Yuwen Hu holds the reins, and the boy wants them.

reigns.tagline: A boy king who tried to sack his cousin
reigns.reignEnded: Deposed and killed by Yuwen Hu
reigns.previously: The last Western Wei emperor steps down for Yuwen Tai's son.
paragraphs: Yuwen Jue was Yuwen Tai's heir because his mother was a Wei princess. In 557 he took the throne of a new dynasty, Zhou, using the old title "Heavenly King" from China's ancient past. The real ruler was his cousin Yuwen Hu, who had stepped in when Yuwen Tai died.

Some of Yuwen Tai's old generals resented Yuwen Hu. One, Zhao Gui, plotted against him and was executed. Another, the great general Dugu Xin, was forced to kill himself. The boy king then built his own little plot with a few guardsmen. Yuwen Hu found out, deposed him and had him killed. He was 15 and had reigned about eight months.

claims.text: Dugu Xin was father-in-law to an emperor of three dynasties: Zhou, Sui and Tang.
claims.note: The Zhou Shu and Sui Shu record his daughters as the wives of Yuwen Yu of Zhou, Yang Jian of Sui and Li Bing, father of the Tang founder.

claims.text: Dugu Xin was so admired that when he rode home with his hat askew, the whole city wore its hats askew next day.
claims.note: From the Zhou Shu. A charming story that tells you about his fame more than about his hat.

reigns.hook: Yuwen Hu has killed one cousin. Now he needs another. He picks the boy's elder half-brother, a quiet, bookish man who seems safe.

images.caption: Not a portrait: the 26-sided jet seal of Dugu Xin, the great general forced to kill himself in this reign.
images.alt: Small black faceted seal shaped like a ball with many square and triangular faces, each carved with characters

reigns.tagline: The bookish emperor and the poisoned cakes
reigns.cameToPower: Chosen by the regent Yuwen Hu
reigns.reignEnded: Poisoned, it is said, by Yuwen Hu
reigns.previously: Yuwen Hu deposes and kills the boy king Xiaomin.
paragraphs: Yuwen Yu was Yuwen Tai's eldest son but his mother was a concubine, so he had been passed over. He was clever, well read and liked by officials. His empress was Dugu Xin's eldest daughter. In 559 he dropped the old title of Heavenly King and called himself emperor, the first Zhou ruler to do so. Yuwen Hu even offered to hand back most of the government.

That was the danger. An emperor who could actually govern was no use to Yuwen Hu. In 560 the emperor fell suddenly ill after eating and died at about 26. On his deathbed he named his younger brother Yuwen Yong as heir. Across the border, Northern Qi had its own troubles: its drunken, violent founder Gao Yang had died in 559.

claims.text: Yuwen Hu had a cook put poison in the emperor's sugar cakes.
claims.note: The Zhou Shu says so. It was written after Yuwen Hu's fall, by people with every reason to blame him.

claims.text: On his deathbed the emperor dictated his own will, naming his brother.
claims.note: The will survives in the Zhou Shu, which quotes it at length.

reigns.hook: Yuwen Hu has now outlived two emperors. The third is 17, quiet and polite. He is also waiting.

images.caption: Not a portrait: a Buddha carved under the Northern Zhou, now in the Forest of Steles at Xi'an.
images.alt: Stone Buddha statue from the Northern Zhou, displayed in the Beilin Stone Museum, Xi'an

reigns.tagline: Waited 12 years, struck once, then took the north
reigns.cameToPower: Named in his dying brother's will
reigns.previously: Emperor Ming dies, poisoned, it is said. His brother Yong inherits.
paragraphs: For twelve years Yuwen Yong let his cousin Yuwen Hu run everything and never complained. In 572 he struck. He asked Yuwen Hu to read a lecture against drink to the empress dowager, then hit him from behind with his jade tablet. A eunuch and the emperor's brother finished the job. At last the state was his.

He ran it hard. In 574 he banned both Buddhism and Daoism, closed monasteries and sent monks and nuns back to farm and pay tax. Then he went after Northern Qi, rotten under the young Gao Wei. In 577 his armies took the Qi capital at Ye, and the north was one again. In 578 he marched against the Turks, fell ill and died at 35.

claims.text: He struck Yuwen Hu with his jade tablet while Hu was reading aloud to the empress dowager.
claims.note: From the Zhou Shu, written by the winners. The killing is certain; the stage-managed details may be polished.

claims.text: Gao Wei, the last Qi emperor, dragged his favourite Feng Xiaolian along on campaign and lost battles waiting for her.
claims.note: Told in the Bei Qi Shu and Bei Shi. Later poets made her a byword for a ruler's ruin.

claims.text: He married Ashina, daughter of the Turkish khan Mughan, in 568 after years of haggling.
claims.note: The Zhou Shu records the match. Her seal was found when their shared tomb near Xianyang was dug in the 1990s.

reigns.hook: The emperor is dead at 35. His heir is his eldest son Yun, whom he beat for drinking and watched like a hawk. Yun has been waiting too.

images.caption: From the Thirteen Emperors Scroll attributed to Yan Liben, painted less than a century after his death.

reigns.tagline: Five empresses, a big stick and no restraint
reigns.previously: Emperor Wu dies on campaign at 35. His eldest son inherits.
paragraphs: Yuwen Yun had grown up afraid of his father. The moment he was emperor he relaxed. He had his uncle Yuwen Xian, the best general in the land, strangled. He gave himself five empresses at once, a thing never seen before. Officials who displeased him were beaten with his "heavenly staff", up to 120 strokes a time.

In 579, after less than a year, he handed the throne to his five-year-old son and named himself Heavenly Emperor. He kept all the power and lost interest in using it. He partly lifted his father's ban on Buddhism, built palaces and partied. His chief empress, Yang Lihua, was the daughter of a powerful general named Yang Jian.
In June 580 he fell ill on an outing and died at about 21. Two courtiers forged an order putting Yang Jian in charge of the government.

claims.text: Touching the scars from his father's beatings, he said, "Old man, you died too late."
claims.note: Told in the Tang-era histories and the Zizhi Tongjian. It sounds like him, but nobody can check.

claims.text: He threatened to kill Empress Yang Lihua until her mother begged at the palace gate for her life.
claims.note: Told in the Zhou Shu and Sui Shu. Her mother, Dugu Qieluo, was Yang Jian's formidable wife.

reigns.hook: The Heavenly Emperor is dead and his son is six. Yang Jian, father of the boy's stepmother, has the seals. Not everyone will accept that.

reigns.tagline: The child who signed away his dynasty
reigns.reignEnded: Gave the throne to Yang Jian
reigns.previously: Emperor Xuan dies. Yang Jian takes over the government for the boy.
paragraphs: Yuwen Chan was a little boy on a throne his father had dumped on him. After his father died in 580, Yang Jian ruled in his name. The old Zhou general Yuchi Jiong rose at Ye in the east, and others joined him. Yang Jian's general Wei Xiaokuan crushed him in about two months. Yuchi Jiong killed himself and the city of Ye was razed.

One by one, the Yuwen princes were called to Chang'an and killed. On 4 March 581 the boy handed the throne to Yang Jian, who named his new dynasty Sui. The child was made a duke and killed a few months later. Yang Jian then had the rest of the Yuwen family wiped out.

claims.text: Yang Lihua, the boy's stepmother and Yang Jian's own daughter, was furious at her father's takeover.
claims.note: The Zhou Shu and Sui Shu both say so. She lived on under Sui, a reminder of the dynasty her father ended.

claims.text: The Chen emperor's song "Jade Tree Flowers in the Back Courtyard" became a byword for music that loses a kingdom.
claims.note: Tang poets made it one. The song is real; blaming a dynasty's fall on it is moralising after the event.

reigns.hook: Yang Jian has the north and a new dynasty, Sui. Across the Yangtze, the Chen crown prince Chen Shubao writes poems for his favourites. Soon he'll be emperor, and the river is all that protects him.

reigns.tagline: He reunited China and was terrified of his wife
reigns.cameToPower: Took the throne from a boy
reigns.previously: The boy Emperor Jing of Zhou hands the throne to Yang Jian.
paragraphs: Yang Jian came from a northern noble family of mixed Chinese and Xianbei blood. In 581 he took the throne, founded the Sui and built a new capital, Daxing, beside old Chang'an. In 589 his armies crossed the Yangtze and took the Chen capital. For the first time in nearly 300 years, north and south were one again.

Then he got to work. New law codes, a census, the equal-field system handing out land, and huge granaries against famine. He started recruiting some officials by examination rather than birth, and began the canal works his son would finish. He was stingy, suspicious and tireless.

At home, Empress Dugu was the boss. She also helped persuade him to drop his heir Yang Yong in favour of the second son, Yang Guang, who was careful to look modest. In 604 the emperor fell ill at his summer palace and died.

claims.text: Empress Dugu made him promise to have no children by any other woman.
claims.note: The Sui Shu and Zizhi Tongjian tell it. All his sons were hers, which fits, but the vow itself is a good story.

claims.text: When she had a palace girl he'd slept with killed, he rode off alone into the hills and his ministers had to fetch him back.
claims.note: Told in the Zizhi Tongjian, with the emperor complaining that the Son of Heaven had no freedom.

claims.text: Yang Guang had his father murdered on his sickbed.
claims.note: Some accounts say so, but they come from the Tang, who wanted Yang Guang to look as bad as possible. Others just say illness.

reigns.hook: The old emperor is dead, perhaps helped along. Yang Guang takes the throne with grand plans: a new capital, a canal across China and a war he cannot lose.

reigns.tagline: He dug the Grand Canal and lost everything in Korea
reigns.previously: Emperor Wen dies at his summer palace, perhaps murdered.
paragraphs: Yang Guang thought big. He built a new eastern capital at Luoyang. He drove the Grand Canal through from the Yellow River to the Yangtze between 605 and 611, using vast gangs of forced labour. Then he sailed it, on great dragon-boat progresses south to Jiangdu (Yangzhou), with a flotilla of staggering size.

His downfall was Korea. Three times, in 612, 613 and 614, he sent huge armies against the kingdom of Goguryeo. In 612 an army was cut to pieces at the Salsu River. Conscription and taxes drove the empire to revolt, and rebels sprang up everywhere.

The emperor retreated south to Jiangdu and gave up on the north. In April 618 his own guards, led by Yuwen Huaji, turned on him and strangled him. The Tang who came next gave him the posthumous name Yang, an insult, and made him the model of a bad last emperor.

claims.text: Near the end he looked in a mirror and asked who would cut off such a fine head.
claims.note: Recorded in the Zizhi Tongjian, written centuries later. Perfect deathbed drama, and that's a reason for caution.

claims.text: His dragon-boat flotilla stretched for miles along the canal.
claims.note: The histories describe thousands of boats. The exact size grows in the telling.

claims.text: He was a monster of vanity and cruelty.
claims.note: The image comes from Tang historians. Modern historians note his canal and capital served China for centuries.

reigns.hook: Even before the emperor dies, his cousin Li Yuan has taken Chang'an and crowned a 12-year-old grandson of his, Yang You. It's the Sui, in name only.

images.caption: From the Thirteen Emperors Scroll attributed to Yan Liben, a Tang painter working for the dynasty that replaced him.

reigns.tagline: A boy emperor kept warm for the Tang
reigns.cameToPower: Set up by Li Yuan in Chang'an
reigns.previously: Emperor Yang is strangled by his own guards at Jiangdu.
paragraphs: Yang You was the son of Emperor Yang's eldest boy, the crown prince who died young in 606. When the emperor sailed south for good in 616, the child, as Prince of Dai, was left as the face of Sui authority in Chang'an. In late 617 Li Yuan's rebel army stormed the city.

Li Yuan did not kill the boy. He crowned him. On 18 December 617 Yang You became emperor, and his grandfather, still alive in the south, was politely 'promoted' to retired emperor. Li Yuan made himself chancellor and Prince of Tang, which gave him every power the throne had while he kept up the look of a loyal Sui servant.

In the spring of 618 news came that Emperor Yang had been murdered. The pretence was no longer needed. On 12 June the boy handed over the throne, and six days later Li Yuan was emperor of the Tang. Yang You was made a duke and died the next year, aged about 14.

claims.text: Li Yuan had Yang You quietly killed in 619.
claims.note: The Tang histories record only his death and Li Yuan's show of mourning. Later historians suspect murder because a living Sui heir was a danger; no source proves it.

claims.text: Li Yuan named the absent Emperor Yang 'retired emperor' without asking him.
claims.note: Recorded in the Sui and Tang histories and the Zizhi Tongjian. Emperor Yang never accepted it.

reigns.hook: In Chang'an the Sui is finished. But in Luoyang, the eastern capital, officials loyal to the old dynasty have their own grandson of Emperor Yang, and they crown him too.

images.caption: A gold necklace from the Chang'an tomb of Li Jingxun, a little girl related to the Sui royal family who died in 608. Not a portrait of Yang You.
images.alt: Gold necklace set with pearls and coloured gemstones, with a large blue pendant

reigns.tagline: He founded the Tang, then his sons fought over it
reigns.previously: Wang Shichong takes the throne in Luoyang and kills the last Sui boy.
paragraphs: Li Yuan, Duke of Tang, was the Sui garrison commander at Taiyuan, and Emperor Yang's cousin through their mothers. In 617, with the empire in flames, he rebelled and marched on Chang'an. He put a Sui child on the throne as a puppet, and when news came that Emperor Yang was dead, he proclaimed his own Tang dynasty in June 618.

His sons did much of the fighting, crushing rival warlords one by one. Even his daughter, Princess Pingyang, raised her own army. But the crown prince Li Jiancheng and his brilliant younger brother Li Shimin grew to hate each other.

On 2 July 626, Li Shimin ambushed his brothers Jiancheng and Yuanji at the Xuanwu Gate of the palace and killed them both. Days later the old emperor made Shimin his heir. In September he stepped down and lived on as retired emperor until 635.

claims.text: It was Li Shimin, not his father, who pushed for the rebellion of 617.
claims.note: The official histories say so, but they were written under Li Shimin, who had good reason to play up his own role.

claims.text: Princess Pingyang raised an army of tens of thousands to help her father.
claims.note: The Old Book of Tang records her army; she was later given a military funeral. The exact numbers are less certain.

claims.text: Li Shimin shot his elder brother with his own bow at the Xuanwu Gate.
claims.note: That's the official account. Since the winner controlled the record, the claim that his brothers struck first is suspect.

reigns.hook: Two princes lie dead at the palace gate. The man who killed them is about to become the emperor China remembers as one of its very best.

reigns.tagline: The last Sui emperor, trapped in Luoyang
reigns.reignEnded: Forced to abdicate to Wang Shichong
reigns.previously: Yang You hands the throne to Li Yuan, who founds the Tang.
paragraphs: Yang Tong, Prince of Yue, was Yang You's elder brother. Emperor Yang had left him in charge of Luoyang, the great eastern capital, which spent 617 besieged by the rebel Li Mi. When word of the emperor's murder arrived, the city's officials made Yang Tong emperor on 22 June 618. His era name was Huangtai.

The court was a nest of rivals. The general Wang Shichong seized control that summer and killed his chief rival among the ministers. In the autumn he beat Li Mi outside the city, and Li Mi fled to the Tang. From then on Wang ruled Luoyang, and the boy emperor signed what he was given.

In May 619 Wang made Yang Tong hand him the throne and declared his own state of Zheng. A month or so later he sent poison. Two years after that Li Shimin took Luoyang, and Wang Shichong was killed on his way into exile.

claims.text: Before drinking the poison, Yang Tong prayed never again to be born into a ruling family. When it worked too slowly, he was strangled.
claims.note: From the Zizhi Tongjian, written 450 years later. The death is certain; the last words may be a moralist's touch.

claims.text: Yang Tong was the Sui's last emperor.
claims.note: After his abdication no Yang held the throne. A Sui pretender in the north, backed by the Turks, lasted until 630 but never ruled China.

reigns.hook: Luoyang has fallen to a usurper. But go back to June 618 and look west. In Chang'an, Li Yuan has just made himself emperor of a brand-new dynasty: the Tang.

images.caption: Wang Shichong, who deposed Yang Tong, as imagined in a 1783 edition of a Tang adventure novel. No portrait of Yang Tong exists.

reigns.tagline: A brother-killer who became the model emperor
reigns.cameToPower: Killed his brothers; father stepped down
reigns.previously: Li Shimin kills his brothers at the Xuanwu Gate. Gaozu steps down.
paragraphs: Li Shimin started with blood on his hands and went on to be one of China's most admired emperors. Part of the trick was listening. Wei Zheng, who had once served his murdered brother, became his conscience and told him off to his face, hundreds of times. When Wei died in 643, the emperor said he had lost the mirror that showed him his faults.

He was a soldier too. In 630 his armies crushed the Eastern Turks, and steppe chiefs hailed him as "Heavenly Khagan". The monk Xuanzang slipped off to India in 629 and came home in 645 to an emperor's welcome. A new law code set the pattern for centuries. His invasion of Goguryeo in 645 failed.
His family was another matter. In 643 his crown prince, Li Chengqian, was caught plotting and deposed. Taizong chose his gentle ninth son, Li Zhi. He died in July 649.

claims.text: Taizong hid a pet hawk in his robe when Wei Zheng came in, and Wei talked so long the bird suffocated.
claims.note: A Tang anecdote, not in the main histories. It sums up their relationship a bit too neatly.

claims.text: Wei Zheng criticised him to his face more than 200 times.
claims.note: The figure comes from the Tang histories, which counted his memorials. Taizong also polished his own image as a listener.

claims.text: He may have been killed by an elixir of long life from an Indian alchemist.
claims.note: The histories say he took such drugs late in life. Whether they killed him is guesswork.

reigns.hook: The new emperor Li Zhi is mild and easily led. And among his late father's concubines, now shaved and sent to a nunnery, is a young woman named Wu Zhao.

reigns.tagline: The emperor who shared his throne with Wu Zhao
reigns.previously: Taizong dies. His mild ninth son Li Zhi takes the throne.
paragraphs: When Taizong died, his young concubines were sent off to a Buddhist convent. One of them, Wu Zhao, did not stay there. Within a few years she was back in the palace as a consort of the new emperor. She rose past Empress Wang and the favourite Consort Xiao, and in 655 Gaozong made her empress. Both rivals were soon dead.

From about 660 the emperor suffered strokes or failing eyesight, and Wu ran government beside him. Courtiers called the pair the "two sages". Abroad, these were the Tang's widest years. Allied with the Korean kingdom of Silla, Tang armies destroyed Baekje in 660 and Goguryeo in 668.
Gaozong died at Luoyang in December 683. His son Li Xian became emperor as Zhongzong. Everyone knew who held the real power.

claims.text: Wu smothered her own baby daughter and blamed Empress Wang.
claims.note: Found in later histories, hostile to Wu. The baby's death is likely; the murder is not proven.

claims.text: She had her fallen rivals' hands and feet cut off and threw them into a wine vat.
claims.note: The Tang histories tell it; most historians accept the women were killed but treat the details with caution.

claims.text: Gaozong was too ill to rule from about 660.
claims.note: The histories describe dizziness and failing sight. How much he was sidelined and how much he chose to share power is debated.

reigns.hook: Gaozong is dead. His son Li Xian takes the throne as Zhongzong, but his mother is now empress dowager, and she has no intention of handing over the seals.

reigns.tagline: Six weeks on the throne, undone by one careless boast
reigns.previously: Gaozong dies at Luoyang. Wu Zhao's son Li Xian is the new emperor.
paragraphs: Li Xian was the third son Wu Zhao had borne Gaozong, and heir only because his two elder brothers had died or been deposed. His father died in December 683 and he took the throne in January 684 as Zhongzong. On paper he was emperor. In practice his mother was now empress dowager, and every order still went through her.

Zhongzong wanted a court of his own. He tried to make his wife's father, Wei Xuanzhen, a chief minister, and when the chancellor Pei Yan objected he lost his temper. Pei Yan went straight to the empress dowager. On 26 February 684 she called the court together, had Zhongzong pulled from the throne and demoted him to Prince of Luling. He was sent into exile in the hills of Hubei with his wife, Lady Wei, for the next fourteen years.

claims.text: Zhongzong shouted that he could give the whole empire to his father-in-law if he liked.
claims.note: Both Tang histories report the outburst and Pei Yan's report of it. They were written long after, by courts that had their own reasons to belittle him.

claims.text: In exile he promised Lady Wei that if they ever got back, she could do whatever she wanted.
claims.note: Told in the Tang histories to explain his later indulgence of her. It reads like hindsight.

reigns.hook: Zhongzong is gone after six weeks. His younger brother Li Dan gets the throne next, but this time Wu Zhao makes sure the new emperor never even gets to speak.

reigns.tagline: An emperor kept in a side palace for six years
reigns.reignEnded: Gave the throne to his mother
reigns.previously: Wu Zhao deposes Zhongzong and sends him into exile.
paragraphs: Li Dan was Wu Zhao's youngest son, and he learned fast from his brother's fall. He was proclaimed emperor the day after Zhongzong went, then shut away in a separate palace. He was not allowed to take part in government. His mother sat in the audience hall and gave the orders herself.

In 684 the official Xu Jingye raised a revolt at Yangzhou in the name of the exiled Zhongzong. The poet Luo Binwang wrote him a scorching manifesto against the empress. The rising was crushed within about two months. Wu then built a regime of informers and secret trials, and the Tang princes who rose against her in 688 were wiped out.
In 690 the courtiers and thousands of petitioners asked Wu to take the throne. Ruizong joined in and asked to take her surname. She accepted. He became her heir, renamed Wu Dan.

claims.text: Luo Binwang's manifesto so impressed Wu that she asked why such a talent had been left unused.
claims.note: A favourite anecdote in the Tang histories and later collections. The manifesto itself survives and is still read.

claims.text: In 693 Wu had Ruizong's wife and his consort Lady Dou, Li Longji's mother, killed after a maid accused them of witchcraft.
claims.note: The Tang histories say the two women vanished after paying their respects to Wu, and their bodies were never found. Ruizong dared not ask about them.

reigns.hook: Ruizong steps down without a fight. His mother is about to do something no woman in China has ever done: take the throne in her own name.

reigns.tagline: The only woman ever to be emperor of China
reigns.cameToPower: Took the throne from her son
reigns.reignEnded: Forced out by a palace coup
reigns.previously: Ruizong, a puppet for six years, offers his mother the throne.
paragraphs: After Gaozong died, Wu deposed her son Zhongzong after about six weeks in 684 and made his brother Ruizong a puppet. A revolt led by Xu Jingye was crushed. In 690 she stopped pretending. She took the throne in her own name and called her dynasty Zhou. She was the only woman in Chinese history to reign as emperor.

She ruled by fear and talent. Bronze boxes invited anyone to inform on anyone, and cruel officials like Lai Junchen and Zhou Xing ran the terror. She invented new characters, including one for her own name. She promoted the exams and brought clever outsiders into government. She poured money into Buddhism, including the giant Vairocana Buddha at Longmen.

Old age brought new favourites, the Zhang brothers. In February 705, with Wu about 80, officers stormed the palace, killed the Zhangs and made her give the throne back to Zhongzong. She died that December.

claims.text: Zhou Xing was asked how to make a stubborn suspect talk. "Put him in a jar and heat it," he said. "Please step into the jar," came the reply.
claims.note: A famous anecdote, now a Chinese proverb. Zhou Xing did fall from power, but the scene is too neat.

claims.text: The face of the great Vairocana Buddha at Longmen was modelled on Wu's own.
claims.note: A popular modern story. She did fund the carving with her own money, according to an inscription there.

claims.text: Her stele at the Qianling tomb was left blank.
claims.note: It still stands uninscribed. Why is unknown: modesty, confidence, or a verdict nobody dared write.

reigns.hook: Zhongzong is back on the throne he lost 21 years ago. But his wife and daughter have watched Wu closely, and they think they could do it too.

reigns.tagline: Back on the throne, and ruled by his wife
reigns.previously: Officers storm the palace. Wu Zetian gives Zhongzong back the throne.
paragraphs: Zhongzong had spent fourteen years in exile, recalled in 698 as his mother's heir. In February 705 the minister Zhang Jianzhi and his officers killed Wu's favourites, the Zhang brothers, and forced her to hand over. Zhongzong was emperor again, and the dynasty was called Tang once more.

He let his wife rule beside him. Empress Wei sat behind a screen at audiences, as Wu once had. She allied with Wu's nephew Wu Sansi, and the coup leaders were exiled and killed. Their daughter Princess Anle sold offices and wanted to be heir. In 707 the crown prince Li Chongjun rose, killed Wu Sansi and stormed the palace. Zhongzong appealed to the rebels from a gate tower, they turned on their leaders, and the prince was killed in flight.
On 3 July 710 Zhongzong died suddenly at 53. Empress Wei kept it quiet for a few days while she placed her men.

claims.text: Princess Anle asked to be made "imperial heir daughter", a crown princess.
claims.note: Reported in the Tang histories. No such title had ever existed, and her father laughed it off rather than granting it.

claims.text: Empress Wei and Princess Anle poisoned Zhongzong with a cake.
claims.note: The Tang histories say so, but they were written for the side that killed the two women soon after.

reigns.hook: Zhongzong is dead and Empress Wei holds the palace. She puts his teenage son on the throne and plans to rule through him. She has forgotten about her husband's nephew, Li Longji.

reigns.tagline: A teenage puppet who lasted seventeen days
reigns.previously: Zhongzong dies suddenly. Empress Wei keeps his death quiet for days.
paragraphs: Li Chongmao was Zhongzong's youngest son, born to a concubine. That made him useful to Empress Wei. With her husband dead she made the boy emperor and herself regent, and filled the palace guard with her own relatives. The plan was to rule as Wu had.

She moved too slowly. On 21 July 710 Ruizong's son Li Longji and his aunt Princess Taiping struck first. Their men broke into the palace that night and killed Empress Wei and Princess Anle. Four days later the boy was made to step down for his uncle Ruizong. He was sent off as Prince of Wen, then to the provinces, and died in 714.

claims.text: Princess Taiping took the boy by the arm and lifted him off the throne, saying it was no seat for a child.
claims.note: Told in the Tang histories. It fits Taiping's role in the coup, but the line is the kind of thing historians liked to add.

claims.text: Empress Wei fled to a guards' camp and was cut down there by a soldier.
claims.note: Both Tang histories and the Zizhi Tongjian describe her death in the coup, though the details differ a little.

reigns.hook: The boy is gone. Ruizong is back on the throne he gave away twenty years ago, and the two people who put him there, his sister and his son, do not trust each other.
