reigns.tagline: Caught between a scheming sister and an ambitious son
reigns.previously: Li Longji and Princess Taiping kill Empress Wei. The boy steps down.
paragraphs: Ruizong owed his second reign to two people. His sister Princess Taiping had brains, money and half the chief ministers. His son Li Longji had led the coup. Ruizong's eldest son stood aside, and Li Longji was named crown prince. Taiping had wanted someone softer, and from then on she worked to bring him down.

Ruizong tried to keep the peace by sharing out favours, which pleased nobody. In 712 a comet appeared, and an astrologer said it meant the heir would become emperor. Taiping hoped it would scare Ruizong into dropping his son. Instead he decided heaven was telling him to retire. On 8 September 712 he handed the throne to Li Longji. He kept the big appointments for himself, so the fight went on.

claims.text: Princess Taiping hired the astrologer to turn her brother against the crown prince.
claims.note: Told in the Zizhi Tongjian, which reads the comet as her plot backfiring. The comet and the abdication are certain; the plot is not.

claims.text: In 711 Ruizong put his son in charge of day-to-day government.
claims.note: Both Tang histories record the crown prince acting for him. He seems to have wanted out of the quarrel long before the comet.

reigns.hook: Li Longji is emperor, his father has retired and his aunt still controls the chief ministers. In 713 he will move first and kill her.

reigns.tagline: The golden-age emperor who lost it all for love
reigns.cameToPower: Father stepped down after a comet
reigns.previously: A comet persuades Ruizong to hand the throne to his son Li Longji.
paragraphs: Li Longji had already helped kill one empress to get here. In 713 he ordered his aunt, Princess Taiping, to kill herself, and then settled in for over 40 years. His Kaiyuan era was the high noon of the Tang. Chang'an was one of the biggest cities on earth, full of Persian merchants, monks and Turkic horsemen. Li Bai, Du Fu and Wang Wei were writing poems. The emperor played music himself and trained performers in his Pear Garden.

Then he fell for Yang Guifei, the wife of his own son, Prince Shou. Her cousin Yang Guozhong became chief minister after the long rule of Li Linfu. The frontier armies grew huge, often under foreign-born generals, and in 751 an Abbasid army beat the Tang at Talas in Central Asia. One general, An Lushan, a vast man of Sogdian and Turkic family, charmed his way into court and was even adopted by Yang Guifei.

In December 755 An Lushan rebelled. He took Luoyang and called himself emperor of Yan. Next summer the old emperor fled west towards Sichuan. At Mawei the guards killed Yang Guozhong and demanded Yang Guifei too. She was strangled. Soon after, at Lingwu, his son made himself emperor without asking. Xuanzong lived on as retired emperor until 762. Bai Juyi's Song of Everlasting Sorrow later turned it all into a love story.

claims.text: Relay riders raced fresh lychees from the far south for Yang Guifei.
claims.note: The Tang histories and Du Mu's poem tell it. Scholars argue over whether the fruit came from distant Lingnan or nearer Sichuan.

claims.text: Yang Guifei had An Lushan bathed and swaddled like a newborn as a palace joke.
claims.note: Told in Sima Guang's Zizhi Tongjian, written three centuries later, and in gossipy unofficial tales. It may be slander.

claims.text: Chinese prisoners taken at Talas taught the Arabs to make paper.
claims.note: The story appears in later Arabic writings. Paper-making was probably already spreading through Central Asia before 751.

reigns.hook: The old emperor has lost his throne and his love. His son Suzong must now win back two capitals from a rebel army, and he will need foreign help to do it.

reigns.tagline: He crowned himself while his father ran for the hills
reigns.previously: At Mawei, Yang Guifei is strangled. The crown prince heads north.
paragraphs: Li Heng had been crown prince for eighteen years, always watched by his father's ministers. After Mawei he did not follow the old emperor to Sichuan. He went north to the frontier town of Lingwu, and on 12 August 756 his officers proclaimed him emperor. His father heard about it later and accepted it.

He had a throne but no capital. With Uyghur cavalry and troops from Central Asia, his generals Guo Ziyi and Li Guangbi took back Chang'an and Luoyang in late 757. The Uyghurs were paid with the right to loot Luoyang. The rebels had their own troubles. An Lushan, half blind and violent, had been killed by his own son that January. But the general Shi Siming took over and kept the war going.

In the palace Suzong leaned on the eunuch Li Fuguo, who grew ever stronger. His father died in May 762. Thirteen days later, as Suzong lay dying, Empress Zhang tried to kill Li Fuguo. He struck first.

claims.text: Li Fuguo's men dragged Empress Zhang out of Suzong's sickroom, and the shock killed him.
claims.note: The Tang histories describe the arrest in the sickroom. Whether it hastened his death is guesswork.

claims.text: An Lushan was murdered by his son An Qingxu in 757.
claims.note: Both Tang histories record it. An was going blind and had become violently abusive to those around him.

reigns.hook: Suzong is dead and Li Fuguo's guards hold the palace. The eunuch puts the crown prince on the throne and tells him to leave the governing to him.

reigns.tagline: The rebellion ended, but the warlords stayed
reigns.cameToPower: Enthroned by the eunuch Li Fuguo
reigns.previously: Suzong dies as Li Fuguo's guards seize Empress Zhang.
paragraphs: Li Yu had led the armies that retook Chang'an. Now he owed his throne to Li Fuguo, who told him to stay in the palace and leave the rest to his old servant. Daizong played along, then stripped him of his posts. That November an unknown killer broke into Li Fuguo's house at night and took his head.

The rebellion finally ended in early 763, when Shi Siming's son killed himself. To get there the court had let the rebel generals keep their provinces. In the north-east they became governors who passed their armies to their sons. Late that year Tibetan troops held Chang'an for about two weeks while Daizong fled.
Then Pugu Huai'en, a Tiele general who had helped win the war, rebelled and brought in Uyghur and Tibetan armies. Daizong reigned seventeen years, but much of the empire no longer obeyed him.

claims.text: Daizong himself sent the assassin who killed Li Fuguo.
claims.note: The killer was never caught. The Tang histories say the emperor was suspected, and he made a show of mourning.

claims.text: When the chancellor Yuan Zai fell in 777, his house held 800 measures of black pepper.
claims.note: The Tang histories list it as proof of his greed. The figure is famous but cannot be checked.

reigns.hook: Daizong dies in 779. His son Dezong is clever, proud and sure he can bring the rebel governors to heel. He is about to find out how wrong he is.

reigns.tagline: He took on the warlords and ended up a refugee
reigns.previously: Daizong dies. The rebel governors still rule the north-east.
paragraphs: Dezong started well. In 780 his minister Yang Yan replaced the old head tax with the two-tax system, levied twice a year on land and property. It lasted for centuries. Then he tried to stop the north-eastern governors from handing their provinces to their sons. That meant war, and the war spread.

In 783 troops passing through Chang'an on their way to the front mutinied over poor rations. Dezong fled to Fengtian, and the mutineers made the general Zhu Ci emperor. In 784 Dezong issued an edict blaming himself for the disaster and pardoning the rebel governors. Chang'an was retaken that summer, but the lesson stuck. He stopped trusting his generals and gave the palace armies to eunuchs, who kept them until the dynasty's last years.

claims.text: Dezong's 784 edict blaming himself moved soldiers to tears when it was read out.
claims.note: The Tang histories say so. The edict is real and was drafted by the scholar Lu Zhi; the tears may be decoration.

claims.text: Palace buyers took goods in the markets for next to nothing, as in Bai Juyi's poem The Old Charcoal Seller.
claims.note: The poem was written soon after Dezong's reign, and Shunzong's reformers abolished the practice in 805.

reigns.hook: Dezong dies early in 805. His heir has had a stroke and can barely speak, but two of his old friends have big plans for the new reign.

reigns.tagline: A speechless emperor and six months of reform
reigns.previously: Dezong dies. His heir is crippled by a stroke.
paragraphs: Shunzong had a stroke months before his father died and could no longer speak. Government passed to two men from his old household: Wang Shuwen, who had taught him the board game go, and the calligrapher Wang Pi. They brought in bright young officials, among them the writers Liu Zongyuan and Liu Yuxi.

Their reforms came fast. They ended the hated palace market purchases, cut taxes owed from the past and tried to take the palace armies away from the eunuchs. That was too far. The eunuchs made Shunzong name his son Li Chun as heir, then in August 805 forced him to abdicate. Wang Shuwen was later ordered to kill himself, and the young reformers were sent to remote posts. Shunzong died the next year.

claims.text: Shunzong was murdered by the eunuchs in 806.
claims.note: Suspected at the time and hinted at in later writings. The official account says he died of illness, which after his stroke is quite possible.

claims.text: Eight of the reformers were exiled together as provincial assistant officials.
claims.note: They are remembered as the "two Wangs and eight assistants". Liu Zongyuan wrote some of his best essays in exile.

reigns.hook: Shunzong is pushed aside. His son Xianzong is 27, tough and stubborn, and he means to bring the rebel provinces back under the throne.

reigns.tagline: The last strong Tang emperor, killed by his own eunuchs
reigns.previously: The eunuchs force Shunzong to give the throne to his son.
paragraphs: Xianzong wanted the provinces back. In 815 agents of the rebel governors had his chief minister Wu Yuanheng murdered in the street at dawn. The emperor did not back down. His minister Pei Du ran the war, and in late 817 the general Li Su marched through a snowstorm at night and took Caizhou by surprise. The rebel governor was sent to Chang'an and executed. Province after province submitted. People called it the Yuanhe revival.

In 819 Xianzong had a finger bone of the Buddha brought into the palace. The official Han Yu sent a furious memorial calling it a rotten bone. He was nearly executed and exiled to the far south. The emperor was taking elixirs of immortality by then. They made him irritable and harsh with his eunuchs. In February 820 he died suddenly.

claims.text: Xianzong was murdered by his eunuchs.
claims.note: The official story was an elixir overdose. The Tang histories say the eunuch Chen Hongzhi was suspected, but nobody was punished.

claims.text: Han Yu called the Buddha's finger bone a rotten, filthy relic that should be thrown in the fire.
claims.note: His Memorial on the Bone of the Buddha survives and is one of the most famous essays in Chinese.

reigns.hook: Xianzong is dead and the eunuchs pick his son Muzong to succeed him. The new emperor would rather play polo, and the provinces his father won back are already slipping away.

reigns.tagline: The party-loving son who let the north-east go
reigns.cameToPower: Eunuch allies killed his rival brother
reigns.reignEnded: Died after a stroke and elixirs
reigns.previously: Xianzong dies suddenly in 820. Many blame his eunuchs.
paragraphs: Li Heng's father was barely cold when the killing started. A powerful eunuch, Tutu Chengcui, had wanted a different prince on the throne, Li Heng's half-brother Li Yun. The eunuchs on Li Heng's side moved first and killed them both. The new emperor didn't look too hard into how his father had died, either. His mother was a granddaughter of the great general Guo Ziyi, and he had the palace army behind him.

Muzong liked feasts, music, polo and hunting far more than paperwork. His ministers decided the army was too big and began cutting it, turning soldiers loose with nothing. In 821 the north-east blew up. Mutineers seized Youzhou, near modern Beijing, and in Chengde the officers murdered their governor. The court sent armies, ran out of money and gave in. The Hebei provinces went back to running themselves, and stayed that way to the end of the Tang.

There was one bright spot. In 821 and 822 Tang and Tibet swore a peace treaty, and its words were carved on a stone pillar that still stands in Lhasa. Late in 822 a eunuch fell from his horse during a polo game, and the emperor was so shaken that he collapsed and could not walk. He never really recovered. He took elixirs of immortality, the same kind that had clouded his father's last years, and died in February 824, aged 28.

claims.text: A polo accident brought on the collapse that wrecked his health.
claims.note: The Tang histories say a eunuch's fall in a polo match frightened him into a fit. What actually happened to him medically can't be known.

claims.text: Muzong's elixirs helped kill him.
claims.note: Later histories say he took mineral elixirs in his last months, as his father had. Tang emperors' deaths were often blamed on them, sometimes to hide worse.

claims.text: The Tang–Tibet peace treaty of 821–822 is carved on a pillar in front of the Jokhang temple in Lhasa.
claims.note: The pillar and its Chinese and Tibetan inscription survive and have been published and translated many times.

reigns.hook: Muzong's eldest son is 14, and he would much rather play polo than meet his ministers. The palace eunuchs think that suits them very nicely.

images.caption: The Tang–Tibet treaty pillar outside the Jokhang in Lhasa, set up in 823 to record the peace sworn in Muzong's reign. No portrait from his lifetime survives.

reigns.tagline: The teenage night-hunter killed by his drinking partners
reigns.cameToPower: Named heir by his dying father
reigns.reignEnded: Murdered by eunuchs after a party
reigns.previously: Muzong dies in 824, after a stroke and a course of elixirs.
paragraphs: Li Zhan was 14 and did exactly as he liked. He turned up late to court, sometimes not at all. He loved polo and wrestling, and best of all he loved riding out at night to hunt foxes. He spent freely on palace building and showered gifts on the wrestlers and grooms who amused him. His ministers wrote him careful warnings. He read them, said kind things about them and carried on.

A few months into the reign, in 824, a labourer from the palace dye works called Zhang Shao and a fortune teller smuggled more than a hundred men into the palace, with weapons hidden in carts of dye plants. The emperor was playing polo. He ran for the camp of the palace army. The raiders reached the throne hall and sat down to eat there before the guards killed them. Nobody at court seemed to learn much from it.

His temper got rougher. He had the eunuchs and polo players around him beaten for small mistakes, and some never forgave him. On a January night in 827 he came back from a fox hunt and sat drinking with a group of them, among them the eunuch Liu Keming. When he went off to change his clothes, the candles went out and he was killed. He was 17. The murderers tried to crown a prince of their own, but rival eunuchs crushed them within days.

claims.text: Jingzong was killed while changing his clothes after a night of drinking.
claims.note: Both Tang histories and the Zizhi Tongjian record it and name the eunuch Liu Keming among the killers.

claims.text: A fortune teller had promised the dyer he would sit on the throne and dine there, and the raiders did just that.
claims.note: Told in the Tang histories and the Zizhi Tongjian. The raid is real; the neatly fulfilled prophecy looks like a storyteller's touch.

claims.text: He hunted foxes by night with his companions.
claims.note: The Tang histories list the night fox hunts among his amusements, as proof that he neglected the government.

reigns.hook: The winning eunuchs put Jingzong's younger brother Li Ang on the throne. He is serious, thrifty and bookish, and he is quietly planning to destroy them.

reigns.tagline: The bookish emperor whose plot against the eunuchs failed
reigns.cameToPower: Put on the throne by eunuchs
reigns.reignEnded: Died of illness, still their captive
reigns.previously: Jingzong is murdered by his eunuchs after a night of drinking.
paragraphs: Li Ang was everything his brother was not. He read history, dressed plainly and cut back on palace luxury. But his court was split by a feud between two groups of officials, one around Niu Sengru and Li Zongmin, the other around Li Deyu. Each side spent years pushing the other out of office. The emperor sighed that beating the rebels in Hebei was easy, and getting rid of factions at court was hard.

His real targets were the eunuchs who had killed his brother. With two clever outsiders, Li Xun and Zheng Zhu, he struck first at the old eunuch Wang Shoucheng, who was sent poisoned wine in 835. Then, on 14 December 835, came the big plan. Officials reported sweet dew, a lucky omen, on a pomegranate tree in a palace courtyard. The senior eunuchs were sent to look, and soldiers were hidden behind curtains to kill them.

The eunuch Qiu Shiliang noticed the general in charge sweating, and then the wind lifted a curtain and showed the soldiers. The eunuchs grabbed the emperor and carried him into the inner palace. Their troops then killed the chief ministers and more than a thousand others. Wenzong lived on for five more years as a captive, drinking and brooding. He died in February 840, aged 30.

claims.text: Wenzong said he was worse off than the last kings of Zhou and Han: they were ruled by strong lords, he by his own house slaves.
claims.note: The Zizhi Tongjian records it as a private talk with the scholar Zhou Chi in 839. Nobody else heard it, so the wording may be polished.

claims.text: The Sweet Dew plot was given away when the wind blew a curtain aside.
claims.note: Told in the Zizhi Tongjian, which also says the general Han Yue's nervousness made Qiu Shiliang suspicious. The accounts mix both.

claims.text: More than a thousand people were killed after the Sweet Dew Incident.
claims.note: The Tang histories give figures of over a thousand dead, including several chief ministers and their families.

reigns.hook: Wenzong wanted his nephew to succeed him. Qiu Shiliang has other plans. He forges an order and brings out the dying emperor's younger brother, Li Yan, instead.

reigns.tagline: The Daoist emperor who emptied China's monasteries
reigns.cameToPower: Made heir by a forged order
reigns.previously: Wenzong dies a prisoner of his eunuchs, five years after Sweet Dew.
paragraphs: Li Yan owed his throne to the eunuch Qiu Shiliang, and the reign began with blood. His brother's chosen heir, a favourite consort and another prince were all forced to kill themselves. Then he did something nobody expected. He called Li Deyu back as chief minister and trusted him. Li Deyu was tough and clever, and for six years the Tang had a government that worked. Even Qiu Shiliang was eased into retirement in 843, and died soon after.

The north was in chaos. In 840 the Kyrgyz smashed the Uyghur empire on the steppe, and Uyghur bands fled south to the Tang frontier, raiding as they went. In 843 a Tang force surprised the camp of their khan and brought home Princess Taihe, a Tang princess married off to the Uyghurs years before. A year later a rebel governor in Zhaoyi, in the hills of modern Shanxi, was crushed too.

Wuzong was a devoted Daoist, and in 845 he turned on Buddhism. Monasteries were shut and their land, bronze bells and slaves seized. Hundreds of thousands of monks and nuns were sent back to farm and pay tax. Zoroastrians, Manichaeans and Christians were banned too. A Japanese monk, Ennin, saw it happen and wrote it all down. Meanwhile Wuzong swallowed Daoist elixirs, grew sick and short-tempered, and died in April 846, aged 31.

claims.text: The 845 edict counted 260,500 monks and nuns sent back to ordinary life.
claims.note: The figure is the court's own, from the edict quoted in the Tang histories. It may be rounded up for effect, but nobody doubts the scale.

claims.text: A Japanese monk, Ennin, witnessed the persecution and described it in his diary.
claims.note: His travel diary survives and was translated into English by Edwin O. Reischauer in 1955.

claims.text: Daoist elixirs killed him.
claims.note: The Tang histories say his pills made him ill and irritable in his last months. The exact cause of death can't be known.

reigns.hook: Wuzong's sons are small. The eunuchs pick his uncle Li Chen, a prince everyone thinks is a bit simple. They are about to find out he has been acting for years.

reigns.tagline: The prince who played the fool, then ruled like a hawk
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Uncle of Wuzong; son of Xianzong
reigns.cameToPower: Chosen by eunuchs who thought him dim
reigns.previously: Wuzong dies of his elixirs in 846, a year after his war on Buddhism.
paragraphs: Li Chen was a son of Xianzong, and for years he said almost nothing at court. His nephews thought he was slow and liked to tease him at parties. That may have been the point: a quiet, harmless prince was a prince nobody bothered to kill. When Wuzong died, the eunuchs chose him because he looked easy to control. At his first audiences he was suddenly sharp, decisive and very much in charge.

He undid his nephew's work. Li Deyu was sent away within days and died in exile on Hainan island. The Buddhist monasteries were allowed to reopen. Xuanzong read reports himself, remembered names and caught officials out on details, and people later called him 'Little Taizong'. In the far west a local leader, Zhang Yichao, drove the Tibetans out of Dunhuang in 848 and sent envoys to hand the Hexi corridor back to the Tang.

He wanted to break the eunuchs too, but never found a way to do it. Like his nephew, he grew fond of elixirs from Daoist masters, and in 859 they poisoned him. He died aged 49 without naming an heir. He had wanted his third son to follow him. The eunuch in charge of the palace army had other ideas and brought out the eldest son instead.

claims.text: As a prince he pretended to be simple-minded so that nobody would see him as a threat.
claims.note: The Tang histories say his nephews mocked him as a dullard. Whether he was acting is a reading of his sudden sharpness as emperor.

claims.text: Wuzong tried to have him killed, and he escaped by hiding as a Buddhist monk.
claims.note: Told in late Tang and Song anecdote collections, not in the official histories. Most historians treat it as a tale.

claims.text: Zhang Yichao won Dunhuang back from Tibet and returned it to Tang rule.
claims.note: Recorded in the Tang histories and in documents found in the Dunhuang library cave.

reigns.hook: The new emperor is Li Cui. He loves music, banquets and spending, and the bill for all of it is about to land on the people.

reigns.tagline: Feasts, mutinies and a parade for the Buddha's finger
reigns.previously: Xuānzong dies of his elixirs. Eunuchs pass over his chosen son.
paragraphs: Yizong liked to be entertained. He kept hundreds of musicians, threw banquet after banquet and went on outings with huge crowds of followers. Meanwhile the money ran short and the provinces came apart. In 859 a rebel called Qiu Fu raised an army in Zhejiang. In 863 the kingdom of Nanzhao, in modern Yunnan, took the Tang protectorate at Hanoi, and it took the general Gao Pian until 866 to win it back.

In 868 soldiers from Xuzhou were kept on frontier duty at Guilin years past their promised time. They mutinied under an officer called Pang Xun and marched home, gathering an army of the poor as they went. The court beat them in 869 only with the help of Shatuo Turk cavalry, and their chief was given the imperial surname, Li. In the middle of all this, in 868, a man named Wang Jie paid for the printing of the Diamond Sutra.

In 870 his favourite daughter, Princess Tongchang, died. Yizong had more than 20 of her doctors executed and threw their families in jail. In 873, against his ministers' advice, he had the Buddha's finger bone brought from Famen Temple to Chang'an in a vast parade. He said that if he could see it, he would die without regret. A few months later he was dead. The relic turned up again in 1987, in the temple's sealed crypt.

claims.text: He had more than 20 doctors executed after his daughter's death.
claims.note: Recorded in both Tang histories and the Zizhi Tongjian. Ministers who protested were sent away from court.

claims.text: He said that if he saw the Buddha's bone he would die without regret.
claims.note: Quoted in the Zizhi Tongjian, written knowing he died that year, so the line may be shaped as a moral.

claims.text: The finger bone relic was found in Famen Temple's crypt in 1987.
claims.note: Archaeologists opened the sealed Tang crypt in 1987 and found the relics with treasures and an inventory from the Tang court.

reigns.hook: His fifth son is 11. Real power will sit with a eunuch the boy calls 'father', just as a salt smuggler named Huang Chao starts gathering an army.

reigns.tagline: The polo-mad boy who lost his capital twice
reigns.cameToPower: Chosen by eunuchs as a child
reigns.previously: Yizong parades the Buddha's finger bone and dies months later.
paragraphs: Li Xuan was 11 when the eunuchs crowned him. He left the government to his old companion, the eunuch Tian Lingzi, whom he called 'father'. The boy wanted to play. He loved polo, cockfights and goose fights, and bragged that if polo were an exam subject he would come top. Drought and hunger spread across the plains. In 874 and 875 two salt smugglers, Wang Xianzhi and Huang Chao, rose in revolt in the east.

Huang Chao's army roamed the whole country, down to Guangzhou in the far south and back north again. In January 881 it took Chang'an. Xizong fled to Chengdu in Sichuan, just as Xuanzong had fled An Lushan. Huang called himself emperor of Qi. It took the Shatuo cavalry of Li Keyong, the one-eyed son of the chief Yizong had honoured, to drive him out in 883. Huang Chao died on the run in 884.

Xizong came home in 885 to a wrecked city, and before the year was out he was on the run again, this time from his own governors, who were fighting Tian Lingzi over the salt revenue. One of them even crowned a rival Tang prince in 886. Xizong finally got back to Chang'an early in 888, already ill, and died that April, aged 25.

claims.text: He gave out governorships in Sichuan to the winners of a polo match.
claims.note: The Zizhi Tongjian says Chen Jingxuan won the western Sichuan post this way. It fits his reputation, and many historians accept it.

claims.text: He boasted that if polo were in the exams he would come first, and an actor told him a strict examiner would fail him.
claims.note: Quoted in the Zizhi Tongjian. Court jesters' sharp replies are a favourite device of the histories, so the exchange may be improved.

claims.text: Huang Chao had failed the imperial exams before he turned rebel.
claims.note: The New Book of Tang says so and later writers attach poems to him. It is plausible but can't be checked.

reigns.hook: Xizong leaves no grown son. The eunuch Yang Fugong brings out his younger brother Li Jie, 21 and eager. He wants a real army, and trying to get one will cost him everything.

reigns.tagline: The last Tang emperor who tried, murdered by a warlord
reigns.cameToPower: Picked by the eunuch Yang Fugong
reigns.previously: Xizong dies at 25, back in a ruined Chang'an.
paragraphs: Zhaozong was bright, energetic and determined to make the throne count again. He raised new armies, and in 890 sent one against Li Keyong. It was crushed. After that the great governors knew the emperor had nothing to scare them with. Li Maozhen of Fengxiang, just west of the capital, marched on Chang'an more than once. In 896 the emperor fled to Huazhou, and in 897 his host there, Han Jian, had eleven Tang princes murdered.

Inside the palace it was worse. In late 900 the eunuch Liu Jishu found the emperor drunk after he had killed some servants. He locked him in a courtyard, passed his food through a hole in the wall and crowned his son. Loyal officers freed him early in 901. Then the eunuchs carried him off to Li Maozhen at Fengxiang, and Zhu Wen, the strongest warlord of all, besieged the city for months until Li handed the emperor over.

Zhu Wen and the chief minister Cui Yin then killed the palace eunuchs, hundreds of them, in 903. A year later Zhu Wen had Cui Yin killed too. He forced the emperor and the people of Chang'an to move to Luoyang, and tore the old capital down, floating its timbers down the river. In September 904 his officers broke into the palace at night and murdered Zhaozong. He was 37.

claims.text: Locked up by Liu Jishu, the emperor was fed through a hole in the wall.
claims.note: The Tang histories and the Zizhi Tongjian describe it. Liu Jishu was killed when the emperor was freed in 901.

claims.text: Zhu Wen pulled down Chang'an and sent its timbers downriver to build at Luoyang.
claims.note: The histories describe the demolition of 904. Chang'an was never again the capital of a united China.

claims.text: His consort Li Jianrong threw herself over him and was killed too.
claims.note: Recorded in the Tang histories and the Zizhi Tongjian, but no eyewitness account survives and loyal heroines were a favourite theme.

reigns.hook: Zhu Wen still needs a Tang emperor, for now. He picks Zhaozong's 11-year-old son, Li Zhu, and means to keep him only until he can take the throne himself.

reigns.tagline: The boy who kept the throne warm for his father's killer
reigns.cameToPower: Set up by his father's murderer
reigns.previously: Zhu Wen's officers murder Zhaozong at night in Luoyang.
paragraphs: Li Zhu was a frightened child in a palace run by Zhu Wen's men. Early in 905 nine of his brothers were invited to a banquet at a pond in Luoyang and strangled there. That summer came the Baima killings. About thirty senior officials, men from the old Tang families, were rounded up at the Baima post station by the Yellow River, killed, and thrown into the water.

Zhu Wen's adviser Li Zhen had failed the exams again and again, and he hated the proud officials who had passed. They call themselves the pure stream, he is supposed to have said, so throw them in the Yellow River and make it muddy. Soon afterwards the boy's mother, Empress Dowager He, was murdered too. Nothing stood between Zhu Wen and the throne except the need to make it look proper.

In May 907 the 14-year-old emperor handed his throne to Zhu Wen, who founded a new dynasty, the Later Liang, with its capital at Kaifeng. The boy was sent to Caozhou with the title Prince of Jiyin. In 908 he was poisoned there, aged 15. After almost 290 years the Tang was over, and so was any pretence that China had a single ruler.

claims.text: Li Zhen said the officials who called themselves the pure stream should be thrown in the Yellow River to make it muddy.
claims.note: Reported by Song historians, including Sima Guang in the Zizhi Tongjian, who blamed the killings on him. The words may be sharpened.

claims.text: Nine of Zhaozong's sons were strangled at a banquet in 905.
claims.note: Both Tang histories and the Zizhi Tongjian record it and name Zhu Wen's officer Jiang Xuanhui as the man who arranged it.

claims.text: Zhu Wen had the former emperor poisoned in 908.
claims.note: The Tang histories and the Zizhi Tongjian say he was poisoned on Zhu Wen's orders.

reigns.hook: Zhu Wen, once an officer in Huang Chao's rebel army, is emperor now. But his rivals refuse to bow, and his own sons are watching the throne very closely.

reigns.tagline: The rebel who switched sides and buried the Tang
reigns.cameToPower: Forced the last Tang emperor out
reigns.previously: Zhu Wen takes the throne from the boy Emperor Ai of Tang.
paragraphs: Zhu Wen was the son of a poor village schoolteacher. He joined Huang Chao's rebels. In 882 he changed sides, and the grateful Tang court gave him a new name: Quanzhong, "Complete Loyalty". It aged badly. By 907 he had killed one emperor and bullied a boy into handing over the throne. He named his dynasty Liang, later called Later Liang, and ruled from Kaifeng and Luoyang.

Half the north refused to bow. Li Keyong, the one-eyed Shatuo Turk who ran Jin from Taiyuan, had hated Zhu for decades. When Li Keyong died in 908, his son Li Cunxu proved even worse news, smashing a Liang siege army at Luzhou that same year and another at Baixiang in 911. Beyond the frontier, the Khitan chief Abaoji was building a power of his own.

At home Zhu turned savage and paranoid. His eldest son was dead, and he leaned towards an adopted son, Zhu Youwen, as heir. In July 912 another son, Zhu Yougui, learned he was being sent away to a distant post. That night he led palace guards into his father's bedroom at Luoyang.

claims.text: Zhu Wen slept with his sons' wives while the sons were away on duty, and the wives competed for his favour.
claims.note: Both Five Dynasties histories tell it, and so does Sima Guang. All were written under dynasties that saw Later Liang as illegitimate, so the tale may be sharpened.

claims.text: His Tang title Quanzhong meant "Complete Loyalty".
claims.note: The name was granted by Emperor Xizong in 882 and appears throughout the official histories.

reigns.hook: Zhu Wen is dead, stabbed by his own son's men. The killer, Zhu Yougui, now has to explain himself to the court, and to his brothers.

reigns.tagline: He murdered his father and lasted eight months
reigns.reignEnded: Killed as rebels stormed the palace
reigns.previously: Zhu Wen is murdered in his bedroom by his son Zhu Yougui's guards.
paragraphs: Zhu Yougui got the throne the bloodiest way possible. His men killed Zhu Wen, and he wrapped the body in a rug and hid it under the palace floor. Then he forged an order in his dead father's name, telling the court that the adopted son Zhu Youwen had plotted against the throne. Zhu Youwen was put to death, and Zhu Yougui announced himself emperor at Luoyang.

Nobody was fooled for long. Zhu Yougui bought support with handouts, but the generals despised him, and his brother Zhu Youzhen, who commanded the guards at Kaifeng, began to plot with the great general Yang Shihou. In March 913 the palace army in Luoyang rose. As the rebels broke in, Zhu Yougui ordered his officer Feng Tingyu to kill him and his wife. Feng did it, then killed himself.

claims.text: Zhu Yougui's mother was a camp prostitute Zhu Wen met at Bozhou.
claims.note: The Old History of the Five Dynasties says so plainly. Nothing contradicts it, though no source outside the official histories survives.

claims.text: He hid his father's body under the floor of the bedchamber, wrapped in a felt rug.
claims.note: The detail comes from Sima Guang's Zizhi Tongjian, written 170 years later from older records. It fits the timeline, but nobody can check it.

reigns.hook: With the parricide dead, the throne goes to his half-brother Zhu Youzhen. He will spend ten years losing a war to Li Cunxu.

reigns.tagline: Ten years of losing, then one last order
reigns.reignEnded: Killed by an officer at his order
reigns.previously: Zhu Yougui dies as the guards storm his palace at Luoyang.
paragraphs: Zhu Youzhen ruled from Kaifeng and liked to keep things in the family. He trusted in-laws and court favourites more than his tough old generals, and it cost him. In 915 he tried to break up the huge Weibo garrison in Hebei. The soldiers mutinied and handed the whole province to Li Cunxu of Jin. After that the war was fought on the Yellow River, and Later Liang slowly bled.

In May 923 Li Cunxu declared himself emperor of a new Later Tang. That autumn Liang's best general, Wang Yanzhang, was captured and refused to change sides. Li Cunxu made a dash straight for Kaifeng. With no army left to stop him, Zhu Youzhen told his officer Huangfu Lin to kill him. Huangfu did, then turned the sword on himself. Later Liang ended the next day, after 16 years.

claims.text: Wang Yanzhang told his captors: "A leopard dies and leaves its skin; a man dies and leaves his name."
claims.note: Ouyang Xiu tells the story as a lesson in loyalty, and he loved a good line. The saying is older than Wang; he may simply have been given it.

claims.text: Zhu Youzhen asked to be killed so that he would not fall into enemy hands.
claims.note: Both Five Dynasties histories agree on his last order to Huangfu Lin, and on Huangfu's suicide.

reigns.hook: Li Cunxu rides into Kaifeng the day after. The Shatuo prince has kept a promise to his father, and he means to enjoy the reward.

reigns.tagline: The warrior king who wanted to be an actor
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Son of Li Keyong, Prince of Jin
reigns.previously: Zhu Youzhen dies at Kaifeng as the Later Tang army arrives.
paragraphs: Li Cunxu was a Shatuo Turk and a brilliant cavalry general. He took over Jin at 22, swallowed the Yan state around modern Beijing, held off the Khitans and ground down Later Liang. In May 923 he named himself emperor of Later Tang, claiming the old Tang's mantle, and by the end of the year he held Kaifeng. He made Luoyang his capital, and in 925 his armies conquered Former Shu in Sichuan.

Then he stopped trying. He loved theatre, painted his face, went on stage under the name Li Tianxia and gave actors posts and favours. His greedy Empress Liu hoarded cash while his soldiers went unpaid. In 926 she had his best general, Guo Chongtao, murdered on a false charge. Mutinies broke out across the north.

In May 926 the palace guard at Luoyang rose under Guo Congqian, a commander who had started out as an actor. Li Cunxu was hit by an arrow in the fighting and died. He had won his empire in 15 years and lost it in three.

claims.text: His dying father gave him three arrows, one for each enemy to destroy: Yan, the Khitans and Zhu Wen.
claims.note: The story is the opening of Ouyang Xiu's preface on actors, a moral essay written more than a century later. It is not in the older history.

claims.text: When he called out "Where is Li Tianxia?" on stage, an actor slapped him, saying only one man rules all under heaven.
claims.note: Told by Ouyang Xiu and Sima Guang. The emperor is said to have laughed and rewarded him. A neat story, probably polished.

claims.text: Actors piled musical instruments over his body and burned it.
claims.note: Ouyang Xiu reports it as a fitting end for a ruler ruined by actors. The moral is obvious; the fact may be too.

reigns.hook: The emperor is dead. Outside the capital, his adopted brother Li Siyuan, a grizzled general who cannot read, has been carried along by mutineers. Now they want him on the throne.

images.caption: A hanging-scroll portrait painted under the Ming, about 500 years or more after his death; now in the National Palace Museum, Taipei.
images.alt: Hanging-scroll painting of Emperor Zhuangzong of Later Tang in imperial robes

reigns.tagline: The illiterate general who prayed for a better emperor
reigns.reignEnded: Died days after his son's coup
reigns.previously: Li Cunxu dies in a palace mutiny at Luoyang.
paragraphs: Li Siyuan was sent to crush a mutiny at Weibo in 926. Instead, his own troops joined it and swept him along to Luoyang. By the time he arrived, Li Cunxu was dead. The old general became emperor at 58. He couldn't read, so ministers read every report aloud to him, and he picked capable ones, among them the famous survivor Feng Dao.

His seven years were the calmest the north had seen in decades. He cut palace spending, punished corrupt officials and had decent harvests. In 932 he approved Feng Dao's plan to print the Confucian classics from carved wooden blocks, a project that took over 20 years.
The end was ugly. In December 933, as he lay ill, his son Li Congrong led troops at the palace gates, fearing he would be passed over. The guards killed him. Days later the heartbroken emperor died.

claims.text: Every night he burned incense and prayed: "I am a barbarian. May Heaven send a sage to rule China."
claims.note: Song-era writers, Ouyang Xiu among them, record the prayer and note that the Song founder was born in 927. The link to Song is pious hindsight.

claims.text: He could not read.
claims.note: Both Five Dynasties histories say reports had to be read to him, and An Chonghui's power rested partly on that.

reigns.hook: Li Siyuan's surviving son Li Conghou, 19, takes the throne. His advisers want to tame the provincial governors. One of those governors is his adoptive brother Li Congke.

images.caption: An imagined likeness from a Qing-dynasty printed edition of a popular historical novel, made some 900 years after his reign.

reigns.tagline: The teenager whose army walked away
reigns.previously: Li Siyuan dies days after his son Li Congrong's failed coup.
paragraphs: Li Conghou was a quiet, bookish young man, and he let two ambitious ministers, Zhu Hongzhao and Feng Yun, steer for him. They decided the provincial governors had grown too strong and started moving them around. One of them, Li Congke at Fengxiang, was the old emperor's adopted son and a famous fighter. He refused to move and rebelled.

The court sent an army to besiege Fengxiang. It never took the city. The besiegers went over to Li Congke and marched with him on Luoyang. Li Conghou fled east and ran into his brother-in-law Shi Jingtang, whose men killed his escort and left him stranded. A few weeks later Li Congke's envoy put him to death.

claims.text: Li Congke climbed the walls of Fengxiang, bared his scars to the besiegers and wept, and the army changed sides.
claims.note: Sima Guang tells the scene. The defection is certain; promises of big rewards probably did more than the tears.

reigns.hook: Li Congke rides into Luoyang as emperor. His soldiers expect the huge reward he promised them, and the treasury is almost empty.

reigns.tagline: Emperor by mutiny, ended in a burning tower
reigns.previously: Li Conghou's army goes over to his adoptive brother Li Congke.
paragraphs: Li Congke was born a Wang. His widowed mother became a concubine of Li Siyuan, who adopted the boy, and he grew into one of the bravest soldiers in the army. As emperor he struggled to pay the reward he had promised his troops, squeezing the people of Luoyang and still falling short.

His real problem was Shi Jingtang, his rival from the old days and now governor at Taiyuan. In 936 Li Congke tried to move him. Shi rebelled and asked the Khitans for help, offering a huge price. In the autumn Yelü Deguang, the Khitan emperor, rode south and smashed the Later Tang army outside Taiyuan. In November he made Shi emperor.
As the Khitans and Shi's men closed on Luoyang, Li Congke gave up. In January 937 he climbed the Xuanwu tower with his family and set it on fire.

claims.text: The ancient Heirloom Seal of the Realm, said to go back to the First Emperor, was lost in the flames with him.
claims.note: Later writers claim the seal vanished here. Whether the Later Tang seal was really the Qin one is doubtful to begin with.

claims.text: He burned himself to death with his family rather than surrender.
claims.note: Both Five Dynasties histories and Sima Guang record the fire in the Xuanwu tower.

reigns.hook: Shi Jingtang has his throne, but he bought it from the Khitans. Now the bill comes due.

reigns.tagline: He bought a crown with sixteen prefectures
reigns.previously: Li Congke burns himself to death as Shi Jingtang's allies close in.
paragraphs: Shi Jingtang was a Shatuo officer and the late Li Siyuan's son-in-law. To win the Khitans' help he promised them the Sixteen Prefectures, a belt of land around modern Beijing and Datong. His general Liu Zhiyuan warned that cash would do and that giving away land would haunt China. He was right. With those prefectures the Khitans held the passes through the mountains for the next two centuries.

Shi also agreed to send 300,000 bolts of silk a year and to treat the Khitan emperor as his father. He ruled from Kaifeng as a client, sending gifts and polite letters north while his own governors rebelled against the shame of it. He put down a revolt at Weizhou in 937 and another in 941. In the summer of 942 he died, worn out at 50, with his sons dead or very young.

claims.text: He called the Khitan emperor "father", though he was ten years older.
claims.note: Recorded in both Five Dynasties histories. Shi was born in 892, Yelü Deguang in 902.

claims.text: Handing over the Sixteen Prefectures shaped Chinese history for 400 years.
claims.note: Song and Ming writers blamed him for the northern invasions that followed. Historians agree the loss mattered, though later failures to win it back were not his doing.

reigns.hook: On his deathbed Shi asked Feng Dao to protect his infant son. Instead the generals pick a grown man: his nephew Shi Chonggui, who has will not call himself anyone's subject.

reigns.tagline: He defied the Khitans and lost everything
reigns.previously: Shi Jingtang dies in 942, a client of the Khitans to the end.
paragraphs: Shi Chonggui was the son of Shi Jingtang's elder brother and grew up as his uncle's adopted son. His minister Jing Yanguang talked him into a bolder line. The new emperor wrote to the Khitans as a grandson, as family manners required, but refused to call himself their subject. To Yelü Deguang, now ruling a state called Liao, that was war.

The Liao invaded in 944 and again in 945 and were beaten back both times. The win went to the court's head. In 946 Shi sent his whole field army north under Du Chongwei, his uncle's brother-in-law. Du, hoping the Liao would make him emperor, surrendered the lot. In January 947 Liao horsemen rode into Kaifeng.
Shi Chonggui gave himself up. The Liao named him "Marquis Who Betrayed Righteousness" and sent him north with his family. He lived 27 more years in exile and died in Liao territory in 974.

claims.text: He declared himself the Khitans' "grandson but not their subject".
claims.note: Both Five Dynasties histories and Sima Guang report the letter and the Khitan fury it caused.

claims.text: At the battle of Yangcheng in 945, Yelü Deguang escaped on a camel.
claims.note: The Chinese histories tell it to show how badly he was beaten. They wrote for the side that won that day.

claims.text: Du Chongwei surrendered because the Liao promised him the throne.
claims.note: Sima Guang says so. The Liao never kept the promise, which makes it plausible.

reigns.hook: Yelü Deguang sits in Kaifeng in Chinese robes while his riders strip the countryside. Revolts break out. At Taiyuan, Shi Jingtang's old general Liu Zhiyuan sees his chance.

reigns.tagline: The Shatuo general who waited for the Khitans to leave
reigns.reignEnded: Died of illness within a year
reigns.previously: The Khitans take Kaifeng and carry Shi Chonggui off to the north.
paragraphs: Liu Zhiyuan was a Shatuo Turk, a hard-bitten cavalry general who had helped Shi Jingtang win the throne in 936. By 947 he held Taiyuan, the old Shatuo stronghold, with a strong army and full storehouses. When the Khitans took Kaifeng he sent polite messages to their emperor, Yelü Deguang, and waited. Early that spring his officers hailed him emperor.

He played it shrewdly. North China rose against the Khitan foragers, and Yelü Deguang soon headed home, grumbling that he had never known the Chinese were so hard to rule. He fell ill and died on the way. Liu marched into Kaifeng that summer and named his dynasty Han, borrowing the glory of the ancient Han emperors.

It was a short triumph. His eldest son, Liu Chengxun, died around the turn of the year, and the grieving father soon followed, early in 948. On his deathbed he warned his ministers about Du Chongwei, the general who had handed a whole Jin army to the Khitans, and they had him executed. The throne went to his second son, Liu Chengyou.

claims.text: Leaving Kaifeng, the Khitan emperor said he had never known the Chinese were so hard to rule.
claims.note: Recorded in Sima Guang's Zizhi Tongjian and the Five Dynasties histories, all Chinese works. It is a neat line that may have been polished in the retelling.

claims.text: The Khitans gutted their dead emperor and packed him with salt for the journey home, and the Chinese jeered at him as 'emperor jerky'.
claims.note: Told by Chinese historians of the period, who had no love for the Khitans. Preserving a body for a long journey is plausible; the nickname is mockery.

claims.text: As a poor soldier he married a farmer's daughter, Li Sanniang, then left her to suffer while he rose to power.
claims.note: This is the plot of the White Rabbit story, told in Jin- and Yuan-era ballads and plays long after his death. It owes little to the record.

reigns.hook: Liu Chengyou is about seventeen, and his father's old generals and ministers run everything. He resents every one of them, and soon he will do something about it.

reigns.tagline: The teenage emperor who struck first and lost it all
reigns.previously: Liu Zhiyuan dies, barely a year after taking Kaifeng.
paragraphs: Liu Chengyou inherited a throne guarded by his father's men: the generals Shi Hongzhao and Guo Wei, the money man Wang Zhang and the chief minister Yang Bin. Almost at once three governors in the west rebelled. Guo Wei spent 948 and 949 crushing them one after another and came home the hero of the army. The young emperor had to sit and nod.

He hated it. His regents overruled him, scolded his favourites and kept him short of cash. Late in 950, egged on by his mother's family and his cronies, he struck. Yang Bin, Shi Hongzhao and Wang Zhang were cut down as they arrived at the palace. Secret orders went north to kill Guo Wei at his base, and Guo Wei's family in Kaifeng was slaughtered.

The orders leaked. Guo Wei's officers told him to march, and he did. The imperial army melted away outside Kaifeng around the turn of 951. The emperor fled with a handful of men and was killed in a village nearby by one of his own attendants. He was about nineteen. The Later Han had lasted less than four years.

claims.text: Shi Hongzhao sneered that long spears and big swords kept the state safe, and asked what use a writing brush was.
claims.note: The quarrel between soldiers and scholars is told in the Zizhi Tongjian and the Five Dynasties histories, written by scholars with every reason to remember it.

claims.text: The emperor was killed by his own favourite, Guo Yunming, not by Guo Wei's soldiers.
claims.note: The histories name Guo Yunming. They were written under Guo Wei's successors, who had every reason to keep his hands clean.

reigns.hook: Guo Wei holds Kaifeng and talks of crowning a Liu prince. Then he marches north to meet the Khitans, and on the way his soldiers tear down a yellow banner.

reigns.tagline: The tattooed soldier who wanted a paper shroud
reigns.cameToPower: Wrapped in a yellow flag by his troops
reigns.previously: Liu Chengyou is dead, killed fleeing Guo Wei's army.
paragraphs: Guo Wei grew up poor and fatherless and joined the army as a rough young man. With Liu Chengyou dead, he talked of crowning a Liu prince and marched north to meet a Khitan raid. At Chanzhou his soldiers tore a yellow banner and wrapped it round him like an emperor's robe. He turned back to Kaifeng and early in 951 founded the Later Zhou.

He ruled like a man who had seen what greed cost. He cut taxes and the savage punishments of earlier regimes, and stopped the provinces sending fancy delicacies to court. The Liu prince he had offered the throne, Liu Yun, was killed. Liu Yun's father, Liu Chong, set up his own Northern Han at Taiyuan with Khitan backing, and the north had a new feud.

Guo Wei's sons had all died in the Kaifeng massacre, so his heir was Chai Rong, his wife's nephew, whom he had raised and adopted. Guo Wei fell ill and died early in 954. He asked to be buried in paper clothes in a pottery coffin, so that no one would bother robbing his grave.

claims.text: He had a sparrow tattooed on his neck, and people called him Guo the Sparrow.
claims.note: Ouyang Xiu's history records the tattoo and the nickname. Tattooed soldiers were common in the period.

claims.text: He smashed jewelled treasures in front of his court, asking what use an emperor had for such things.
claims.note: Told in the Five Dynasties histories as proof of his thrift. Such scenes were a stock way to praise a founder.

claims.text: The yellow banner at Chanzhou was staged, and became the model for Zhao Kuangyin's yellow robe nine years later.
claims.note: The histories present both scenes as surprises. Many historians think both were planned by the men who gained from them.

reigns.hook: Chai Rong, Guo Wei's adopted son, is thirty-two. Within weeks the Northern Han and the Khitans invade, betting the new man will crack.

reigns.tagline: He planned thirty years of work and got five
reigns.reignEnded: Fell ill on campaign, died at 38
reigns.previously: Guo Wei dies, asking for paper clothes and a pottery coffin.
paragraphs: Chai Rong had grown up in Guo Wei's household. Weeks after he took the throne, the Northern Han and the Khitans invaded. At Gaoping, in 954, part of his army broke and ran, but he rode into the fight himself and won. Back in camp he executed the officers who had fled. A young commander who had fought hard that day, Zhao Kuangyin, was promoted.

Then he set about building a state. He cut the dead wood from the army and made the palace guard the best force in China. In 955 he closed thousands of unlicensed Buddhist monasteries and melted their bronze statues into coins. From 956 to 958 he took the rich lands between the Huai and the Yangtze from the Southern Tang, whose ruler stopped calling himself emperor.

In 959 he turned north to win back the Sixteen Prefectures from the Liao. He took three passes and a clutch of towns in weeks with hardly a battle, then fell ill and was carried back to Kaifeng. He died that summer, aged 38. He had wanted thirty years: ten to win the empire, ten to feed the people, ten to bring peace. He got five and a half.

claims.text: He said the Buddha, who gave his own body to help others, would not grudge his statues being melted for coins.
claims.note: Quoted in Sima Guang's Zizhi Tongjian. Buddhist writers later counted him among the great persecutors of their faith.

claims.text: He told a minister he needed ten years to conquer, ten to care for the people and ten to bring peace.
claims.note: Recorded by Song-era writers, who admired him as the man who built the army their own founder inherited.

claims.text: On campaign he found a plank inscribed 'The Inspector-General will become Son of Heaven' and sacked the officer who held that post.
claims.note: Told in Song sources. The man promoted to the post was Zhao Kuangyin, which makes the story look like hindsight, or a plant.

reigns.hook: Chai Rong's son is a small boy. The post of Inspector-General, the one the plank named, now belongs to Zhao Kuangyin, and the palace army adores him.

reigns.tagline: Six months on the throne, then a yellow robe for another
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Eldest surviving son of Chai Rong
reigns.reignEnded: Gave the throne to Zhao Kuangyin
reigns.previously: Chai Rong dies at 38, his northern campaign unfinished.
paragraphs: Chai Zongxun came to the throne in the summer of 959 as a small boy. His father's older sons had been killed in the Kaifeng massacre of 950, so there was no one else. The young Empress Dowager Fu stood beside him, and the experienced ministers Fan Zhi and Wang Pu ran the government. On paper the Later Zhou looked secure.

Real power lay with the palace army, and Chai Rong had handed its top commands to trusted officers, above all Zhao Kuangyin and his sworn brothers. A child emperor gave ambitious generals the same itch it always had, and rumours ran round Kaifeng that the commander would soon be emperor. At the lunar new year of 960, word came that the Northern Han and the Khitans were invading.

Zhao Kuangyin led the army out of the capital. Within days he was back, as emperor. The boy gave up the throne without a fight and was made Prince of Zheng. He was later moved to Fangzhou, far from the capital, and died there in 973, aged about 20. The Song looked after the Chai family for generations.

claims.text: The invasion that sent the army out of Kaifeng was invented.
claims.note: No invasion followed, and the alarm went quiet once Zhao was emperor. Song histories tell it straight; most modern historians think the coup was planned.

claims.text: Song Taizu left a secret stone tablet ordering his heirs to protect the Chai family for ever.
claims.note: The oath tablet appears in Song writings from the 12th century. No such tablet has been found, and many historians doubt it existed.

reigns.hook: The army camps for the night at Chenqiao, a day's march from Kaifeng. Before dawn, Zhao Kuangyin's officers come to his tent carrying a yellow robe.

reigns.tagline: The general who got crowned in his own army camp
reigns.previously: The army marches out, leaving a boy of six on the Zhou throne.
paragraphs: Early in 960 Zhao Kuangyin marched out of Kaifeng to meet a reported Khitan attack. At Chenqiao, a day's march away, his officers woke him, threw a yellow imperial robe over his shoulders and hailed him emperor. He turned round, took the capital almost without a fight and named his dynasty Song. He treated the boy emperor and his family kindly, which was rare for the time.

Zhao knew what killed dynasties: generals. So in 961, the story goes, he threw a banquet for his top commanders and told them over wine he couldn't sleep for fear one of them would get a yellow robe too. They took the hint, retired to rich estates and gave up their armies. For the rest of the dynasty, scholar-officials outranked soldiers. He picked off the south: Later Shu in 965, Southern Han in 971, Southern Tang in 975, whose last ruler was the poet Li Yu.

He never got the Sixteen Prefectures back from the Liao. In November 976 he died suddenly at 49. His younger brother Zhao Kuangyi had been with him that night, and it was the brother, not one of his sons, who took the throne.

claims.text: Zhao was taken by surprise when his officers made him emperor.
claims.note: Song histories tell it that way, but the robe was ready and the plan ran smoothly. Most historians think he and his brother set it up.

claims.text: Taizu talked his generals into retirement over a cup of wine.
claims.note: The scene appears in Song accounts written decades later. The generals did lose their commands, but probably over years, not at one banquet.

claims.text: 'Candle shadows and the sound of an axe': Taizu was killed by his brother.
claims.note: A monk's account from the next century describes shadows and an axe that night. Nothing proves murder, but the brother's quick takeover fed suspicion for centuries.

reigns.hook: Taizu's younger brother, Zhao Kuangyi, takes the throne as Taizong. He wants to finish the conquest, but the Khitan cavalry of the Liao are waiting in the north.

reigns.tagline: The brother who took the throne and never quite explained
reigns.cameToPower: Took over the night Taizu died
reigns.previously: Taizu dies suddenly in the night. His brother takes the throne.
paragraphs: Zhao Kuangyi had helped plan the coup of 960 and ran the capital for his brother. Now he wanted to finish the job. In 978 the last southern rulers, Qian Chu of Wuyue among them, handed over their lands. In 979 he besieged Taiyuan and ended the Northern Han. The Ten Kingdoms were gone. Then he pushed on towards Liao-held Beijing.

At the Gaoliang River, outside the city, Khitan cavalry smashed his tired army, and the emperor got away with an arrow wound. A second great offensive in 986 failed too. The general Yang Ye was captured and starved himself to death, the start of the Yang family legends of later opera. After that the Song mostly stayed on the defensive.

At home he built a state run by scholars. Exam intakes soared, and he sponsored huge compilations such as the Taiping Yulan encyclopedia. Taizu's sons did not prosper: one killed himself in 979 after a rebuke, the other died young in 981. Taizong's own eldest son went mad and set fire to his palace, so in 997 the throne went to his third son, Zhao Heng.

claims.text: Their mother had made Taizu swear the throne would pass to his brother: the 'Golden Casket' promise.
claims.note: The document only surfaced in 981, produced by the minister Zhao Pu. Many historians think it was made up to cover a doubtful succession.

claims.text: He fled the Gaoliang River in a donkey cart with an arrow wound.
claims.note: The colour comes from later accounts. The official Song record says little about the rout, so the details are hard to check.

claims.text: He had the captive poet-king Li Yu of Southern Tang poisoned for writing a homesick poem.
claims.note: Song anecdote collections tell it. The official history just says Li Yu died in 978.

reigns.hook: Zhao Heng inherits an empire that cannot beat the Khitans. In 1004 their cavalry ride deep into Song land, and some of his ministers beg him to flee south.

reigns.tagline: He bought a century of peace, then found letters from heaven
reigns.previously: Taizong dies. His third son, Zhao Heng, inherits a stalemate.
paragraphs: Zhenzong was a cautious man in a dangerous spot. In 1004 the Liao emperor and his formidable mother, the Empress Dowager Xiao, led their cavalry south almost to the Yellow River. Some ministers urged him to flee south. The chief minister Kou Zhun pushed him the other way, to the front at Chanyuan, where the sight of the emperor's banner cheered the troops.

Early in 1005 the two sides made a deal. The Song would send 100,000 taels of silver and 200,000 bolts of silk a year, and the two emperors would call each other brothers. It was cheaper than war, and it held for more than a century. Critics at court called it a treaty signed under the city walls, a surrender in all but name, and Kou Zhun soon lost his post.

Stung, Zhenzong looked for glory elsewhere. In 1008 'heavenly texts' were found hanging from a palace gate, and he went to Mount Tai for the ancient feng and shan rites. More usefully, in 1012 he had quick-ripening Champa rice sent to farmers in the lower Yangtze. In his last years he was ill and his clever empress, Liu, took charge. He died in 1022.

claims.text: Under the Treaty of Chanyuan the Song paid the Liao 100,000 taels of silver and 200,000 bolts of silk a year.
claims.note: The terms are recorded in both Song and Liao sources. The payments were raised in 1042.

claims.text: The heavenly texts were staged, with the emperor in on it.
claims.note: Song historians blamed the minister Wang Qinruo for the scheme. Zhenzong certainly went along with it, but how much he planned is unclear.

claims.text: He wrote the verses promising that books hold houses of gold and girls as fair as jade.
claims.note: The poem 'Encouragement to Study' goes under his name in later collections, but nothing from his lifetime ties it to him.

reigns.hook: The new emperor is eleven. The real ruler is his father's widow, the Empress Dowager Liu, and she is keeping a secret about who the boy's mother really is.

reigns.tagline: The longest Song reign, and a mother he never knew
reigns.previously: Zhenzong dies, leaving a boy of eleven and a powerful widow.
paragraphs: For his first eleven years Renzong reigned and the Empress Dowager Liu ruled. She ran the court with a firm hand, and in 1023 her government took over the jiaozi, the paper notes Sichuan merchants had been issuing, and printed them itself. Only when she died in 1033 did the young emperor learn that his real mother was a palace woman, Consort Li, who had died the year before.

Renzong was gentle, cautious and long-lived. His reign brought war with the Tangut Western Xia, whose ruler Li Yuanhao declared himself emperor in 1038. Years of defeats ended with the Song paying the Tanguts off. Fan Zhongyan's Qingli reforms of 1043 tried to clean up the bureaucracy and were dropped within two years. In the far south the general Di Qing crushed Nong Zhigao's rising in 1053.

It was a golden age of talent all the same: the essayist Ouyang Xiu, the upright judge Bao Zheng, the young Su Shi passing the exams in 1057, and a commoner named Bi Sheng making movable type. But every one of Renzong's sons died young. In 1062 he named a cousin's son, Zhao Shu, as his heir, and died the next spring.

claims.text: Rivals swapped the newborn prince for a skinned civet cat.
claims.note: The story comes from Yuan and Ming plays and novels about Judge Bao. The history only says Empress Liu raised Consort Li's son as her own.

claims.text: From 1023 the Song state issued paper money, the jiaozi, the first government banknotes anywhere.
claims.note: The official note bureau in Sichuan is well recorded. Merchants there had issued notes before the state took over.

claims.text: He deposed his first empress after she lashed out at a rival consort and scratched his neck instead.
claims.note: Told in the Song history. The quarrel and the deposition in 1033 are real; the scratch may be tidied-up court gossip.

reigns.hook: The new emperor, Yingzong, is a cousin's son who never wanted the job. Days after his accession he falls ill and starts behaving strangely.

reigns.tagline: The reluctant heir who picked a fight over his father
reigns.previously: Renzong dies with no son. A cousin's son is his heir.
paragraphs: Zhao Shu was a great-grandson of Taizong, raised for a time in Renzong's palace as a spare heir. When he was named crown prince he pleaded illness again and again to get out of it. Days after he took the throne in 1063 he really did fall ill, behaving so wildly that Renzong's widow, the Empress Dowager Cao, ran the government from behind a screen.

He recovered and quarrelled with her, and in 1064 the chief minister Han Qi eased her out of power. Then came the great row of the reign. Yingzong wanted to honour his birth father, the Prince of Pu, as his father. Sima Guang and the censors said an adopted heir must call him 'uncle'. The Puyi controversy raged for over a year and ended with the critics sent away.

He did one lasting thing. In 1066 he asked Sima Guang to write a history of the past, which grew into the great Zizhi Tongjian. Early in 1067, after less than four years on the throne, Yingzong died at 34. His eldest son, Shenzong, was eighteen and impatient to change everything.

claims.text: Officials fought for more than a year over what Yingzong should call his birth father.
claims.note: The Puyi debate is fully recorded in Song sources. Han Qi and Ouyang Xiu backed the emperor; Sima Guang and the censors opposed him.

claims.text: He tried again and again to refuse the title of crown prince.
claims.note: The Song history records his refusals. Heirs were expected to decline politely, but his went on unusually long.

claims.text: His illness after the accession was a mental breakdown.
claims.note: The sources describe raving and erratic behaviour. Whether it was fever, nerves or something else can't be known.

reigns.hook: Shenzong is eighteen, the treasury is empty and the army keeps losing. He is about to hand power to the most controversial minister in Song history.

reigns.tagline: The young emperor who bet everything on reform
reigns.previously: Yingzong dies after four years. His teenage son takes over.
paragraphs: Shenzong came to the throne set on fixing two things: an empty treasury and an army that kept losing. In 1069 he handed power to Wang Anshi, a brilliant, stubborn official with a plan. The New Policies poured out: cheap state loans to farmers at planting time, called the 'green sprouts'; village militias; state trading; new ways to collect tax. Wang wanted the state to grow the economy and then tax the growth.

Half the court hated it. Sima Guang led the opposition, then retired to Luoyang, where he finished his giant history, the Zizhi Tongjian, in 1084. The poet Su Shi mocked the reforms in verse, was put on trial by the Censorate, the 'Crow Terrace', in 1079, and sent into exile. Wang Anshi left office for good in 1076, but Shenzong kept many of his policies.

He wanted a war too. The campaigns against the Western Xia went badly, and in 1082 the new fortress of Yongle fell with terrible losses. Meanwhile the polymath Shen Kuo wrote down how a magnetised needle points south. Shenzong died in 1085, aged about 36. His son was a small boy, so Shenzong's mother, the Empress Dowager Gao, took charge and called Sima Guang back.

claims.text: Su Shi was put on trial for poems mocking the reforms.
claims.note: The Crow Terrace case of 1079 is well documented. He escaped with exile to Huangzhou.

claims.text: Shen Kuo gave the first clear description of the magnetic compass needle.
claims.note: His Dream Pool Essays (about 1088) are the earliest clear account of a magnetised needle used to find direction.

claims.text: The New Policies ruined ordinary farmers.
claims.note: That was the opponents' charge, repeated by later Confucian historians. Modern historians see a mixed record, with real gains for the treasury.

reigns.hook: Shenzong's son Zhezong is only eight. His grandmother, the Empress Dowager Gao, takes charge, and her first move is to send for Sima Guang.

reigns.tagline: The boy who spent eight years staring at ministers' backs
reigns.previously: Shenzong dies at about 36. His mother calls Sima Guang back.
paragraphs: Zhezong was eight when his father died, so his grandmother, the Empress Dowager Gao, ruled. She loathed the New Policies and brought back Sima Guang, who scrapped them as fast as he could before dying in 1086, the same year as his old rival Wang Anshi. The Yuanyou years that followed belonged to the conservatives, and the boy emperor was politely ignored.

Gao died in 1093 and Zhezong struck back. He named his era Shaosheng, 'carrying on the sage', meaning his father, and brought the reformers home under Zhang Dun. The conservatives were purged. Su Shi was sent further and further south, ending up on Hainan island in 1097. Zhezong also deposed his empress, Meng, in 1096 and later raised his favourite, Consort Liu, in her place.

Against the Western Xia his armies did well, pushing forts deep into contested land. But Zhezong was sickly. He died in February 1100, aged 23, and his only son had died as a baby. The Empress Dowager Xiang chose his brother Zhao Ji, Prince of Duan, a gifted painter, over Zhang Dun's loud objections.

claims.text: He later complained that in the regency years all he ever saw of his ministers were their backsides.
claims.note: The remark is reported in Song sources. It fits his anger at being sidelined, but it can't be checked word for word.

claims.text: Zhang Dun warned that the Prince of Duan was too frivolous to rule the empire.
claims.note: The exchange is in the Song history. How prophetic it sounds owes a lot to hindsight.

reigns.hook: The new emperor, Huizong, is seventeen and dazzlingly gifted with a brush. Zhang Dun said he was too frivolous to rule. Kaifeng is about to find out.

reigns.title: Huizong and the Fall of Kaifeng
reigns.tagline: The artist emperor who painted while his empire fell
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Brother of Zhezong; Qinzong his son
reigns.reignEnded: Both carried off by the Jurchens
reigns.previously: Zhezong revives his father's reforms, then dies young without a son.
paragraphs: Huizong was one of the finest artists ever to sit on a throne. He painted birds and flowers with uncanny precision and invented his own elegant 'slender gold' calligraphy. His Auspicious Cranes scroll shows birds wheeling over a palace gate. He loved Daoism, collected rare rocks and plants, and left government to the minister Cai Jing. Kaifeng was rich, crowded and busy, like the scene in the scroll Along the River During the Qingming Festival.

The convoys hauling rocks for his gardens, the Huashigang, squeezed the south-east and helped spark Fang La's huge rebellion in 1120. An outlaw named Song Jiang raided in the north, the seed of the later novel Water Margin. Then Huizong made his big mistake. In 1120 he allied with the Jurchens, whose new Jin empire was tearing apart the Liao. The Liao fell in 1125, and the Jin, having seen how feeble Song armies were, turned on the Song.

In January 1126 Huizong panicked and handed the throne to his son Qinzong. It didn't help. Kaifeng fell in January 1127. In the Jingkang Incident both emperors, thousands of the imperial clan and much of the court were marched north as prisoners. Huizong died in captivity in the far north-east in 1135. Qinzong lived on as a captive until around 1156.

claims.text: Huizong painted the Auspicious Cranes himself.
claims.note: It carries his inscription, but many 'Huizong' paintings were made by his court academy artists, and scholars argue over which are his own.

claims.text: Along the River During the Qingming Festival shows Kaifeng in Huizong's time.
claims.note: The scroll is attributed to Zhang Zeduan and usually dated to the early 12th century, but some scholars date it later or doubt it shows Kaifeng at all.

claims.text: Huizong died a prisoner of the Jin in 1135.
claims.note: Song and Jin records agree. His coffin was sent back to the Southern Song under the peace of 1141.

reigns.hook: Every prince in Kaifeng has been taken north. Every prince but one. Huizong's ninth son, Prince Kang, was away from the city, and now he is the dynasty's last hope.

reigns.tagline: The prince who got away, and the general he let die
reigns.cameToPower: Only prince to escape the Jin
reigns.previously: Kaifeng falls. Huizong, Qinzong and the court are marched north.
paragraphs: Prince Kang had been sent out of Kaifeng on a mission and missed the disaster. In June 1127 he was crowned at Yingtian, today's Shangqiu. The Jin came after him fast. Their general Wuzhu chased him over the Yangtze, and the emperor fled to sea, riding out the winter of 1129–1130 on ships off the coast. On its way back north, the Jin fleet was trapped at Huangtiandang by the general Han Shizhong.

Gaozong settled at Lin'an, today's Hangzhou. This was the Southern Song. In 1140 his best general, Yue Fei, was winning battles and pushing towards the old capital when he was ordered back. Gaozong and his chancellor Qin Hui wanted peace with the Jin. The Treaty of Shaoxing in 1141 made the Song a vassal of the Jin, with the border on the Huai River.

Yue Fei was arrested and killed in prison in January 1142. Asked for proof of his treason, Qin Hui is said to have answered: 'Perhaps there was something.' Iron statues of Qin Hui, his wife and two accomplices still kneel at Yue Fei's tomb in Hangzhou. Gaozong had no surviving son. In 1162 he handed the throne to his adopted heir, a descendant of Taizu, and lived on in comfort until 1187.

claims.text: Yue Fei was recalled by twelve gold-lacquered orders in a single day.
claims.note: The story comes from Song accounts sympathetic to Yue Fei, many gathered by his grandson Yue Ke. The number may be dramatised.

claims.text: Yue Fei's mother tattooed 'serve the country with utmost loyalty' on his back.
claims.note: The Song Shi says words like these were on his back at his trial. The scene with his mother is a much later addition from fiction and opera.

claims.text: Gaozong let Yue Fei die because victory might bring his brother Qinzong home to reclaim the throne.
claims.note: A popular explanation since the Ming. Historians point out that Gaozong also shared the old Song fear of over-mighty generals.

reigns.hook: Gaozong hands the throne to his adopted son Xiaozong, from the founder Taizu's line. Xiaozong's first act is to clear Yue Fei's name. His second is to march north.

reigns.tagline: The emperor who wanted the north back, and settled for peace
reigns.previously: Gaozong steps down, handing the throne to his adopted son Xiaozong.
paragraphs: Zhao Shen was not Gaozong's son at all. He came from the line of the founder Taizu, which had lost the throne to Taizu's brother back in 976, and he was picked out of a crowd of distant cousins as a small boy and raised in the palace. When Gaozong retired in 1162, the throne went back to Taizu's family for good.

Within weeks he cleared Yue Fei's name and gave the dead general a proper burial. Then he went to war. In 1163 his army marched north and fell apart at Fuli. The Longxing peace of 1164 was still better than the old deal: the Song emperor became the Jin emperor's 'nephew' instead of his vassal, and the yearly payments shrank.

After that Xiaozong ruled a rich, calm south for 25 years, the best-run stretch of the Southern Song. He waited on old Gaozong dutifully in his retirement palace. When Gaozong finally died in 1187, Xiaozong mourned hard, and in 1189 he handed the throne to his son and retired too.

claims.text: Xiaozong gave up the throne so he could mourn Gaozong properly.
claims.note: That's the reason he gave, and the Song Shi accepts it. Historians add that he was over 60, tired, and had seen his northern hopes fail.

claims.text: Gaozong chose between two boys after one kicked a cat that walked past, and picked the one who sat still.
claims.note: A story told in Song anecdote collections. The real choice took years, with both boys raised in the palace.

claims.text: Xiaozong posthumously restored Yue Fei's titles and gave him a state reburial.
claims.note: Recorded in the Song Shi. Later emperors kept adding honours, and Yue Fei's temple at Hangzhou grew from it.

reigns.hook: Xiaozong retires to watch his son rule. But the new emperor is fragile, and his wife is the most feared woman in the palace.
