reigns.tagline: A broken emperor who would not visit his own father
reigns.reignEnded: Forced to abdicate by his ministers
reigns.previously: Xiaozong steps down to mourn Gaozong. His son Zhao Dun takes over.
paragraphs: Zhao Dun had waited a long time, and the throne did not suit him. He was nervous and sickly, and within a couple of years his mind seemed to be going. His wife, Empress Li, ran the inner palace and made sure nobody came between them. She also made sure he stayed away from his father.

The story goes that Guangzong once admired the hands of a palace maid who was helping him wash. Soon after, the empress sent him a food box. Inside were the maid's hands. While he was away at a sacrifice she had his favourite consort killed too, and he came back half mad with shock.

The retired Xiaozong lived just across the city, but his son refused to visit him, even when he was dying. When Xiaozong died in June 1194, Guangzong would not lead the funeral. For a filial Confucian court this was a scandal. The ministers Zhao Ruyu and Han Tuozhou, with the old dowager Empress Wu, put his son on the throne in July 1194. Guangzong lived on, confused, until 1200.

claims.text: Empress Li sent Guangzong the severed hands of a maid he had admired.
claims.note: Told in the Song Shi's life of Empress Li. Official historians disliked her, and the tale may have grown in the telling.

claims.text: Guangzong suffered from a mental illness that left him unfit to rule.
claims.note: Song records describe his breakdown in detail. What exactly was wrong with him can't be diagnosed now.

claims.text: The emperor refused to lead his own father's funeral.
claims.note: The Song Shi and other Song records agree. It was the excuse the court needed to replace him.

reigns.hook: The court pushes the imperial robe on Guangzong's son, Zhao Kuo. He doesn't want it. The men who made him emperor will soon be at each other's throats.

reigns.tagline: Two strongmen ran his empire, and one lost his head
reigns.cameToPower: Put on the throne in a palace coup
reigns.previously: Guangzong won't bury his father. The ministers force him to step down.
paragraphs: Zhao Kuo cried that he couldn't do it, and had to be pushed into the yellow robe. He was a gentle, quiet man and stayed in the background for 30 years. Real power went to Han Tuozhou, a nephew of the old dowager Empress Wu. Han pushed out his partner Zhao Ruyu and banned the 'false learning' of Zhu Xi and his followers in 1196. Zhu Xi died in disgrace in 1200.

In 1206 Han went to war with the Jin to win back the north. It failed. In late 1207 the minister Shi Miyuan and Empress Yang had Han ambushed and killed on his way to court, and his head was sent to the Jin to buy peace. Shi Miyuan then ran the government for the rest of the reign and beyond, 25 years in all.

Far to the north, Genghis Khan took the Jin capital, today's Beijing, in 1215. The Song stopped paying the Jin and the two fought on. Ningzong's sons all died young. His adopted heir, Zhao Hong, hated Shi Miyuan and said so. When Ningzong died in September 1224, Shi Miyuan acted that same night.

claims.text: Ningzong burst into tears and ran from the robe when told he was emperor.
claims.note: Song accounts tell it to show his modesty. Reluctance was expected of a new ruler, so it may be partly ritual.

claims.text: Han Tuozhou's head was sent to the Jin as the price of peace.
claims.note: The Song Shi records that his head was handed over under the peace of 1208.

claims.text: Zhao Hong pointed at a map of Hainan and said he would send Shi Miyuan there.
claims.note: The story says a lute girl planted by Shi Miyuan reported it. It explains Shi's coup neatly, which makes it suspect.

reigns.hook: Shi Miyuan has a secret candidate ready: Zhao Yun, a distant cousin who grew up far from the palace. By morning the heir is out and Zhao Yun is emperor.

reigns.tagline: He helped the Mongols kill the Jin, and invited them in
reigns.cameToPower: Shi Miyuan's swap on the night
reigns.previously: Ningzong dies. Shi Miyuan swaps the heir for his own man overnight.
paragraphs: Zhao Yun was a tenth-generation descendant of Taizu who had grown up with a commoner's life in Shaoxing. Shi Miyuan found him, trained him, and swapped him in for the heir. The pushed-aside Zhao Hong was killed after rebels used his name in 1225. Lizong let Shi Miyuan rule until the old man died in 1233, and only then began to govern himself.

In 1234 the Song joined the Mongols to finish off the Jin. Then the Song tried to grab the old capitals of Kaifeng and Luoyang for themselves. The Mongols threw them out and war began. It dragged on for decades. In 1259 the Great Khan Möngke died besieging the Song fortress of Diaoyu, and his brother Kublai, fighting at Ezhou, hurried north to claim the throne.

Lizong made Zhu Xi's teaching the official orthodoxy in 1241, a choice that shaped Chinese schooling for centuries. In later years he let the chancellor Jia Sidao take charge. He died in 1264 with no son, and his nephew followed. Even death gave him no peace: when the Mongols ruled, a Tibetan monk dug up the Song tombs and turned Lizong's skull into a drinking bowl.

claims.text: Jia Sidao made a secret deal with Kublai at Ezhou in 1259 and hid it from the court.
claims.note: Yuan sources say he offered tribute. Song records called the Mongol retreat a victory. Historians still argue how much he promised.

claims.text: The monk Yang Lianzhenjia made Lizong's skull into a ritual drinking bowl.
claims.note: Recorded in Yuan and early Ming writings. The Hongwu Emperor is said to have found the skull and reburied it in 1369.

claims.text: Lizong made Zhu Xi's Neo-Confucianism state orthodoxy in 1241.
claims.note: Song records show Zhu Xi and other masters placed in the Confucian temple that year. The Yuan made his commentaries the exam texts.

reigns.hook: Lizong is dead and his heir is his nephew Zhao Qi, a young man people whisper is slow. Jia Sidao is happy to do his thinking for him.

reigns.tagline: The slow emperor who left it all to Jia Sidao
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Nephew and adopted son of Lizong
reigns.previously: Lizong dies with no son. His nephew Zhao Qi takes the throne.
paragraphs: Zhao Qi was the son of Lizong's brother. Court gossip said his mother had tried to end the pregnancy with drugs, and that he was slow because of it. He learned to talk late and was never sharp. Lizong had made him heir anyway, because there was nobody else.

Jia Sidao ran the empire. He was clever and hard-working, but he lived grandly by West Lake and was famous for loving cricket fights, even writing a book about them. Meanwhile Kublai renamed his empire the Yuan in 1271 and turned on the Song for good.

The key was Xiangyang, a twin fortress on the Han River. It held out for five years from 1268. Then in 1273 engineers from Persia built counterweight trebuchets that threw huge stones over the walls, and the city surrendered. The road to the Yangtze was open. A year later, in August 1274, Duzong died at 34, leaving three little sons.

claims.text: Duzong was slow because his mother took drugs to end her pregnancy.
claims.note: Told in Song sources. It is the kind of explanation courts gave for a weak ruler, and can't be checked.

claims.text: Jia Sidao wrote a book on fighting crickets.
claims.note: A Book of Crickets has long carried his name. Whether he wrote it or it was pinned on him is not certain.

claims.text: Persian engineers' counterweight trebuchets broke the siege of Xiangyang.
claims.note: The Yuan Shi names Ismail and Ala al-Din, sent by the Ilkhan Abaqa. Persian historians also record them.

reigns.hook: Duzong leaves three small boys. The middle one, aged two, gets the throne. Kublai's great general Bayan is already marching down the Yangtze.

reigns.tagline: A toddler handed over his empire, then became a monk
reigns.previously: Duzong dies at 34. Xiangyang has fallen and Bayan is coming.
paragraphs: Zhao Xian was a toddler, so his grandmother, the Grand Empress Dowager Xie, ruled. Bayan's army came down the Yangtze in 1275. Jia Sidao led out the Song army and it collapsed at Dingjiazhou. The court sent him into exile, and on the road an officer who hated him killed him.

Nothing could stop Bayan now. In early 1276 the empress dowager sent the imperial seal to his camp and Lin'an surrendered without a fight. The boy emperor, his mother and the court were taken north to Kublai's capital. Kublai treated them kindly and made the boy a duke.

His later life was stranger than his reign. As a young man he was sent to Tibet, became a Buddhist monk, and translated scriptures. In 1323, now about 52, he was ordered to kill himself. One story says a poem he wrote seemed to long for the Song.

claims.text: Zhao Xian was put to death in 1323 because of a poem.
claims.note: Later Chinese accounts say a poem about a swallow was read as missing the Song. The exact charge and place are uncertain.

claims.text: Jia Sidao was killed in a latrine by the officer Zheng Huchen, who was escorting him into exile.
claims.note: Told in Song and Yuan accounts. That Zheng killed him is widely accepted; the latrine is the detail that may be embroidery.

claims.text: The ex-emperor became a respected Buddhist monk and translator in Tibet.
claims.note: Tibetan sources record a monk of royal Song birth working on translations at Sakya.

reigns.hook: Lin'an has surrendered, but two of Duzong's sons slipped away first. Loyalists crown the elder, Zhao Shi, at Fuzhou, and the Song fights on from the sea.

reigns.tagline: A boy emperor on the run along the south coast
reigns.previously: Lin'an surrenders. The boy emperor is taken north to Kublai.
paragraphs: Two of Duzong's sons had been smuggled out of Lin'an before it fell. In June 1276 loyalists crowned the elder, Zhao Shi, aged six, at Fuzhou. Around him were Chen Yizhong, the general Zhang Shijie and the scholar Lu Xiufu. Out in the field, Wen Tianxiang raised troops for them.

The Yuan kept coming, and the court took to the sea. They tried the great port of Quanzhou, but its trade commissioner Pu Shougeng shut the gates and went over to the Yuan. The fleet drifted down the coast from one island and harbour to the next.

In a storm the boy's ship was wrecked and he fell into the sea. He was pulled out, but he never recovered. He died in May 1278 on a small island off Guangdong, aged eight. Many wanted to give up. Lu Xiufu refused: as long as one Song prince lived, there was still a Song.

claims.text: Pu Shougeng closed Quanzhou to the Song court and went over to the Mongols.
claims.note: Song and Yuan records agree. He was a powerful merchant of Arab or Persian descent who had run the port's sea trade.

claims.text: Duanzong never recovered from nearly drowning when his ship was wrecked.
claims.note: The Song Shi links his illness and death to the shipwreck. Exactly what killed a boy on the run can't be known.

claims.text: Duanzong died on Gangzhou, an island off Guangdong.
claims.note: Which island Gangzhou was is argued over: Naozhou near Zhanjiang and Lantau, now part of Hong Kong, are both claimed.

reigns.hook: Duanzong is dead at eight. Lu Xiufu crowns his little brother Zhao Bing and leads the last Song fleet to the bay of Yamen.

reigns.tagline: The last Song emperor went into the sea at seven
reigns.cameToPower: Crowned by Lu Xiufu on the run
reigns.previously: Duanzong dies at eight on an island off Guangdong.
paragraphs: Zhao Bing was six when he was crowned. Lu Xiufu and Zhang Shijie took him to Yamen, a bay on the Pearl River delta, and built a camp there. Zhang Shijie chained more than a thousand ships together into a floating fortress. It was hard to break, but it couldn't move either.

Wen Tianxiang, captured on land, was brought along as a prisoner on the enemy fleet. Asked to write to Zhang Shijie urging surrender, he wrote out a poem instead, 'Crossing the Lingding Sea', ending with a line about leaving a loyal heart to shine in history.

The Yuan commander Zhang Hongfan cut the Song off from fresh water and attacked on 19 March 1279. By evening the chained fleet was lost. Lu Xiufu dressed the boy in his imperial robes, took him on his back and jumped into the sea. Thousands are said to have followed. The Song dynasty, 319 years old, was over.

claims.text: Lu Xiufu jumped into the sea with the boy emperor on his back.
claims.note: Recorded in the Song Shi. Later loyalist writings add many details, like the gold seal tied to the boy's body.

claims.text: A hundred thousand Song soldiers and courtiers drowned themselves after the emperor.
claims.note: Loyalist sources give huge figures, and bodies were said to cover the sea. The real number is unknown.

claims.text: Wen Tianxiang answered the call to surrender with his poem 'Crossing the Lingding Sea'.
claims.note: The poem survives in his collected works, with his own account of when he wrote it.

reigns.hook: The Song is gone. For the first time all of China belongs to a conqueror from the steppe: Kublai, grandson of Genghis Khan, Emperor of the Yuan since 1271.

reigns.tagline: The Mongol khan who made himself Emperor of China
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Brother of the Great Khan Möngke
reigns.previously: The Song are drowned at Yamen. Now, the man who beat them.
paragraphs: Kublai was a grandson of Genghis Khan, but he grew up curious about the settled farming world his grandfather had smashed. When his brother, the Great Khan Möngke, died in 1259, Kublai had himself elected khan at Kaiping, his summer capital, the Xanadu of later poems. His younger brother Ariq Böke claimed the title too. Kublai won the four-year civil war, but the wider Mongol empire never truly obeyed one khan again.

He built a new capital, Dadu, where Beijing stands today, and in 1271 named his dynasty Yuan. Once the Song fell in 1279 it became the first non-Han dynasty to rule all of China. He ran on paper money, pushed the Grand Canal up to his capital and had the Tibetan lama 'Phags-pa design a new script. Subjects were ranked: Mongols first, southern Chinese last. The captured Song minister Wen Tianxiang refused every offer and was executed in 1283.

Japan was the one that got away. Invasion fleets sailed in 1274 and 1281, and the second was wrecked by a typhoon the Japanese called kamikaze, the divine wind. At home Kublai lost his beloved wife Chabi in 1281 and his heir Zhenjin in 1285. He ate and drank too much, suffered badly from gout, and died in 1294 aged 78. The throne went to Zhenjin's son Temür.

claims.text: Marco Polo served Kublai for 17 years as a trusted official.
claims.note: Polo's book is the only source. No Chinese record names him, so some scholars doubt his role, though many of his details about Yuan China ring true.

claims.text: A typhoon destroyed the 1281 invasion fleet off Japan.
claims.note: Japanese and Chinese records agree on the storm. The size of the fleet, often given as over 4,000 ships, is probably inflated.

claims.text: The four-class ranking of Mongols, semu, northern and southern Chinese was a rigid caste system.
claims.note: The ranking was real in appointments and some laws, but historians argue it was applied unevenly and never set out as one formal code.

reigns.hook: Kublai has outlived his son. His grandson Temür inherits the richest empire on earth, and a family that is about to start killing each other for it.

reigns.tagline: Kublai's grandson, who decided to stop conquering
reigns.cameToPower: Chosen by the kurultai at Shangdu
reigns.previously: Kublai Khan dies at Dadu. His grandson Temür inherits.
paragraphs: Kublai's chosen heir, his son Zhenjin, had died in 1285, so the throne sat empty for three months while the family argued. Zhenjin had two grown sons. Temür had the better backers: Bayan, the general who had conquered the Song, and his own mother, Kökejin. In May 1294 the princes gathered at Shangdu and made him khan. The Chinese remember him as Chengzong.

He called off his grandfather's plans for a third go at Japan and stopped the costly wars in Vietnam. The real enemy was in Central Asia: Kaidu, a grandson of Ögedei, who had defied the Great Khans for thirty years. After a big battle in 1301 Kaidu died, and by 1304 his heirs and the other western khans made peace and accepted Temür as their overlord.

At home he kept Kublai's machinery ticking over without adding much. He liked his drink, and as his health failed his wife Bulughan took more of the work. Their only son died in 1306. When Temür died in February 1307 at 41, no heir had been named.

claims.text: Kökejin settled the contest by having the two brothers recite Genghis Khan's sayings, and Temür won.
claims.note: The story comes from the Persian historian Rashid al-Din. Chinese sources stress the backing of Bayan and the princes instead.

claims.text: Kublai had his grandson punished more than once for heavy drinking.
claims.note: Rashid al-Din tells it. It fits what is known of the family's drinking, but no Chinese source confirms it.

claims.text: The peace of about 1304 united the Mongol khanates again under one Great Khan.
claims.note: The western khans did recognise Temür, but each kept ruling his own lands. How much it meant in practice is debated.

reigns.hook: Temür is dead with no son. His widow Bulughan wants a cousin of her choosing on the throne. Out on the Altai frontier his nephew Khaishan has an army, and Khaishan's brother is riding for Dadu.

reigns.tagline: The frontier general who spent the treasury dry
reigns.cameToPower: Backed by his army and his brother
reigns.previously: Temür dies with no son. His widow Bulughan has her own candidate.
paragraphs: Khaishan was a soldier. For years he had commanded the armies on the Altai frontier against Kaidu's heirs, and his men were loyal to him. While he marched east, his younger brother Ayurbarwada and their mother Targi got to Dadu first. They arrested Bulughan and her candidate, the prince Ananda, and held the capital. Ananda was put to death. Khaishan was enthroned at Shangdu in June 1307 and is remembered in China as Wuzong.

The brothers struck a deal. Ayurbarwada became crown prince, and after him the throne would go back to Khaishan's sons. Then Khaishan opened the treasury. Princes and loyal officers got rich gifts and grand titles, and the money ran out fast. In 1309 he tried to fix it with a new paper currency tied to silver and fresh copper coins.
None of it had time to work. In January 1311 Khaishan died at Dadu, aged just 29, and his brother took over as agreed.

claims.text: The brothers agreed that Khaishan's sons would inherit after Ayurbarwada.
claims.note: The arrangement is recorded in the Yuan Shi. It was later broken, which fed twenty years of feuding.

claims.text: Drink killed Khaishan.
claims.note: Heavy drinking ran in the family and is often blamed, but no source gives a clear cause of death.

reigns.hook: Ayurbarwada is emperor now, a prince who loves the Confucian classics. He has promised to pass the throne to Khaishan's son. Promises in this family don't last long.

reigns.tagline: The Confucian khan who brought back the exams
reigns.previously: Khaishan dies at 29. His brother steps up, as agreed.
paragraphs: Ayurbarwada had grown up with Chinese tutors and could read the classics. Remembered as Renzong, he started by sweeping out his brother's big spenders, executing several of them, and scrapping the new money. Then came his big reform. In 1313 he ordered the civil service exams brought back, with Zhu Xi's commentaries on the classics as the syllabus. The first were held in 1315, and that syllabus stayed at the heart of China's exams until 1905.

He did not rule alone. His mother Targi was a power at court, and her favourite, the minister Temüder, was greedy and hated by officials. Ayurbarwada also broke the family deal. In 1316 he made his own son Shidebala heir and sent Khaishan's elder son Kusala off to the far south-west. Kusala rebelled on the way and fled to the Chagatai khans in Central Asia. Ayurbarwada died in March 1320, aged 34.

claims.text: The Yuan held its first civil service examinations in 1315.
claims.note: Recorded in the Yuan Shi. Quotas let Mongols and Central Asians compete on easier terms than Chinese candidates.

claims.text: Zhu Xi's commentaries stayed the core of the exams until 1905.
claims.note: The Ming and Qing kept the Yuan syllabus. The Qing abolished the exam system in 1905.

claims.text: Targi and Temüder really ran the government.
claims.note: The Yuan Shi paints them as all-powerful, but historians argue over how far the emperor was sidelined.

reigns.hook: Ayurbarwada is dead. His son Shidebala is 18, keen to reform, and surrounded by his grandmother's men. Khaishan's sons have not forgotten the broken promise.

reigns.tagline: The young reformer murdered in his tent
reigns.previously: Ayurbarwada dies. His teenage son inherits the throne, and the feud.
paragraphs: Shidebala, remembered as Yingzong, was 18 and serious. For his first two years his grandmother Targi and her minister Temüder still called the shots, and Temüder had critics put to death. The young emperor leaned on another minister, Baiju, a descendant of one of Kublai's great generals, and waited.

In 1322 both Temüder and Targi died. Shidebala moved fast. He stripped Temüder of his honours, purged his people, cut court spending and in 1323 issued a new law code, the Da Yuan tongzhi. Temüder's friends saw where it was going. On 4 September 1323, while the court camped at Nanpo on the road from Shangdu to Dadu, plotters led by Tegshi, Temüder's adopted son, burst into the imperial tent and killed Shidebala and Baiju. He was 21.

claims.text: Shidebala and Baiju were murdered in the imperial tent at Nanpo by Tegshi's band.
claims.note: The assassination is recorded in the Yuan Shi and was a public scandal at the time.

claims.text: Yesün Temür knew about the plot before it happened.
claims.note: The plotters sent word to him in advance, and his warning came too late. Historians are unsure how innocent he was.

reigns.hook: The emperor is dead and the killers need a new one. Far away on the Mongolian steppe sits a prince with the old homeland's armies behind him: Yesün Temür.

reigns.tagline: The steppe khan who punished his cousin's killers
reigns.previously: Shidebala is stabbed to death in his tent at Nanpo.
paragraphs: Yesün Temür was a great-grandson of Kublai through Zhenjin's eldest son, Kammala. He had spent his life on the steppe guarding the Mongol homeland and its great camps, and he had the soldiers there behind him. In October 1323 he was enthroned by the Kherlen river in Mongolia. Then he did something the plotters hadn't bargained for. He came south and had Tegshi and the other killers executed.

After that he ruled quietly. Much of the work went to his Muslim minister, Dawlat Shah, and the court leaned towards steppe ways more than Chinese ones. In 1324 he named his small son Ragibagh crown prince. He died at Shangdu in August 1328, aged 34. He never got a temple name, the honour every Chinese emperor received, so he is known by his era name: the Taiding Emperor.

claims.text: Yesün Temür has no temple name because the side that won in 1328 refused him one.
claims.note: The Yuan Shi lists him without one; he is named after his reign era, Taiding. His son's line lost the civil war that followed.

claims.text: He let the killers in on the deal and only turned on them once he was safe.
claims.note: His execution of the plotters is recorded. Whether he had agreed to anything beforehand rests on suspicion, not proof.

reigns.hook: Yesün Temür is dead at Shangdu, and his minister Dawlat Shah dithers about crowning the boy. In Dadu a general named El Temür has other plans, and they involve Khaishan's sons.

reigns.tagline: The boy khan who vanished from the record
reigns.cameToPower: Crowned at Shangdu by Dawlat Shah
reigns.previously: Yesün Temür dies at Shangdu. Two capitals, and two khans coming.
paragraphs: Ragibagh had been crown prince since he was four. When his father died, the court at Shangdu was slow to crown him, and that gave the other side its chance. On 8 September 1328 the general El Temür, whose family had served Khaishan, seized Dadu and declared for Khaishan's sons. Only in October did Dawlat Shah crown the boy at Shangdu, under the era name Tianshun.

This was the War of the Two Capitals. Shangdu's armies pushed towards Dadu through the mountain passes, and El Temür beat them back. Then another force swung round and surrounded Shangdu itself, which surrendered in November 1328. Dawlat Shah was later put to death. Of the eight-year-old khan, nothing more is heard.

claims.text: Nobody knows what happened to Ragibagh.
claims.note: After Shangdu surrendered he simply drops out of the record. Most historians assume he was quietly killed.

claims.text: Ragibagh was a real emperor.
claims.note: The official Yuan Shi, following the winners, does not count him. Many modern lists do, since he was properly crowned at Shangdu.

reigns.hook: Dadu has won. Khaishan's younger son Tugh Temür is on the throne, but he says he is only keeping it warm. His elder brother Kusala is still in Central Asia.

images.caption: No portrait of Ragibagh exists; these are the ruins of Shangdu, where he was crowned and where his side surrendered.

reigns.tagline: Crowned by a coup, he promised the throne away
reigns.cameToPower: Put up by El Temür's coup at Dadu
reigns.reignEnded: Stood down for his elder brother
reigns.previously: Shangdu surrenders and the boy khan Ragibagh disappears.
paragraphs: Tugh Temür, Khaishan's younger son, had spent the 1320s being moved out of the way. Shidebala sent him to Hainan island, and Yesün Temür kept him in the south at Jiankang and Jiangling. Then in September 1328 El Temür took Dadu in his name and sent for him. He was enthroned there on 16 October 1328. The Chinese remember him as Wenzong.

He made a striking promise. He held the throne, he said, only until his elder brother Kusala could come home from Central Asia. Once Shangdu fell he kept his word, at least on paper. Envoys went west, Kusala was enthroned in Mongolia in February 1329, and that spring Tugh Temür handed over the imperial seal. Kusala named him crown prince in return.

claims.text: Tugh Temür was exiled to Hainan island under Shidebala.
claims.note: The Yuan Shi records the banishment in 1321. It kept a possible rival far from both capitals.

claims.text: Tugh Temür never meant to give up real power.
claims.note: He did hand over the seal. But El Temür, who had made him, stood to lose everything if Kusala's own men took over, and many historians read the abdication as a holding move.

reigns.hook: Kusala is emperor at last, after thirteen years in exile. He is travelling south with his Central Asian followers to meet the brother who stood aside for him.

reigns.tagline: Thirteen years in exile, six months as emperor
reigns.previously: Tugh Temür wins the civil war, then offers his brother the throne.
paragraphs: Kusala was Khaishan's elder son, the one his uncle Ayurbarwada had cheated. Sent to the far south-west in 1316, he rebelled, failed and fled to the Chagatai khans in Central Asia. He lived there for thirteen years, and his son Toghon Temür was born there. The Chinese remember him as Mingzong.

On 27 February 1329 the princes enthroned him north of Karakorum, and he named his brother Tugh Temür crown prince. El Temür came out to bring him the imperial seal. Kusala's Central Asian followers expected the top jobs. He travelled slowly south and on 26 August met his brother at Ongghuchad, near Shangdu. There was a feast. Four days later Kusala was dead, and Tugh Temür was emperor again.

claims.text: Kusala was poisoned on the orders of El Temür, with or without his brother's knowledge.
claims.note: Widely suspected then and now, given who gained. The Yuan Shi says only that he died suddenly.

claims.text: Kusala spent his exile in the lands of the Chagatai khans.
claims.note: The Yuan Shi and Persian sources agree he took refuge with the Chagatai khan after his failed revolt of 1316.

reigns.hook: Kusala is dead four days after the family feast. Tugh Temür takes the throne back, and El Temür is now the most powerful man in the empire.

reigns.tagline: The scholar emperor who ruled in El Temür's shadow
reigns.previously: Kusala dies four days after a family feast at Ongghuchad.
paragraphs: Tugh Temür was restored at Shangdu on 8 September 1329. El Temür took the top offices, married into the imperial family and ran the government. The emperor turned to culture. He was a gifted calligrapher and painter, founded the Kuizhang Pavilion as an academy for art and learning, and had scholars compile a vast handbook of how the empire was governed, the Jingshi dadian, finished in 1331.

Kusala's family was a threat, so he dealt with it. Kusala's son Toghon Temür was sent into exile, first to an island off Korea and then to Guangxi in the far south, and Tugh Temür had it put about that the boy was not really Kusala's son. Then Tugh Temür fell ill. He died at Shangdu on 2 September 1332, aged 28, and left word that Kusala's line should have the throne.

claims.text: On his deathbed Tugh Temür asked for Kusala's son to succeed, out of remorse for his brother's death.
claims.note: The wish itself is reported in the Yuan Shi and was why his widow chose Kusala's sons. The guilty motive is guesswork.

claims.text: Tugh Temür declared that Toghon Temür was not Kusala's son.
claims.note: The Yuan Shi records the claim; it was a way to bar the boy from the throne. Later legends ran wild with it.

reigns.hook: The emperor is dead. His widow Budashiri chooses Kusala's younger son, a little boy of six, over her own child. El Temür is not pleased.

reigns.tagline: The six-year-old emperor who lasted 53 days
reigns.previously: Tugh Temür dies at Shangdu, asking for Kusala's line to rule.
paragraphs: El Temür wanted Tugh Temür's son El Tegüs on the throne. The widowed empress Budashiri said no. Her husband had asked for Kusala's line, and she held to it, passing over her own son. So on 23 October 1332 Kusala's younger son Rinchinbal, aged six, was enthroned at Dadu. He is remembered as Ningzong.

He fell ill almost at once and died on 14 December 1332, after 53 days on the throne. El Temür tried again for El Tegüs. Budashiri again refused and sent for Kusala's elder son, Toghon Temür, still in exile in Guangxi. El Temür stalled for months, and the throne stood empty until he died in 1333.

claims.text: Rinchinbal reigned for only 53 days.
claims.note: The dates of his enthronement and death are both recorded in the Yuan Shi.

claims.text: Budashiri chose Kusala's sons over her own to obey her husband's dying wish.
claims.note: That is the official account. She may also have feared that El Temür would rule through El Tegüs and sideline her.

reigns.hook: With El Temür dead, the way is clear. A 13-year-old boy is fetched from exile in the far south to be crowned. He will be the last Mongol emperor to rule China.

reigns.tagline: The last Yuan emperor in China, who ran from Dadu
reigns.reignEnded: Ming founded; fled Dadu that year
reigns.previously: The boy emperor Rinchinbal dies after 53 days.
paragraphs: Toghon Temür was 13 when he was crowned in July 1333. The Ming would call him Shundi. For seven years the minister Bayan ran everything. Bayan distrusted the Chinese, cancelled the exams in 1335 and, the story goes, suggested killing everyone named Zhang, Wang, Liu, Li or Zhao. In 1340 Bayan's own nephew Toghto turned on him with the emperor's blessing, and Bayan died in exile. Toghto brought the exams back and had the histories of the Song, Liao and Jin compiled by 1345.

In 1344 the Yellow River burst its banks and changed course. In 1351 Toghto sent a huge workforce to dig a new channel. That year the Red Turbans, followers of the White Lotus sect, rose in revolt. Paper money collapsed and the south broke up into rebel states. Toghto was winning at Gaoyou in 1354 when the emperor, listening to his enemies, dismissed him.

Out of the chaos rose Zhu Yuanzhang, an orphan who had been a monk and a beggar. He took Nanjing in 1356, crushed his rival Chen Youliang on Lake Poyang in 1363 and on 23 January 1368 proclaimed the Ming. That September his army reached Dadu. Toghon Temür fled north to the steppe and died at Yingchang in 1370.

claims.text: Bayan proposed killing everyone named Zhang, Wang, Liu, Li or Zhao.
claims.note: It comes from the Yuan Shi, compiled by the Ming, who had reason to make the Yuan look monstrous. It was never carried out.

claims.text: The rebels dug up a one-eyed stone man in the Yellow River works, carved with a prophecy of revolt.
claims.note: Told in accounts of the Red Turban rising. If the statue existed, rebel leaders most likely buried it there to be found.

claims.text: Lake Poyang in 1363 was one of the largest naval battles in history.
claims.note: The Ming histories give hundreds of thousands of men on each side. Historians accept it was huge but doubt the exact figures.

reigns.hook: A beggar monk now sits on the throne at Nanjing. He remembers having no land to bury his parents in, and he trusts nobody with power.

reigns.tagline: From begging bowl to the dragon throne
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Rebel who drove out the Yuan
reigns.previously: The Mongols flee Dadu. A peasant rebel has founded the Ming.
paragraphs: Zhu Yuanzhang was born dirt poor. In 1344 famine and plague killed his parents and eldest brother within weeks, and he later wrote that the family had no land to bury them in. He became a novice monk, begged on the roads, then joined the rebels. Twenty-four years later he was emperor. He ruled from Nanjing as the Hongwu Emperor, with Empress Ma at his side, remembered by the histories as brave and kind.

He rebuilt the countryside with land surveys and the Yellow Registers, which listed every household for tax and labour. But he was ferociously suspicious. In 1380 he had his chancellor Hu Weiyong executed for treason, abolished the post for good and ran the government himself. The purge rolled on for years, and another hit the general Lan Yu in 1393. His secret police, the Embroidered Uniform Guard, made the arrests, and officials were flogged in open court.

His heir, Zhu Biao, died in 1392. Hongwu passed over his own grown sons and named Zhu Biao's teenage son, Zhu Yunwen. When the old emperor died in June 1398, the young man became the Jianwen Emperor, with a ring of powerful uncles watching him.

claims.text: The Hu Weiyong purge killed about 30,000 people.
claims.note: The figure comes from Ming records and later histories and covers executions spread over more than a decade. It can't be checked precisely.

claims.text: Empress Ma had big, unbound feet.
claims.note: A popular tradition that fits her humble origins and her bold character. It comes from later stories, not from her official biography.

claims.text: Hongwu's ugly portraits show his real face, and the handsome ones were painted to flatter him.
claims.note: Both types survive. Why there are two is unknown; the tale that he punished honest painters is a later story with no solid evidence.

reigns.hook: Jianwen's advisers want to cut his uncles down to size. The toughest uncle, the Prince of Yan, sits in Beijing with a battle-hardened army.

reigns.tagline: The grandson who took on his uncles and vanished
reigns.previously: The Hongwu Emperor dies. His grandson Zhu Yunwen inherits.
paragraphs: Zhu Yunwen was a gentle, bookish young man, raised on the classics. His grandfather had given his many sons big princedoms along the frontier, with real armies. The new emperor's advisers, Huang Zicheng and Qi Tai, told him those uncles were a threat. So he struck first. Within a year five princes were stripped of their titles. The Prince of Xiang, facing arrest, set fire to his own palace and died in it.

The most dangerous uncle, Zhu Di, Prince of Yan, held Beijing. In August 1399 he rebelled, claiming he only wanted to rescue his nephew from bad advisers. The court's armies outnumbered him, but its generals were poor. Yan's cavalry won battle after battle, then cut south past the strongholds. In July 1402 the general Li Jinglong opened a gate of Nanjing to the rebels.

The palace went up in flames. Bodies were pulled from the ashes and said to be the emperor's, but nobody could be sure. Zhu Di took the throne and wiped his nephew's years out of the official calendar, counting them as the last years of Hongwu. The Jianwen reign title was only restored in 1595, under the Wanli Emperor.

claims.text: The Jianwen Emperor escaped the burning palace disguised as a Buddhist monk and lived out his life in hiding.
claims.note: Stories of his wanderings spread within decades and grew in later Ming fiction. No body was clearly identified, which kept them alive, but nothing proves he survived.

claims.text: The Yongle Emperor erased the Jianwen years from the records, dating them as Hongwu 32 to 35.
claims.note: The official Ming records follow this. The Jianwen era name was restored in 1595, and he got a temple name only in 1644, as the dynasty fell.

reigns.hook: The Prince of Yan is now the Yongle Emperor. Nanjing's scholars must decide whether to serve the man who burned out their emperor, and one of them will refuse.

reigns.relationToPredecessor: Uncle of Jianwen; son of Hongwu
reigns.previously: Nanjing falls, the palace burns and the Jianwen Emperor vanishes.
paragraphs: The young Jianwen Emperor began stripping his uncles of their princedoms. In 1399 the eldest surviving one, Zhu Di, Prince of Yan, rebelled from Beijing. After three years of war he took Nanjing in July 1402. The palace went up in flames and Jianwen vanished. Zhu Di became the Yongle Emperor and punished anyone who had stayed loyal. The scholar Fang Xiaoru refused to draft his proclamation and was executed along with hundreds of his relatives.

Then he went big. The eunuch admiral Zheng He led huge fleets to South-East Asia, India, Arabia and East Africa, seven voyages between 1405 and 1433. In 1414 a giraffe from East Africa reached the court and was hailed as a qilin, a lucky beast of legend. Scholars compiled the Yongle Encyclopedia, over 11,000 volumes. His armies invaded Vietnam in 1407. And he moved the capital to Beijing, where the new Forbidden City was ready in 1421.

He led five campaigns into Mongolia in person. Coming home from the last one, in August 1424, he died in the field aged 64. His son, a heavy, bookish man, took the throne and began cancelling his father's costly schemes.

claims.text: The Jianwen Emperor escaped the burning palace disguised as a monk.
claims.note: The official line was that he died in the fire, but no body was clearly identified. The Ming Shi says rumours of his escape were one reason Zheng He's fleets were sent out.

claims.text: Fang Xiaoru's family was wiped out to the 'ten degrees', 873 people in all.
claims.note: Later accounts give totals in the hundreds, often 873. Adding his students as a tenth 'degree' of kin may be a later embellishment.

claims.text: A giraffe brought to the court in 1414 was hailed as a qilin.
claims.note: A court painting of the animal with the official Shen Du's poem of praise survives in a later copy.

reigns.hook: Yongle dies on the steppe. His heavy, bookish son Zhu Gaozhi, the Hongxi Emperor, has waited twenty years as heir. He has very different ideas about what the empire should spend.

reigns.tagline: Ten months to undo his father's grand schemes
reigns.previously: The Yongle Emperor dies on his way home from Mongolia.
paragraphs: Zhu Gaozhi was nothing like his warrior father. He was heavy, slow on his feet and happiest with books. Yongle often thought about passing him over for his bold younger brother, Zhu Gaoxu, but the bookish son kept his place as heir for twenty years. While his father campaigned, he ran the government, and he learned exactly what the wars and the fleets were costing.

As emperor he moved fast. He stopped the treasure voyages and the buying missions abroad, and freed officials his father had jailed for objecting, among them the finance minister Xia Yuanji. He leaned on a trio of grand secretaries, the Three Yangs, who would guide the court for twenty years. He even ordered the capital moved back to Nanjing. Then, in May 1425, after about ten months on the throne, he died suddenly at 46.

claims.text: The Hongxi Emperor was so heavy and lame that he needed two eunuchs to hold him up.
claims.note: Accounts of his weight and bad legs come from Ming anecdotes and fit his portrait, but the vivid details are hard to check.

claims.text: He ordered the court to move back to Nanjing.
claims.note: The order is in the Ming records for 1425. His death stopped it, and Beijing stayed the capital.

reigns.hook: His son Zhu Zhanji is away in Nanjing when the news comes. He races back to Beijing. His uncle Zhu Gaoxu is watching, and thinking about another rebellion.

reigns.tagline: The painter emperor who sent out the last great fleet
reigns.previously: The Hongxi Emperor dies suddenly after ten months.
paragraphs: Zhu Zhanji had been Yongle's favourite grandson, and he had ridden on campaign with him. Within a year his uncle Zhu Gaoxu, Prince of Han, rose in revolt. The emperor marched out in person and the uncle gave up without a real fight. He was locked up in Beijing. He did not live long.

Xuande cut his losses. The Ming army in Vietnam had been bogged down for years by Lê Lợi's rebels, and in 1427 he pulled it out. In 1431 he sent Zheng He on a seventh and last great voyage, which came home in 1433. He set up a school inside the palace to teach eunuchs to read, which would give them real power later. He was a skilled painter himself, and the porcelain and bronzes made in his reign are still prized.
In 1428 he set aside Empress Hu, who had no son, and raised his favourite, Lady Sun, whose baby boy was now heir. Xuande died in January 1435, aged 35. His son was seven.

claims.text: Zhu Gaoxu tripped the emperor during a visit, so Xuande had him trapped under a huge bronze vat and roasted to death with charcoal.
claims.note: A grisly story told in later Ming writings. The official record simply has the prince and his sons put to death in prison.

claims.text: Xuande was mad about cricket fighting.
claims.note: Later Ming anecdotes say so, and fine cricket jars are linked to his kilns, but the court records are silent.

claims.text: Lady Sun's son was really the child of a palace maid, passed off as hers.
claims.note: A rumour repeated in unofficial Ming histories. The Ming Shi does not confirm it.

reigns.hook: A seven-year-old is on the throne, with his tough grandmother keeping watch. Beside the boy stands his favourite tutor, a eunuch named Wang Zhen.

reigns.tagline: The emperor who rode out to war and came back a prisoner
reigns.reignEnded: Captured by the Oirats at Tumu
reigns.previously: The Xuande Emperor dies at 35, leaving a seven-year-old son.
paragraphs: For seven years the boy's grandmother, Grand Empress Dowager Zhang, kept things steady with the Three Yangs. When she died in 1442, the young emperor turned to the man he trusted most: Wang Zhen, the eunuch who had taught him as a child. Wang Zhen ran the court, grew rich and sent armies into long, costly wars in the far south-west.

In the north, the Oirat Mongol leader Esen was squeezing the Ming over trade and tribute. In the summer of 1449 he raided the frontier. Wang Zhen talked the 21-year-old emperor into leading a vast army out himself, with no real plan. It wandered, turned back, and was caught at the post station of Tumu, without water. On 1 September 1449 the Oirats fell on it.

The army was destroyed. Wang Zhen was killed, along with dozens of senior officials. The emperor was found sitting calmly on the ground and taken prisoner. The Mongols now held the Son of Heaven, and Beijing was nearly undefended.

claims.text: Wang Zhen was killed at Tumu by one of the emperor's own officers, furious at the disaster.
claims.note: Later accounts name the guard officer Fan Zhong, who is said to have clubbed him to death. Earlier reports only say he died in the rout.

claims.text: The army that marched to Tumu was half a million strong.
claims.note: The figure appears in Ming sources but is almost certainly inflated. Frederick Mote's study of Tumu treats the numbers with caution.

reigns.hook: In Beijing, panicking officials want to flee south. The minister of war, Yu Qian, says no. He needs a new emperor, and fast: the captive's younger brother.

reigns.tagline: Crowned in a crisis, then pushed out by his own brother
reigns.cameToPower: Enthroned while his brother was captive
reigns.previously: The Zhengtong Emperor is taken prisoner by the Oirats at Tumu.
paragraphs: Zhu Qiyu, Prince of Cheng, never expected to rule. With his brother a prisoner, the minister Yu Qian and the court put him on the throne three weeks after Tumu. Some officials wanted to abandon Beijing and run to Nanjing. Yu Qian refused. In October 1449 Esen brought his captive to the walls, expecting the gates to open. They didn't. Yu Qian's troops fought him off and the Oirats rode home.

A prisoner nobody would pay for was useless, so in 1450 Esen sent the old emperor back. Jingtai gave his brother a title and locked him in the Southern Palace for seven years. In 1452 he demoted his brother's son as heir and named his own boy instead. The child died the next year, and Jingtai named nobody else.

Early in 1457 he fell seriously ill. A group of ambitious men, the general Shi Heng, the eunuch Cao Jixiang and the official Xu Youzhen, saw their chance. In February they broke into the Southern Palace at night and put the old emperor back on the throne.

claims.text: After his overthrow, Jingtai was murdered on his brother's orders.
claims.note: He died about a month later, in March 1457. Some Ming writers claimed a eunuch strangled him. The official record says he died of illness.

claims.text: Jingtai was not buried among the Ming tombs.
claims.note: He was buried as a prince in the Western Hills near Beijing. His title of emperor was only restored in 1475.

reigns.hook: The captive of Tumu is emperor again. The men who put him back want rewards. The man who saved Beijing, Yu Qian, is about to pay for it.

reigns.tagline: Back from captivity, back on the throne
reigns.previously: A night coup frees the captive of Tumu from the Southern Palace.
paragraphs: Zhu Qizhen took a new era name, Tianshun, 'Obedient to Heaven'. Within days Yu Qian, the minister who had saved Beijing in 1449, was accused of plotting and executed. The men behind the coup took the rewards. The general Shi Heng and the eunuch Cao Jixiang grew rich and arrogant, and the emperor came to fear them.

Shi Heng was arrested and died in prison in 1460. In August 1461 Cao Jixiang's adopted son, Cao Qin, launched a desperate revolt inside Beijing and set fire to palace gates before it collapsed. Cao Qin threw himself down a well, and his father was executed. The emperor had learned something in his years as a prisoner and a recluse, and he ruled more carefully this time.
Dying in February 1464, he left one order that mattered. For generations, palace women had been forced to die and be buried with Ming emperors. He banned it.

claims.text: The restored emperor ended the custom of burying consorts with dead emperors.
claims.note: His deathbed order is in the Ming records, and the practice stopped with him.

claims.text: Yu Qian was executed on a charge everyone knew was false.
claims.note: The Ming court itself cleared him in 1466. He is honoured today with a temple in Hangzhou.

reigns.hook: His heir is sixteen and deeply attached to a palace woman who once looked after him as a child. She is about seventeen years older than he is.

reigns.tagline: Devoted to a woman seventeen years older
reigns.previously: The restored emperor dies, after banning burial of his consorts.
paragraphs: Zhu Jianshen had a rough start. He was a toddler when his father was captured at Tumu, and his uncle Jingtai later took away his place as heir. Through it all a palace woman, Lady Wan, looked after him. When he became emperor he kept her as his favourite, and she ruled his heart for more than twenty years. Within a month his first empress was demoted for having Lady Wan beaten.

He cleared the name of Yu Qian, the hero his father had executed, and restored his uncle Jingtai's title. The general Yu Zijun built a long new wall along the Ordos frontier in the 1470s. But the court filled up with favourites, Daoist priests and eunuchs. In 1477 the eunuch Wang Zhi got his own secret police office, the Western Depot, which spread fear until it was closed down.
The emperor had no son he knew of until 1475, when he learned of a five-year-old boy kept hidden in the palace. Lady Wan died early in 1487. He followed her a few months later, aged 39.

claims.text: Lady Wan had other consorts' babies killed, so the heir was raised in hiding until he was five.
claims.note: The story is in the Ming Shi and later accounts. Many historians think the secret upbringing has been dramatised.

claims.text: A tiny porcelain 'chicken cup' from his kilns sold for about HK$281 million in 2014.
claims.note: The sale at Sotheby's Hong Kong was widely reported. The buyer, Liu Yiqian, then drank tea from it.

reigns.hook: The secret boy is now the emperor. He's seventeen, his mother died mysteriously when he was small, and he has a court full of his father's favourites to clear out.

reigns.tagline: The model emperor with only one wife
reigns.previously: The Chenghua Emperor dies, months after Lady Wan.
paragraphs: Zhu Youtang's mother, Lady Ji, had come to the palace as a captive from the south-west. She died suddenly soon after her son was revealed. As emperor he cleared out his father's crowd of Daoist priests, Buddhist monks and fixers. He brought in serious ministers like Liu Jian, Xie Qian and Li Dongyang, held audiences, read memorials and listened to criticism.

Ming historians later called his reign a restoration of good government. Life was not perfect: the Turfan rulers took Hami in the far west, and his empress's brothers got away with a great deal. But the court was calmer than it had been in decades. He also did something no other Ming emperor did. He had one wife, Empress Zhang, and no concubines.

Their only surviving son was a lively boy named Zhu Houzhao. In June 1505 the emperor fell ill and died at 34. On his deathbed he told his ministers his son was clever but loved to play, and asked them to guide him.

claims.text: The Hongzhi Emperor had only one wife, Empress Zhang.
claims.note: The records list no other consorts, which makes him unique among Ming emperors.

claims.text: Lady Wan had Hongzhi's mother poisoned.
claims.note: Unofficial Ming histories say so, and the timing looks suspicious. Nothing proves it.

reigns.hook: His thirteen-year-old son is emperor now. The boy loves soldiers, animals and parties, and a band of eunuchs is ready to give him all three.

reigns.tagline: He made himself a general and the palace a playground
reigns.reignEnded: Died at 29 after a boating accident
reigns.previously: The good Hongzhi Emperor dies, leaving a playful teenage son.
paragraphs: The Zhengde Emperor wanted fun, and a group of eunuchs known as the Eight Tigers gave it to him. Their leader, Liu Jin, ran the government while the emperor played. Liu Jin was finally arrested in 1510, after a fellow eunuch accused him of treason. He was executed by slicing. Zhengde moved into the Leopard Quarter, a private compound with animals, soldiers and entertainers.

He loved the army. He gave himself a made-up general's name, Zhu Shou, and in 1517 rode out to fight the Mongols at Yingzhou. When the Prince of Ning rebelled in 1519, the scholar-general Wang Yangming beat him in a matter of weeks, before the emperor had even reached the front. Zhengde marched south anyway.

On the way home in 1520 he fell out of a boat while fishing and never really recovered. He died the following April, aged 29, with no son. His mother and Grand Secretary Yang Tinghe had to pick his successor from the family.

claims.text: Zhengde wanted to capture the defeated Prince of Ning himself, so the prince was set free to be caught again.
claims.note: A colourful story from later writings. The records show the prince was handed over to the emperor and executed in 1521.

claims.text: Liu Jin's estate held vast sums of gold and silver.
claims.note: Ming sources give huge totals for what was seized from his house. Historians think the figures are inflated.

claims.text: The emperor gave orders under the name of General Zhu Shou.
claims.note: Edicts in that name survive in the Ming records, much to his ministers' horror.

reigns.hook: The choice falls on a thirteen-year-old cousin from Hubei. He arrives in Beijing and at once refuses to enter by the gate they've chosen for him.

reigns.tagline: The Daoist who hid from his own government
reigns.cameToPower: Chosen by the court as heir
reigns.reignEnded: Died after 45 years on the throne
reigns.previously: Zhengde dies with no son. His teenage cousin is chosen.
paragraphs: Zhu Houcong was a prince's son from Hubei. The officials wanted him adopted as Hongzhi's son. He refused and insisted on honouring his own father as an emperor. The row, the Great Rites Controversy, ran for years. In 1524 hundreds of officials knelt at a palace gate in protest. They were arrested and flogged, and some died of it.

He grew obsessed with Daoist rites and elixirs. In 1542 a group of palace women tried to strangle him in his sleep, but the cord was tied in a knot that wouldn't tighten. After that he barely saw his ministers, and Grand Secretary Yan Song ran things for twenty years. In 1550 Altan Khan's Mongols raided up to Beijing's walls. Along the coast pirates raided for years until generals like Qi Jiguang beat them back.

In January 1556 an earthquake in Shaanxi killed an enormous number of people; the official count was about 830,000. Near the end, the official Hai Rui sent a memorial telling the emperor bluntly he had failed his people. Jiajing had him jailed. The emperor died in January 1567 at 59, after 45 years.

claims.text: Palace women tried to strangle the Jiajing Emperor in his bed in 1542.
claims.note: The plot is in the court records. The women and two consorts accused with them were executed by slicing.

claims.text: Hai Rui bought his own coffin before sending his memorial, expecting to die for it.
claims.note: The story is in his official biography, which may have polished it to make him a model of courage.

claims.text: Jiajing was killed by his Daoist elixirs.
claims.note: His last illness fits poisoning by the mercury and arsenic in such elixirs, but the cause can't be proved.

reigns.hook: The new emperor is a son Jiajing kept at arm's length for years. He opens the prisons, Hai Rui walks free, and the court waits to see what else changes.

reigns.tagline: Five quiet years that opened the ports
reigns.previously: The Jiajing Emperor dies after 45 years on the throne.
paragraphs: Zhu Zaihou grew up barely knowing his father. Jiajing put off naming an heir for years, and the prince lived quietly outside the palace. As emperor he let his grand secretaries do the work: first Xu Jie, then Gao Gong and Zhang Juzheng. Hai Rui and others jailed by his father were freed.

Two big changes came fast. In 1567 the court let private merchants sail abroad legally from the port of Yuegang in Fujian, easing the old ban on sea trade. Silver from Japan and the Americas would soon pour in. Then in 1570 Altan Khan's grandson fled to the Ming. The court made a deal: in 1571 Altan Khan was made a Ming prince, the raids stopped and border horse markets opened.
The Longqing Emperor fell ill and died in July 1572, aged 35. His heir was an eight-year-old boy.

claims.text: Jiajing avoided his son because a Daoist told him that 'two dragons should not meet'.
claims.note: Told in later accounts of Jiajing's court. It fits his superstition, but the official record does not prove it.

claims.text: The 1571 peace with Altan Khan ended decades of Mongol raiding on the northern frontier.
claims.note: Ming records and Mongol sources agree on the deal, the title and the horse markets that followed.

reigns.hook: An eight-year-old is emperor. The grand secretary Zhang Juzheng has the boy's mother on his side, and he means to run the empire hard.

reigns.tagline: The emperor who went on strike for decades

start.note: enthroned two weeks after Longqing died

reigns.previously: The Longqing Emperor dies. His young son inherits.
paragraphs: The Wanli Emperor was eight when he came to the throne, and for ten years the grand secretary Zhang Juzheng ran the empire for him, strictly and well. He cut waste, chased tax dodgers and pushed the 'single whip' reform, rolling taxes and labour duties into one payment in silver. The treasury filled up. Then Zhang died in 1582, and the emperor, free at last, turned on him. Zhang was stripped of his honours and his family was ruined.

Wanli wanted the son of his favourite, Lady Zheng, as his heir. His ministers insisted on the eldest son. The row dragged on for some fifteen years, and the emperor answered by going on strike: for years he refused audiences, ignored memorials and left posts empty. He did not ignore everything. He sent armies to help Korea fight off Toyotomi Hideyoshi's invasions (1592–1598), and let the Jesuit Matteo Ricci live in Beijing from 1601.

Eunuchs sent out to squeeze mining and commercial taxes set off riots in city after city. In the north-east a Jurchen chief named Nurhaci was building an army, and in 1619 he smashed a big Ming force at Sarhu. Wanli died in August 1620 after 48 years on the throne, the longest Ming reign. Centuries later his tomb, Dingling, became the only Ming imperial tomb ever excavated.

claims.text: Wanli stopped running the government for decades.
claims.note: He largely stopped holding audiences from the 1590s and left many posts unfilled, but he still dealt with some business, especially war. Ray Huang's 1587 tells the story.

claims.text: The emperor was delighted by the chiming clocks Ricci gave him.
claims.note: Ricci's own journals say the clocks won him his place in Beijing. Wanli never actually received Ricci face to face.

claims.text: Red Guards burned the remains of Wanli and his empresses in 1966.
claims.note: Widely reported, including by people involved in the dig. Accounts differ on exactly what was destroyed, and many finds had already decayed after the 1950s excavation.

reigns.hook: Up in the north-east, Nurhaci has already declared his own dynasty. The Ming have a rival now, and he's only getting started.

reigns.title: Nurhaci and Hong Taiji
reigns.tagline: Thirteen suits of armour and a dream of an empire
reigns.cameToPower: Proclaimed khan of the Later Jin
reigns.previously: The Wanli Emperor sulks in Beijing while the frontier slips away.
paragraphs: Nurhaci was a chief of the Jianzhou Jurchens, in the forests north-east of the Ming border. In 1583 his father and grandfather were killed by the Ming's allies, and he set out for revenge with, the story goes, thirteen suits of armour. He fought and married his way to leading the Jurchens, organised them into the Eight Banners and had a script adapted from Mongolian in 1599. In 1616 he proclaimed himself khan of the Later Jin.

In 1618 he declared Seven Grievances against the Ming and went to war. At Sarhu in 1619 he destroyed a Ming army that had marched in four separate columns. He took Liaodong and made Shenyang, which the Manchus called Mukden, his capital in 1625. Then at Ningyuan in 1626 he met Yuan Chonghuan and his Portuguese-style cannon, and lost a battle for the first time. He died that September.

His son Hong Taiji turned a war band into a state. He welcomed Chinese officers and gunners who came over, renamed his people Manchus in 1635 and proclaimed the Qing dynasty in 1636. Korea was forced to submit in 1637. He died suddenly in September 1643, and the princes chose his five-year-old son, with Hong Taiji's half-brother Dorgon as regent.

claims.text: Nurhaci started out with just thirteen suits of armour inherited from his father and grandfather.
claims.note: Told in the Qing official records, it's the dynasty's founding story of rising from almost nothing.

claims.text: A cannon wound at Ningyuan killed Nurhaci.
claims.note: Ming sources claimed he was hit. Qing records say only that he fell ill months later.

claims.text: Hong Taiji renamed the Jurchens 'Manchu' in 1635.
claims.note: His decree is in the Qing records. Where the word Manchu itself came from is still argued over.

reigns.hook: Back in Beijing, the Ming have troubles of their own. Wanli's son Zhu Changluo, the Taichang Emperor, is about to take the throne, swallow a red pill and die within the month.

reigns.tagline: Kept waiting 38 years, then gone in a month
reigns.previously: The Wanli Emperor dies after 48 years on the throne.
paragraphs: Zhu Changluo's mother was a palace maid, and his father never loved either of them. Wanli wanted Lady Zheng's son as heir. Officials fought him for some fifteen years until, in 1601, Changluo was finally named crown prince. In 1615 a man carrying a wooden club got into his palace and hurt a eunuch before he was caught. Rumours pointed at Lady Zheng's people.

He came to the throne at last in August 1620 and made a good start. He sent a million taels of silver from his father's hoard to the troops in the north-east and scrapped the hated mining taxes. Then, about ten days in, he fell ill. A eunuch gave him a purge. An official named Li Kezhuo offered red pills. He took two, and died the next morning, 26 September, after about a month on the throne.

claims.text: The red pills killed the Taichang Emperor.
claims.note: The Red Pill Case was fought over by court factions for years. He was already seriously ill, and some blamed the purge given to him earlier.

claims.text: Lady Zheng was behind the man with the club in 1615.
claims.note: The attacker was linked to eunuchs in her service, but Wanli had the case closed quickly and the full story never came out.

reigns.hook: His fourteen-year-old son is heir. But the dead emperor's favourite consort has the boy with her in the emperor's palace, and she won't move out.

reigns.tagline: The boy who loved his workbench more than his court
reigns.previously: The Taichang Emperor dies a month into his reign.
paragraphs: First the officials had to get the boy out of a consort's hands. Lady Li had kept him with her in the emperor's palace, and officials led by Yang Lian and Zuo Guangdou forced her to move out. Once crowned, the Tianqi Emperor left the government to his old wet nurse, Madam Ke, and her ally, the eunuch Wei Zhongxian. Wei ran the secret police, and officials across the empire built shrines to him while he was still alive.

The Donglin scholars who attacked him were destroyed. In 1625 Yang Lian, Zuo Guangdou and others were tortured to death in prison, and more fell in 1626. That May a huge blast at the Wanggongchang gunpowder works flattened a district of Beijing. On the frontier Yuan Chonghuan, with Western-style cannon, held Ningyuan against Nurhaci early in 1626.
In 1627 the emperor fell ill, weakened, some said, by a boating accident on a palace lake. He died on 30 September, aged 21. None of his children had lived, so the throne went to his younger brother.

claims.text: Tianqi cared more about carpentry than ruling.
claims.note: Widely told in later Ming and Qing writings. His woodworking may have been exaggerated to explain how Wei Zhongxian got so much power.

claims.text: Officials across the empire built living shrines to Wei Zhongxian.
claims.note: Dozens of shrines went up in 1626 and 1627, recorded in the Ming archives. They were torn down when he fell.

claims.text: The cause of the 1626 Wanggongchang explosion is a mystery.
claims.note: Accounts at the time describe strange effects and no clear cause. Most historians suspect an accident in the gunpowder stores.

reigns.hook: Tianqi's brother, a serious sixteen-year-old, inherits a court run by Wei Zhongxian. His first job is to bring the eunuch down.

reigns.tagline: The last Ming emperor and the tree on Coal Hill
reigns.previously: The Tianqi Emperor dies at 21 with no son.
paragraphs: The Chongzhen Emperor started well. Within months he had Wei Zhongxian banished, and the eunuch hanged himself on the road. Chongzhen worked hard and trusted nobody. He went through about 50 grand secretaries in 17 years. His worst mistake came in 1630, after Hong Taiji raided past the Great Wall to the edge of Beijing: he had his best frontier commander, Yuan Chonghuan, executed by slicing for treason.

Meanwhile the north-west was starving. Years of drought, famine and unpaid soldiers turned into rebellion. Cuts to the government courier service threw men out of work, among them Li Zicheng, who became the most dangerous rebel of all. He and Zhang Xianzhong roamed the north and west for years with growing armies. Early in 1644 Li proclaimed his own dynasty, Shun, and marched on Beijing.

On 25 April 1644 the capital fell. The emperor ordered his empress and consorts to die, struck at his daughter Princess Changping with a sword, cutting off her arm, and climbed Coal Hill behind the Forbidden City. There he hanged himself from a tree. A rebel now held Beijing, but the Manchus were waiting beyond the Great Wall.

claims.text: Yuan Chonghuan was framed by a Manchu trick.
claims.note: Qing records later said Hong Taiji let captured eunuchs overhear a fake plot. How much it swayed the emperor, who already distrusted Yuan, is debated.

claims.text: Princess Changping lost an arm to her father's sword.
claims.note: Her biography in the Ming Shi tells it. She survived and died in 1646.

claims.text: Cutting the courier service drove Li Zicheng into rebellion.
claims.note: Li was a courier laid off in the cuts around 1629, but how much the cuts fuelled the wider revolts is argued over.

reigns.hook: Li Zicheng sits in Beijing. At Shanhai Pass the Ming general Wu Sangui must choose: the rebels who hold his family, or the Manchus beyond the wall.

reigns.tagline: The boy who took Beijing and dreamed of a monastery
reigns.cameToPower: Chosen by the princes; Dorgon regent
reigns.previously: Li Zicheng takes Beijing. The Chongzhen Emperor hangs himself.
paragraphs: Fulin was crowned at Mukden in October 1643, aged five, with his uncle Dorgon running things. Then Beijing fell to the rebel Li Zicheng. The Ming general Wu Sangui, guarding Shanhai Pass where the Great Wall meets the sea, threw in his lot with the Manchus. Together they smashed Li's army at the pass in May 1644. In June Dorgon rode into Beijing, and the new Shunzhi Emperor's Qing dynasty claimed the Mandate of Heaven.

The conquest was brutal. In 1645 Chinese men were ordered to shave the front of the head and wear the Manchu queue. People put it bluntly: keep your hair and lose your head. At Yangzhou the Ming commander Shi Kefa made a last stand, and when the city fell the Qing troops killed for days. Ming princes fought on in the south, and the loyalist Koxinga, Zheng Chenggong, raided from the sea.

Dorgon died in 1650 and was disgraced after his death. The 12-year-old emperor now ruled himself. He grew close to the German Jesuit Adam Schall and became a devout Buddhist. When his beloved Consort Donggo died in 1660 he was heartbroken. A few months later, in February 1661, smallpox killed him. He was 22.

claims.text: Wu Sangui opened the pass to the Manchus out of love for the courtesan Chen Yuanyuan, whom Li Zicheng's men had seized.
claims.note: The romance was made famous by Wu Weiye's poem 'Song of Yuanyuan'. Wu had plenty of hard political reasons to side with the Manchus.

claims.text: Over 800,000 people were killed in the ten days after Yangzhou fell.
claims.note: The figure comes from Wang Xiuchu's eyewitness 'Record of Ten Days in Yangzhou'. The massacre is not in doubt, but historians think the number is inflated.

claims.text: Shunzhi did not die of smallpox but slipped away to become a monk on Mount Wutai.
claims.note: A popular tale, linked to his Buddhism and his grief for Donggo. Court records and the Jesuits both describe his death from smallpox.

reigns.hook: The dying emperor's heir is his third son, a boy of six. The court likes him for one practical reason: he has already had smallpox and survived.

reigns.tagline: Sixty-one years on the throne, and he still studied Euclid
reigns.previously: Smallpox kills the Shunzhi Emperor at 22. A small boy takes over.
paragraphs: Xuanye, the Kangxi Emperor, started with four regents. The toughest, Oboi, bullied the rest. In 1669 the teenage emperor had him seized and locked up. Then came the real test. Three Chinese generals who ran the south like private kingdoms, Wu Sangui among them, rose in 1673. The Revolt of the Three Feudatories took eight years to crush. In 1683 his fleet took Taiwan from Koxinga's heirs.

In 1689 he signed the Treaty of Nerchinsk with Russia, fixing the northern border, with Jesuits translating in Latin. It was China's first treaty with a European state. He led his armies in person against the Mongol leader Galdan in 1696 and 1697 and toured the south six times. He studied geometry and astronomy with the Jesuits, and the dictionary he sponsored in 1716 still bears his name.

His great failure was his heir. Crown Prince Yinreng was deposed in 1708, restored, then deposed for good in 1712. The emperor died in December 1722 after 61 years, the longest reign in Chinese history, and nobody was quite sure whom he had chosen.

claims.text: Kangxi was picked over his brothers because he had already survived smallpox, on the advice of Adam Schall.
claims.note: The story comes from Jesuit sources. Chinese records do not credit Schall, though immunity was a sensible reason after Shunzhi's death.

claims.text: The teenage emperor trapped Oboi using a band of young palace wrestlers.
claims.note: A favourite story in later Qing accounts. The official record simply says Oboi was arrested and charged.

claims.text: Jesuit missionaries cured the emperor's malaria with quinine in 1693.
claims.note: The Jesuits described it in their letters home, and the grateful emperor gave them land for a church in Beijing.

reigns.hook: Kangxi leaves more than twenty grown sons and no crown prince. A single name is announced at his deathbed. People are still arguing about whether it was the right one.

reigns.tagline: The workaholic who answered every memo in red ink
reigns.previously: Kangxi dies after 61 years without a clear heir.
paragraphs: Prince Yinzhen said his father had named him on his deathbed. Several of his brothers had their doubts. The new Yongzheng Emperor dealt with them quickly. Rivals were locked up, and two of them were stripped of their names and given insulting Manchu ones. Then he got to work, and for thirteen years he hardly stopped.

He read thousands of reports from officials and covered them in comments in vermilion ink, some kind, many sharp. He set up the Grand Council, a small war cabinet that became the real centre of government. He brought the fees officials skimmed into the budget and paid them extra 'silver to nourish honesty'. He freed some hereditary outcast groups and banned Christianity in 1724.

When a scholar named Zeng Jing plotted against him, Yongzheng spared him and published a book arguing with him. To stop succession fights he wrote his heir's name and locked it in a box behind a plaque in the Palace of Heavenly Purity. In October 1735 he died suddenly, aged 56.

claims.text: Yongzheng forged his father's will, changing 'to the fourteenth son' into 'to the fourth son'.
claims.note: A rumour spread by his enemies. It depends on a trick with Chinese characters, and such edicts were also written in Manchu, where the trick fails.

claims.text: His jailed brothers were renamed 'dog' and 'pig'.
claims.note: The names Akina and Seshe are often translated that way, but scholars disagree on what the Manchu words really meant.

claims.text: He was killed by Lü Siniang, a swordswoman who cut off his head to avenge her family.
claims.note: A tale from popular fiction. Historians who doubt a natural death point instead to the Daoist elixirs he was taking.

reigns.hook: The box behind the plaque is opened. Inside is the name of Prince Hongli. He will rule so long that he steps down only to avoid beating his grandfather's record.

reigns.tagline: Biggest empire, most poems, and a seal on every painting
reigns.previously: Yongzheng dies suddenly. His secret box names his son Hongli.
paragraphs: The Qianlong Emperor inherited a rich, peaceful empire and made it bigger. He boasted of 'Ten Great Campaigns'. The darkest was against the Dzungar Mongols between 1755 and 1758. Most of the Dzungar people were killed, died of smallpox or fled, and their land became Xinjiang, the 'New Frontier'. Qing China was now the largest it would ever be, and its population passed 300 million.

He loved culture and wanted the credit. He ordered the Siku Quanshu, a vast library copying thousands of works, while his censors hunted down books that insulted the Manchus and destroyed thousands. He wrote over 40,000 poems and stamped his seals all over the old masterpieces in his collection. In old age he doted on a young favourite, Heshen, who grew fabulously rich.

In 1793 Lord Macartney arrived from Britain asking for trade. The emperor's letter to George III said, in effect, we have everything we need. In 1796 he stepped down so he would not reign longer than his grandfather Kangxi. He kept the real power anyway.

claims.text: Of perhaps 600,000 Dzungars, about 40 per cent died of smallpox and 30 per cent were killed.
claims.note: The breakdown comes from the Qing scholar Wei Yuan, writing decades later. Historians accept the scale of the destruction but treat the exact figures as estimates.

claims.text: Qianlong wrote more than 40,000 poems.
claims.note: His collected works do hold over 40,000, but court scholars almost certainly drafted or polished many of them.

claims.text: Macartney refused to kowtow to the emperor.
claims.note: Macartney wrote that he knelt on one knee, as to his own king. Some Chinese accounts say he went down on both knees. What he actually did is still argued over.

reigns.hook: The old man still sits on the real throne while his son waits. Heshen, the richest man in China, should be worried about what happens when his patron dies.

reigns.tagline: He waited three years for power, then went after Heshen
reigns.previously: Qianlong abdicates in 1796, but keeps hold of the real power.
paragraphs: For three years the Jiaqing Emperor was emperor in name only. His father lived on and Heshen ran the court. Then in February 1799 the old man died. Within days Heshen was arrested, charged with a long list of crimes and allowed to hang himself instead of being executed. His enormous fortune went to the state.

There was a lot to fix. The White Lotus rebellion, a religious rising in the hills of central China, dragged on from 1796 to 1804 and drained the treasury. In 1813 rebels of the Eight Trigrams sect broke into the Forbidden City itself. Prince Minning, the emperor's son, grabbed a musket and fired on them.

Britain tried again in 1816 with Lord Amherst's embassy, which was sent away without even meeting the emperor. Meanwhile, more and more opium was being smuggled in from India. In September 1820 Jiaqing died suddenly at the summer palace at Chengde.

claims.text: Heshen's fortune equalled years of the empire's revenue.
claims.note: Later stories put it at hundreds of millions of taels. The confiscation lists are real, but the famous totals are probably inflated.

claims.text: Prince Minning shot attackers in the Forbidden City in 1813.
claims.note: Qing court records describe it, and his father rewarded him with a princely title for his courage.

claims.text: Jiaqing was struck by lightning.
claims.note: A story told afterwards. Official records say only that he fell ill suddenly at Chengde and died.

reigns.hook: Jiaqing's heir is Minning, the prince with the musket. He'll need more than a gun: the opium trade is about to turn into a war with Britain.

reigns.tagline: The thrifty emperor who lost the Opium War
reigns.previously: Jiaqing dies suddenly at Chengde. His son Minning takes over.
paragraphs: The Daoguang Emperor hated waste. He cut palace spending and wore patched clothes. But money was draining away faster than thrift could save it. British merchants were shipping opium from India into China in huge amounts, and silver was flowing out of the country to pay for it.

In 1839 he sent the incorruptible official Lin Zexu to Canton. Lin blockaded the foreign merchants until they gave up their opium, then in June destroyed over 1,000 tons of it at Humen. He even wrote to Queen Victoria, asking how her people would like being poisoned. Britain answered with warships. The First Opium War ended with the Treaty of Nanjing on 29 August 1842.

China paid an indemnity, opened five ports to trade and gave up Hong Kong Island. It was the first of the 'unequal treaties'. Far from the court, a failed exam candidate called Hong Xiuquan had strange visions in 1837 and later read some Christian tracts. Daoguang died in February 1850.

claims.text: Courtiers patched their own clothes to match the emperor's.
claims.note: A favourite anecdote about his thrift, told in later Qing writings. Some say officials bought new clothes and paid to have patches sewn on.

claims.text: Lin Zexu destroyed over 1,000 tons of opium at Humen.
claims.note: About 20,000 chests were surrendered and mixed with lime and salt in trenches before being flushed out to sea.

claims.text: Lin's letter to Queen Victoria reached its target.
claims.note: The letter survives and was printed in the British press, but there is no sign the queen ever read it.

reigns.hook: Daoguang's box names his fourth son, Yizhu. Within a year, Hong Xiuquan, who believes he is the younger brother of Jesus Christ, will be leading a rebel army.
