reigns.tagline: A heavenly king in the south, foreign troops in Beijing
reigns.previously: Daoguang dies. Opium pours in and Hong Kong is British.
paragraphs: The Xianfeng Emperor inherited a disaster. Hong Xiuquan, convinced he was the younger brother of Jesus, rose in revolt in the south in 1850. His Taiping Heavenly Kingdom swept north and made Nanjing its capital in 1853. The war that followed was one of the deadliest in history. Estimates vary widely; 20 to 30 million dead is a common figure. Imperial armies failed, and Zeng Guofan built a new Hunan Army to fight back.

Then Britain and France went to war again, the Second Opium War, from 1856. In 1860 their troops marched on Beijing. Xianfeng fled to his hunting retreat at Chengde and left his brother Prince Gong to negotiate. In October the troops looted the Old Summer Palace, and Lord Elgin ordered it burned. Russia used the crisis to take the lands north of the Amur and east of the Ussuri.

His only son had been born in 1856 to a concubine, Lady Yehenara. Xianfeng never came back to Beijing. He died at Chengde in August 1861, aged 30, leaving the boy, now five, to a council of eight regents.

claims.text: Hong Xiuquan believed he was the younger brother of Jesus Christ.
claims.note: He said so in his own writings, describing a vision in which God the Father and his elder brother Jesus gave him a mission.

claims.text: The Taiping war killed 20 to 30 million people.
claims.note: There was no census. The figures are historians' reconstructions from population losses, and estimates range from below 20 to over 50 million.

claims.text: Lord Elgin ordered the Old Summer Palace burned.
claims.note: He did so in October 1860 as reprisal for the torture and killing of British and French envoys, and said so in his own letters.

reigns.hook: Eight regents now hold the boy emperor. But his mother, Lady Yehenara, has no intention of fading away. As the court heads back to Beijing, she makes her move.

reigns.tagline: The boy in front of the curtain
reigns.previously: Cixi steps back in 1889 as her nephew Guangxu comes of age.
paragraphs: Zaichun became emperor at five, the day his father died at Chengde. The eight regents gave his reign the name Qixiang, 'auspicious'. After his mother's coup it was changed to Tongzhi, which can be read as 'ruling together'. It was a fair description. He sat on the throne while two empresses dowager listened from behind a screen.

Officials hailed a 'Tongzhi Restoration': the Taiping crushed, new arsenals, a foreign office, order returning. The boy had little to do with it. He was a poor student and, by his tutors' accounts, more interested in escaping the palace. He took over in February 1873, having married a bride his mother did not want. That June he received foreign envoys, who bowed instead of kowtowing.

His one big project was rebuilding the Old Summer Palace, burned in 1860, with money the state did not have. When Prince Gong and others objected, he stripped them of rank in 1874, and the empresses dowager had to step in and undo it. In December he fell ill. He died on 12 January 1875, aged 18, with no son.

claims.text: He died of smallpox.
claims.note: The official cause, backed by the court physicians' records. Gossip at the time said syphilis from secret trips to the city; most historians accept smallpox.

claims.text: His young empress was driven to her death by Cixi in 1875.
claims.note: She died two months after him. Rumours spoke of suicide or starvation; the court said illness. Nothing settles it.

claims.text: At his 1873 audience the foreign envoys bowed instead of performing the kowtow.
claims.note: Reported by the diplomats present and in the Qing records. The court had resisted the change for over a decade.

reigns.hook: Tongzhi is dead without a son. That same night Cixi calls the princes together. She already has a candidate: her sister's little boy, aged three.

reigns.tagline: The concubine who ruled from behind a screen
reigns.reignEnded: Retired as Guangxu came of age
reigns.previously: Xianfeng dies at Chengde, leaving a boy of five and eight regents.
paragraphs: In November 1861 the dead emperor's widow, Empress Dowager Ci'an, and the boy's mother, now Empress Dowager Cixi, struck with Prince Gong's help. The eight regents were arrested. Their leader Sushun was beheaded and two princes were made to kill themselves. From then on the two women 'listened to government from behind the curtain', a screen in the audience hall, while the boy, the Tongzhi Emperor, sat in front.

Her government finally broke the Taiping, retaking Nanjing in 1864. Zeng Guofan, Li Hongzhang and Zuo Zongtang built arsenals and shipyards in what was called the Self-Strengthening Movement. Tongzhi began to rule in 1873 but died in January 1875, aged 18. Cixi then made her three-year-old nephew emperor, breaking the rule that an heir should come from the next generation.

Ci'an died suddenly in 1881. Prince Gong was dismissed in 1884, and a war with France in 1884 and 1885 cost China its hold over Vietnam. In 1889 the Guangxu Emperor took charge and Cixi retired to the Summer Palace, at least nominally.

claims.text: Tongzhi died of syphilis caught on secret trips to Beijing's brothels.
claims.note: The court said smallpox, and the records of his illness fit it. The syphilis story was court gossip that later writers loved.

claims.text: Cixi poisoned Ci'an.
claims.note: Rumours started at once because the death was so sudden. There is no evidence, and illness is the likelier explanation.

claims.text: Cixi was a far-sighted moderniser held back by others.
claims.note: This is the case made in Jung Chang's 2013 biography. Many historians think it is too admiring and leans on weak sources.

reigns.hook: Cixi ruled from behind a curtain. Now rewind to 1861 and meet the boy in front of it: her son, the Tongzhi Emperor.

reigns.tagline: A three-year-old chosen to keep his aunt in power
reigns.cameToPower: Picked by Cixi the night Tongzhi died
reigns.previously: Tongzhi dies at 18, leaving no son.
paragraphs: Zaitian was the son of Prince Chun, Xianfeng's brother, and of Cixi's younger sister. He was taken from his bed on the night of 12 January 1875 and carried to the Forbidden City. Choosing a boy of Tongzhi's own generation broke the rules, since an heir was meant to perform the rites as the dead emperor's son. It also meant the empresses dowager would rule again for years.

His father resigned his posts and stayed out of sight. The boy grew up apart from his parents, schooled from 1876 by the scholar Weng Tonghe, who became the closest thing he had to a father. Officials described a sickly, nervous, clever child. In 1881 Empress Dowager Ci'an died suddenly, leaving Cixi in sole charge.

The empire he would inherit kept shrinking: France took control of Vietnam after the war of 1884 and 1885. In 1887 he was declared old enough to rule, with Cixi still guiding him. In February 1889 he married her niece, and in March she finally handed over and retired.

claims.text: A censor, Wu Kedu, killed himself at Tongzhi's tomb in 1879 in protest at how the heir had been chosen.
claims.note: Widely recorded at the time; his last memorial survives. It complained that Tongzhi had been left without a son to keep up his rites.

claims.text: Cixi chose him chiefly to keep her own power.
claims.note: His age made a long regency certain, and many historians read it that way. Her defenders argue that few suitable boys were available.

reigns.hook: The emperor is 17, married and finally in charge. Cixi has retired to her Summer Palace. But she chose his bride, and the key officials still answer to her.

reigns.tagline: A hundred days of reform, then a prison on an island
reigns.cameToPower: Came of age; Cixi stepped back
reigns.previously: Cixi steps back in 1889. Her nephew Guangxu takes the reins.
paragraphs: The Guangxu Emperor was married in 1889 to Cixi's niece, a match he never wanted. He much preferred a lively young concubine, the Pearl Consort. Meanwhile Cixi's Summer Palace was being rebuilt on a lavish scale, partly with money meant for the navy. Its most famous sight is a boat made of marble.

In 1894 China went to war with Japan over Korea. Japan destroyed the Beiyang fleet, and the Treaty of Shimonoseki in 1895 handed it Taiwan. Shaken, the young emperor listened to the reformer Kang Youwei. From 11 June 1898 he poured out decrees: modern schools, a university in Beijing, a new army, leaner government. It became known as the Hundred Days' Reform.

Conservative officials ran to Cixi. On 21 September 1898 she took power back. Guangxu was locked up on Yingtai, an island in the palace lake. Six reformers were executed, among them Tan Sitong, who could have run but chose not to. Kang Youwei and Liang Qichao escaped to Japan.

claims.text: Cixi spent the navy's money on the Summer Palace, which is why China lost to Japan.
claims.note: Funds were diverted, but historians argue over how much. The fleet's defeat had many causes, including poor training and bad ammunition.

claims.text: Yuan Shikai betrayed a reformers' plot against Cixi.
claims.note: The reformers asked Yuan for troops, and he reported to Cixi's ally Ronglu. Whether his report started the coup or came after it is still argued.

claims.text: Tan Sitong said no country had ever reformed without bloodshed, so let it begin with him.
claims.note: The words come from his friend Liang Qichao, who wrote them up in exile. They may have been polished.

reigns.hook: The emperor is now Cixi's prisoner. And in the dusty north, bands of young men who say magic makes them bulletproof are starting to attack foreigners.

reigns.title: Cixi Takes Back the Throne
reigns.tagline: Boxers, a siege, a flight, and a last-minute makeover
reigns.previously: Cixi's coup ends the Hundred Days. Guangxu is her prisoner.
paragraphs: The Boxers called themselves the Righteous and Harmonious Fists. They practised martial arts, said their rituals made them bulletproof, and attacked missionaries and Chinese Christians across the north. In June 1900 Cixi backed them and declared war on the foreign powers. Boxers and imperial troops besieged the foreign legations in Beijing for 55 days.

In August an Eight-Nation Alliance fought its way in and lifted the siege. Cixi fled to Xi'an, taking the emperor with her, and the Pearl Consort was drowned in a palace well. The Boxer Protocol of 1901 made China pay 450 million taels. Back in Beijing, Cixi changed her tune. She invited foreign ladies to tea, posed for photographs, scrapped the old exam system in 1905 and promised a constitution.

On 14 November 1908 Guangxu died, aged 37. In 2008 a forensic study found a lethal dose of arsenic in his remains; nobody knows who gave it. Cixi died the next day, after naming his two-year-old nephew Puyi as heir. In 1928 a warlord's soldiers blew open her tomb and looted it.

claims.text: Cixi ordered the Pearl Consort thrown down a well before fleeing.
claims.note: The consort did die in a well in the palace. Accounts of who gave the order come from eunuchs and others years later, and they differ.

claims.text: Cixi escaped from Beijing disguised as a peasant woman.
claims.note: Told by courtiers and repeated in many books. She certainly left in haste and in plain clothes, but details vary.

claims.text: Guangxu was poisoned with arsenic.
claims.note: A 2008 study by Chinese scientists of his hair and clothing found arsenic far above lethal levels. Who did it is unknown.

reigns.hook: A toddler is Son of Heaven now, with his young father as regent. The empire that began in 221 BC has just over three years left.

reigns.tagline: Crowned at two, gone at six, a citizen at 53
reigns.previously: Guangxu and Cixi die a day apart. Puyi, aged two, is heir.
paragraphs: At his enthronement in December 1908 the two-year-old Xuantong Emperor screamed and cried. His father, Prince Chun, was regent. The court promised a constitution, but in 1911 it named a cabinet packed with princes. That year a plan to nationalise the railways enraged local investors, and the Railway Protection Movement spread through Sichuan.

On 10 October 1911 soldiers rose at Wuchang, and province after province declared independence. The court brought back Yuan Shikai to command the army, and Yuan started bargaining with the revolutionaries. On 12 February 1912 Empress Dowager Longyu, Guangxu's widow, issued the abdication in the boy's name. More than 2,000 years of empire were over.

Puyi kept his title and lived on in the Forbidden City. He was restored for twelve days in 1917 and thrown out in 1924. Japan made him puppet ruler of Manchukuo from 1932 to 1945. He was a Soviet prisoner, then spent ten years in a re-education camp at Fushun. Pardoned in 1959, he wrote a memoir, From Emperor to Citizen, and died in 1967. In 1987 Bertolucci filmed his life as The Last Emperor.

claims.text: As the toddler wailed on the throne, his father whispered, 'Don't cry, it'll soon be over.'
claims.note: It comes from Puyi's own memoir, retelling what others said. Courtiers later saw the words as an omen.

claims.text: The abdication deal let Puyi keep his title, his palace and a state allowance.
claims.note: These were the Articles of Favourable Treatment agreed with the new Republic in 1912.

claims.text: After his pardon, the last emperor worked as a gardener.
claims.note: He did work at the Beijing Botanical Garden and then at a historical archive, but the state publicised his new life heavily, so details are hard to pin down.

reigns.hook: The boy is no longer emperor. In Nanjing a revolutionary doctor has already been sworn in as president, and in Beijing a general wants the job.

reigns.title: Sun Yat-sen and Yuan Shikai
reigns.tagline: The doctor makes a republic, the general wants a throne
reigns.previously: Puyi abdicates in February 1912. Over 2,000 years of empire are over.
paragraphs: No more emperors, so from here the deck follows whoever really held power, whatever they were called. First up, a doctor. Sun Yat-sen trained in Western medicine in Hong Kong, then became a full-time revolutionary, raising money from Chinese communities abroad. In 1896 Qing diplomats held him prisoner inside their London legation until his old teacher James Cantlie and the British press got him out. When Wuchang rose in October 1911, Sun was in Denver, Colorado.

He hurried home and on 1 January 1912 was sworn in at Nanjing as provisional president. The man with the army, though, was Yuan Shikai, the Qing's top general. Yuan squeezed the court into abdicating, and Sun stood aside for him. In the first elections the Nationalist Party, the Kuomintang, came out on top. In March 1913 its leader Song Jiaoren was shot at Shanghai station. Sun's “Second Revolution” against Yuan failed, and he fled to Japan.

Yuan ruled more and more like a monarch, and in 1915 accepted a cut-down version of Japan's Twenty-One Demands. That December he went all the way and made himself the Hongxian Emperor. Yunnan rose against him, other provinces followed, and his own generals backed away. After about 83 days he gave up the throne in March 1916. On 6 June he died of kidney failure, his grip on China already gone.

claims.text: Yuan Shikai ordered the murder of Song Jiaoren.
claims.note: Telegrams linked the killers to men in Yuan's government, but no order from Yuan himself has ever been found.

claims.text: Sun was held prisoner in the Chinese legation in London in 1896.
claims.note: Sun told the story in Kidnapped in London (1897), and British press reports and Foreign Office papers cover his release.

claims.text: Sun was in Denver, Colorado, when the Wuchang uprising began.
claims.note: Sun's own account and his biographers place him there; he learned the news from the papers.

reigns.hook: Yuan is dead and nobody inherits his power. The generals who served him are already carving China up between them.

reigns.title: The Warlord Era
reigns.tagline: Generals, students and a new party fight over a broken China
reigns.cameToPower: Yuan died and nobody took over
reigns.previously: Yuan Shikai's empire collapses, and then so does he.
paragraphs: With Yuan gone, the government in Beijing became a prize for whichever general held the city. Military cliques rose and fell: the Anhui clique, the Zhili clique, and Zhang Zuolin's Fengtian clique from Manchuria. In July 1917 the general Zhang Xun, whose troops still wore the Qing pigtail, marched in and put Puyi back on the throne. It lasted twelve days.

In 1919 the peace conference at Versailles handed Germany's rights in Shandong to Japan. On 4 May students marched in Beijing, and the May Fourth Movement grew into a wider push for science, democracy and writing in everyday Chinese. In July 1921 a small group met in Shanghai to found the Chinese Communist Party. One of the delegates was a young man from Hunan named Mao Zedong.

Sun Yat-sen built a base in Guangzhou with Soviet help and opened the Whampoa Military Academy in 1924 under Chiang Kai-shek. Sun died of cancer in Beijing in March 1925. Chiang led the Northern Expedition from 1926, then turned on his Communist allies in Shanghai in April 1927. In June 1928 a Japanese bomb killed Zhang Zuolin on his train, and the Nationalists took Beijing and renamed it Beiping.

claims.text: Chiang's purge of the Communists in April 1927 killed thousands.
claims.note: No reliable count exists. Figures run from a few hundred in Shanghai in the first days to many thousands as the purge spread to other cities.

claims.text: Zhang Zuolin was killed by a bomb planted by Japanese officers.
claims.note: Officers of Japan's Kwantung Army, led by Colonel Kōmoto Daisaku, planned it; Japan's own later inquiries admitted it.

claims.text: Mao Zedong was a delegate at the Party's founding congress in 1921.
claims.note: He was one of about a dozen Chinese delegates; Party records and the delegates' memoirs agree.

reigns.hook: Chiang Kai-shek now rules most of China, on paper at least. Warlords, Communists in the hills and an ambitious Japan are all waiting.

reigns.tagline: The Generalissimo who fought Japan and lost China
reigns.previously: The Nationalists take Beijing. A Japanese bomb kills Zhang Zuolin.
paragraphs: In October 1928 Chiang Kai-shek became head of the new Nationalist government at Nanjing. A year earlier he had married Soong Mei-ling, whose sister was Sun Yat-sen's widow. The “Nanjing decade” brought railways, roads and a modern civil service, though warlords still ran large parts of the country. In September 1931 Japan seized Manchuria and set up the puppet state of Manchukuo, later with Puyi on its throne.

Chiang went after the Communists first, and in 1934–35 they fled his encirclement campaigns on the Long March. In December 1936 his own general Zhang Xueliang kidnapped him at Xi'an and freed him only once he agreed to unite with the Communists against Japan. Full war began at the Marco Polo Bridge on 7 July 1937. At Nanjing that winter Japanese troops killed civilians and prisoners on a vast scale; estimates vary from tens of thousands to around 300,000.

In 1938 Chiang's forces broke the Yellow River dykes to slow the Japanese, and the floods killed hundreds of thousands of Chinese. He ran the war from Chongqing and met Roosevelt and Churchill at Cairo in 1943. Civil war with the Communists resumed in 1946, and runaway inflation wrecked his support. Li Zongren was acting president in 1949, but Chiang kept the real power. On 10 December he flew to Taiwan, where he ruled the Republic of China until his death in 1975.

claims.text: Japanese troops killed between tens of thousands and around 300,000 people at Nanjing.
claims.note: The mass killing is not in doubt; the toll is. China's official figure, from the postwar Nanjing tribunal, is over 300,000; the Tokyo tribunal said over 200,000; some historians give lower counts, depending on dates, area and who is counted.

claims.text: The 1938 Yellow River flood killed hundreds of thousands of people.
claims.note: Records are poor. Chinese postwar figures and historians' estimates range from about 400,000 to around 900,000 dead from the floods and the famine after.

claims.text: Chiang was kidnapped at Xi'an in 1936 by his own general, Zhang Xueliang.
claims.note: Fully documented. Zhang went back to Nanjing with Chiang and spent more than half a century under house arrest.

reigns.hook: Two months before Chiang's flight, Mao Zedong had stood on the Tiananmen gate in Beijing and proclaimed a new state.

reigns.tagline: A new People's Republic, and the deadliest famine on record
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Beat Chiang in the civil war
reigns.previously: Chiang's armies are falling apart. By December he will be on Taiwan.
paragraphs: On 1 October 1949 Mao Zedong stood on the Tiananmen gate in Beijing and proclaimed the People's Republic of China. In the villages, land reform followed. Land was seized and shared out, and landlords were denounced at mass meetings and killed in large numbers; estimates commonly run from about one million to two million or more. In 1950 China entered the Korean War, and that November Mao's son Anying was killed in an air raid.

Tibet was occupied in 1950–51, and Soviet advisers helped launch the first Five-Year Plan. In 1956–57 Mao invited criticism in the Hundred Flowers campaign. When it came, he answered with the Anti-Rightist Campaign, and over half a million people were labelled “rightists”. In 1958 came the Great Leap Forward: vast communes, backyard steel furnaces, and a campaign to wipe out sparrows.

The result was famine, the deadliest in recorded history. Scholarly estimates of excess deaths run from about 15 million to 45 million or more. When the defence minister Peng Dehuai criticised the Leap at Lushan in 1959, Mao purged him. Liu Shaoqi and Deng Xiaoping took over the repairs. China split with the Soviet Union around 1960 and tested its first atomic bomb in October 1964. In May 1966 Mao turned on his own party.

claims.text: The famine after the Great Leap Forward killed between about 15 million and 45 million people.
claims.note: Estimates vary. Demographers' reconstructions from census data mostly give about 15 to 30 million; Yang Jisheng puts it at 36 million and Frank Dikötter at 45 million or more.

claims.text: Land reform killed between about one million and two million or more people.
claims.note: Estimates vary widely. They rest on scattered official reports and historians' reconstructions, and no full count exists.

claims.text: Mao's son Mao Anying was killed in an air raid in Korea in November 1950.
claims.note: He died on 25 November 1950 when aircraft bombed Peng Dehuai's headquarters, where he was serving as a Russian interpreter.

reigns.hook: In May 1966 the Party warns that enemies have wormed their way into its own ranks. Mao is about to turn China's young people loose on them.

reigns.title: The Cultural Revolution
reigns.tagline: Ten years of upheaval, launched by the Chairman himself
reigns.previously: Sidelined after the famine, Mao turns on his own Party.
paragraphs: On 16 May 1966 the Party issued a notice warning that enemies had got inside it. In July Mao, now 72, swam in the Yangtze at Wuhan to show he was fit and back. From August he reviewed huge rallies of Red Guards in Tiananmen Square. Students turned on their teachers, on officials and on the “Four Olds”: old customs, culture, habits and ideas. Temples, books and art were destroyed, and many people were beaten, driven to suicide or killed.

Liu Shaoqi, the head of state, was hounded and died in custody in 1969. Deng Xiaoping was sent to work in a tractor factory in Jiangxi. Millions of city teenagers were sent “up to the mountains and down to the countryside”. Estimates of deaths across the decade range from several hundred thousand to around two million. Lin Biao, named Mao's successor in 1969, died in September 1971 when his plane crashed in Mongolia as he fled.

Then the world shifted. China took the UN seat in October 1971, and Nixon came to Beijing in February 1972. Mao's wife Jiang Qing led the radical group later called the Gang of Four. Zhou Enlai died in January 1976, and in April mourners filled Tiananmen until they were cleared. On 28 July the Tangshan earthquake killed about 242,000 people by the official count. Mao died on 9 September 1976.

claims.text: Between several hundred thousand and around two million people died in the Cultural Revolution.
claims.note: Estimates vary. They draw on local Party histories published in the 1980s and historians' reconstructions; no full count exists.

claims.text: State media said Mao swam nearly 15 km of the Yangtze in about an hour.
claims.note: The swim on 16 July 1966 happened, but the reported speed would have beaten world records. He was mostly floating with the current.

claims.text: The Tangshan earthquake killed about 242,000 people.
claims.note: This is the official Chinese figure; some outside estimates are higher.

reigns.hook: Mao is dead. The man he picked, Hua Guofeng, must now face Jiang Qing and her allies, who think the future belongs to them.

reigns.tagline: Mao's chosen heir, and the man who arrested his widow
reigns.previously: Mao dies in September 1976, after ten years of upheaval.
paragraphs: Hua Guofeng was a quiet party official who had made his career in Hunan, Mao's home province, and risen fast in the 1970s. Mao had picked him as heir, and Hua had a note in Mao's hand to prove it: “With you in charge, I'm at ease.” Less than a month after Mao died, Hua struck first. On 6 October 1976 Jiang Qing and the rest of the Gang of Four were arrested, and crowds celebrated across the country.

Hua became Party chairman, but his line was the “two whatevers”: uphold whatever Mao decided, follow whatever Mao instructed. Many wanted change. University entrance exams came back in 1977, and so did Deng Xiaoping. In 1978 people pasted up posters on Beijing's Democracy Wall. At the Third Plenum in December 1978 real power swung to Deng. Hua lost his top posts by 1981 but kept a Central Committee seat, and he died in 2008.

claims.text: Mao wrote Hua a note: “With you in charge, I'm at ease.”
claims.note: The 1976 note is real and Hua used it as proof he was the chosen heir. Critics said Mao was only reassuring him about routine work.

claims.text: The “two whatevers” were Hua's official line.
claims.note: The slogan appeared in a People's Daily editorial in February 1977 and became the target of Deng's allies.

claims.text: Hua had the Gang of Four arrested on 6 October 1976.
claims.note: He acted with the defence minister Ye Jianying and the guard commander Wang Dongxing. The four were seized after being called to meetings.

reigns.hook: Deng Xiaoping, purged twice, is back on top. He will never take the grandest titles, but he has a plan to make China rich.

reigns.tagline: Never the top title, always the final word
reigns.previously: At the Third Plenum, the Party swings behind Deng Xiaoping.
paragraphs: Deng Xiaoping never held the top formal posts, but from late 1978 his word decided things. His programme was “reform and opening up”. Farm families could work their own plots and sell their surplus, and the communes faded away. Special Economic Zones opened to foreign investors, starting with Shenzhen in 1980. Back in 1962 he had said it didn't matter if a cat was black or white, so long as it caught mice. Now he could act on it.

In 1979 he fought a short, costly border war with Vietnam. The Gang of Four went on trial in 1980, and in 1981 the Party ruled that Mao had made grave mistakes late in life while keeping him as founder. The one-child policy began in 1980. In 1984 Britain agreed to hand back Hong Kong under “one country, two systems”. Time magazine named him Man of the Year for 1978 and 1985.

In April 1989 the death of the reformer Hu Yaobang brought students into Tiananmen Square. Protests spread, students went on hunger strike and martial law was declared. On the night of 3–4 June the army cleared the city and the square with live fire. The official toll was about 200 to 300 dead, soldiers included; other estimates run from several hundred to several thousand. Party chief Zhao Ziyang was purged. In November Deng gave up his last post.

claims.text: Between several hundred and several thousand people were killed on 3–4 June 1989.
claims.note: The government's figure was about 200 to 300, soldiers included. Diplomatic cables, early hospital and Red Cross reports and later researchers give higher figures; no full count has been allowed.

claims.text: Deng said “to get rich is glorious”.
claims.note: No record shows him saying it. The line seems to have been pinned on him later, mostly by Western writers.

claims.text: On 5 June 1989 a lone man stood in front of a column of tanks.
claims.note: Filmed and photographed by several foreign news crews from a hotel above Chang'an Avenue. Who he was has never been confirmed.

reigns.hook: Deng hands the army to Jiang Zemin, the Shanghai party boss promoted after Tiananmen. Can this cautious engineer keep reform alive?

reigns.tagline: The Shanghai engineer who took China into the world market
reigns.previously: Deng gives up his last post. Jiang Zemin has the Party and the army.
paragraphs: Jiang Zemin, a trained electrical engineer and the Shanghai party chief, was made general secretary in June 1989 and took the military chair from Deng that November. At first he played it safe. Then in early 1992 the retired Deng toured the south, praising Shenzhen and calling for faster reform. Jiang took the hint. The Party now spoke of a “socialist market economy”, and Zhu Rongji, later premier, shook up state industry.

Deng died in February 1997. That July Hong Kong returned to China, and Macau followed in December 1999. In May 1999 NATO bombs hit the Chinese embassy in Belgrade, killing three journalists, and angry crowds besieged US missions in China. In July the government banned Falun Gong. Work went on at the Three Gorges Dam. In 2001 Beijing won the 2008 Olympics, and on 11 December China joined the World Trade Organization.

Jiang's “Three Represents” theory opened the Party to private entrepreneurs. In November 2002 he handed the general secretary's job to Hu Jintao, but he kept the military chair until September 2004. He died in Shanghai on 30 November 2022, aged 96.

claims.text: Deng's Southern Tour of 1992 restarted economic reform.
claims.note: His remarks in Shenzhen and elsewhere were spread through the Party press and are widely seen as the turning point.

claims.text: NATO's bombing of the Chinese embassy in Belgrade was an accident.
claims.note: The US said it had used an out-of-date map and apologised. China called it deliberate, and some journalists later argued it was.

claims.text: Jiang kept command of the army after giving up the Party leadership.
claims.note: He stayed chair of the Central Military Commission until September 2004, nearly two years after leaving the top Party job.

reigns.hook: Hu Jintao takes over the Party. He is a quiet engineer, and he has been waiting near the top since 1992.

reigns.tagline: The quiet engineer of a booming decade
reigns.previously: Jiang Zemin hands over the Party, though not yet the army.
paragraphs: Hu Jintao trained as a hydraulic engineer at Tsinghua University and worked his way up through Gansu and the Communist Youth League. In 1989 he was party chief in Tibet when unrest broke out in Lhasa and martial law was declared there. He joined the Party's top committee in 1992, widely reported as Deng Xiaoping's pick for the next generation. He became general secretary in November 2002 and president in March 2003.

His first test was the SARS outbreak in 2003. That October Yang Liwei became China's first astronaut, aboard Shenzhou 5. Hu's slogans were a “harmonious society” and the “scientific outlook on development”. In 2008 came unrest in Tibet in March, the Sichuan earthquake in May, with about 69,000 confirmed dead, and the Beijing Olympics in August. Unrest in Urumqi followed in July 2009. In 2010 China passed Japan as the world's second-largest economy.

He handed the Party to Xi Jinping in November 2012 and the presidency in March 2013. At the closing session of the 20th Party Congress on 22 October 2022, he was led out of the hall in front of the cameras. State media said it was for health reasons.

claims.text: Hu was party chief in Tibet when martial law was declared in Lhasa in March 1989.
claims.note: Martial law was declared on 8 March 1989 and lasted more than a year; it is well documented in news reports of the time.

claims.text: The Sichuan earthquake of 12 May 2008 left about 69,000 confirmed dead.
claims.note: This is the official figure, with nearly 18,000 more listed as missing.

claims.text: Hu was led out of the closing session of the 20th Party Congress on 22 October 2022.
claims.note: Filmed by journalists in the hall. The state news agency Xinhua said he had not been feeling well.

reigns.hook: Xi Jinping, son of a revolutionary veteran, takes over. He will break the two-term pattern of the leaders before him.

reigns.tagline: From a cave home in Shaanxi to a third term at the top
reigns.previously: Hu Jintao steps down after two terms as Party leader.
paragraphs: Xi Jinping is the son of Xi Zhongxun, a revolutionary veteran who was purged under Mao. In 1969, as a teenager, Xi was sent down to the village of Liangjiahe in Shaanxi, where he lived in a cave dwelling until 1975. He rose through posts in Hebei, Fujian, Zhejiang and Shanghai. He is married to the singer Peng Liyuan. He became general secretary on 15 November 2012 and president in March 2013.

He launched a sweeping anti-corruption campaign that has punished officials high and low, and in 2013 the Belt and Road Initiative to build trade links abroad. “Xi Jinping Thought” was written into the Party constitution in 2017, and in March 2018 presidential term limits were removed. In Hong Kong a National Security Law took effect on 30 June 2020.

In Xinjiang, large numbers of Uyghurs and other mainly Muslim minorities have been held in detention camps. A 2022 report by the UN human rights office said this may amount to crimes against humanity; China rejects the finding. COVID-19 was first identified in Wuhan in late 2019, and Xi's “zero-COVID” policy lasted until December 2022. He began a third term as general secretary in October 2022 and as president in March 2023. As of October 2026 he remains in power.

claims.text: Xi lived in a cave dwelling in Liangjiahe as a sent-down youth.
claims.note: It is in his official biography and has been reported by many journalists; the village is now a stop on official tours.

claims.text: Presidential term limits were removed in March 2018.
claims.note: The National People's Congress approved the constitutional amendment on 11 March 2018.

claims.text: A UN human rights office report said abuses in Xinjiang may amount to crimes against humanity.
claims.note: Published on 31 August 2022 by the Office of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights. China's government rejected it.
